In long channels, under concavity and a spectral condition, a new Rayleigh vorticity quantity tames the hard terms and yields nonlinear stability. The work gives sharp decay rates and stability thresholds for this inflow setup.
arxiv-2602-17159: Levent Ali Mengütürk, writing alone, proposes a new way to gauge how far apart two Gaussian distributions sit. The paper sets out a duality linking the spherical squared-Hellinger distance with a hyperbolic invariant of the Poincare disc under the general Mobius group. That link motivates using the L2-embedded hyperbolic invariant as another gauge of divergence for Gaussian measures. The idea speaks to information theory and machine learning alike, offering a geometry-flavored yardstick for statistical difference where standard measures now rule.
arxiv-2602-17359:
Artur Dróżdż led a three-author experimental study of wavy-wall control for turbulent boundary layer separation on a convex plate. The wavy-wall method, first proposed for a flat plate, is tested here at high Reynolds number on the suction side shape of an airfoil. Applying the method raises the friction coefficient by more than forty percent, substantially delaying turbulent separation from the convex wall while maintaining total momentum, as tracked by momentum-loss thickness.

Other efficiency signs include a steady friction Reynolds number and a thinner boundary layer. Together the signs promise aerodynamic gains for airfoils, similar to active suction on the suction side. New insight into the mechanism suggests small-scale turbulent activity drives the benefit, enhancing streamwise convection and sweeping motion for superior momentum transport. Poorly chosen geometry, however, can induce large-scale motions like trough separation that counteract the mechanism and harm efficiency.
arxiv-2602-17459:
Ting-Wei Chao led a three-author team on set systems with uniform witnesses. Frankl, Pach, and Erdos conjectured a size bound for uniform families with VC-dimension at most d, for large n. Ahlswede and Khachatrian disproved it with a larger counterexample. For such a family, the VC-dimension condition restates in terms of witness sets. For any set F in the family, some witness set B_F governs how F relates to the sets.

The lead author and colleagues conjectured the bound holds if every witness set has size s, with s between zero and d. The case s equals zero is the Erdos-Ko-Rado theorem. Here the team shows the claim holds when s is at most half of d. The maximal constructions are stars. They build non-star families of the bound's size for s between half of d and d minus one.
arxiv-2602-17659:
Yu Fang and team study a failure mode of vision-language-action models for robots: language gets overridden by vision. Such models promise to ground language in robot control, yet they often act on vision shortcuts from dataset biases, repeating well-learned acts and picking familiar objects no matter what the words say.

To study this systematically, the team built LIBERO-CF, the first counterfactual benchmark for these models, which assigns alternative instructions under visually plausible layouts. Tests show counterfactual failures are common yet underexplored across leading models. Their fix, Counterfactual Action Guidance, pairs a standard policy with a language-free vision-action module for counterfactual comparison at action choice. It cuts vision-shortcut failures and lifts task success, with no extra demos or architecture changes.
arxiv-2602-17759:
Isabelle John and team analyze cosmic-ray travel using time-varying AMS-02 measures spanning a full solar cycle. They fit two Galactic travel scenarios, convection models and re-accel models, combined with three solar modulation recipes. These are the standard force-field take, an extended force-field model with a stiffness break, and the heliospheric code HelMod.

Time-varying antiproton data offer a unique probe of charge-sign effects and low-energy errors. The force-field take describes plus-charged nuclei fairly well outside solar maximum in convection models, but fails during high solar activity and for antiprotons at all times. In re-accel scenarios, strong mix-ups between modulation and low-energy travel yield unreal results under simple modulation models. Across all models, doubts of about ten to fifteen percent in rebuilt between-star spectra and numbers limit precision, far above the percent-level error of current measures.
arxiv-2602-18759:
Recommender systems learn mostly from clicks. So they must invent negatives, items a user presumably did not want. A bad choice of negatives teaches bad taste. Chen Chen, with two co-authors, proposes ICPNS in 2026. It is a negative sampling method grounded in the communities users actually belong to.

The insight is that exposure runs through latent communities. An item that is popular inside a user's own community yet still unclicked is a far more trustworthy negative than a random unseen item. By estimating exposure from in-community popularity, the method picks negatives that are real, hard, and interpretable. Tests on four benchmarks improve graph-based recommenders and stay competitive on matrix-factorisation models.
arxiv-2602-18959:
In trauma surgery, knowing where hands are, and whether each is left or right, supports rapid, precise choices. Kedi Sun, with one co-author, proposes a YOLOv10-based framework in 2026 that localises hands and classifies laterality at once in complex surgical scenes.

Training uses first-person surgical videos from a trauma challenge dataset, with marked hand bounding boxes. Heavy augmentation and a multi-task design improve robustness against motion blur, lighting variation, and diverse hand appearances. Evaluation shows moderate left-hand and right-hand classification accuracy, while separating hands from background remains challenging. Mean average precision is modest, yet inference stays real-time. The work lays a foundation for hand-instrument interaction analysis in emergency surgery. Real time matters in theatre. This model keeps pace.
arxiv-2602-19259:
Quantum computers raise a tempting hope: squeeze a large nearest-neighbor search structure into very few qubits, using quantum states as a kind of hash. Sajjad Hashemian tests that hope in a broad model where a dataset is stored as a quantum state and each question is answered by measuring a fresh copy. The question is whether a handful of qubits, growing only slowly with dataset size, could ever suffice.

The answer is no. For any approximation quality and any success chance above one half, the paper builds hard examples that no such sketch can handle. In these examples, points are bit strings and distance counts differing bits. The result closes off a whole family of quantum shortcuts for nearest-neighbor search. It shows the hoped-for compression would need a fundamentally different model, not just a cleverer encoding.
arxiv-2602-19359:
Matching a robot simulator to real hardware often relies on hand tuning or black-box optimizers that cannot say which physical mismatch drives the error. Kevin Qiu and three co-authors present Vid2Sid, a pipeline that identifies systems from video. It couples foundation-model perception with a vision-language model optimizer. That optimizer studies paired simulation and real videos, diagnoses concrete mismatches, and suggests physics parameter updates, each with a written rationale.

Tests cover a tendon-actuated finger in MuJoCo and a deformable continuum tentacle in PyElastica. On held-out real controls, Vid2Sid ranks best on average, matching or beating black-box optimizers while explaining each step. Simulation-to-simulation checks show it recovering true parameters most accurately, with mean relative error under 13 percent versus 28 to 98 percent for rivals.
arxiv-2602-19759:
A geometric view of heat and energy assigns curvature to a system's state space. The sign of that curvature has long hinted at whether particles effectively attract or repel. A 2026 arXiv paper by Hosein Mohammadzadeh and three co-authors extends that geometric view to fast-moving ideal gases.

Using a metric drawn from the partition function, the team studies curvature for classical, boson, and fermion cases. Exact results cover two dimensions; the three-dimensional case is numerical. The usual signs survive fast motion: positive for bosons, negative for fermions. One effect of fast motion shifts curvature singular points to a mass-set threshold. The condensation temperature for fast-moving gases also gains mass-based corrections. The paper unifies geometry, particle statistics, and fast motion in one picture.
arxiv-2602-20359:
Rayan Mazouz and three co-authors present StochasticBarrier.jl, an open-source Julia toolbox for building stochastic barrier functions. Such functions certify the safety of discrete-time stochastic systems with additive Gaussian noise. The toolbox covers linear, polynomial, and piecewise affine systems, with the last class opening verification to a wide range of dynamics, including general nonlinear types.

Two optimization routes are offered: a sum-of-squares route using semi-definite programming solvers, and a piecewise-constant route with three engines, two based on linear programming and one on gradient descent. Benchmarks against the state of the art show the tool beats rivals on computation time, safety probability bounds, and scalability across more than thirty case studies. Against its closest rival, it runs faster by orders of magnitude, gives better safety bounds, and supports higher-dimensional systems.
arxiv-2602-20459:
Can AI trained on the science record foresee the gains that follow? Anirudh Ajith and nine co-authors offer PreScience, a dataset and benchmark for science forecasting. It builds from ninety-eight thousand recent AI research papers, plus linked papers on author records and links for five hundred two thousand papers. Records include titles, abstracts, named authors, key sources, topic labels, cite paths, and details frozen at time cutoffs.

Seven sample tasks cover work generation, partner forecast, prior work choice, cite-count forecast, future mix forecast, and two topic trend outlooks. Starting points range from simple rules to frontier models and agentic systems, with a new LACER metric judging made contributions more like humans do. Building task models into a twelve-month made-up corpus yields papers clearly less diverse and less novel than human research from the same period.
arxiv-2602-20759:
Human values rarely speak with one voice, yet most chat models answer as if they do. Yu Fu and two co-authors train a single language model to give varied, fair views on one query, with no extra prompts and no separate parts bolted on.

Their method first tunes a text-similarity tool to judge how well replies cover real views. Then a two-part reward trains the model to cover many views while keeping each one distinct. A small 3-billion-parameter model trained this way beat a much larger 20-billion baseline on a test of inference, gaining 37.4 percent, and also beat a modular rival system.
arxiv-2602-20859:
Financial prediction from long documents is noisy work: useful signals are sparse, and the best embedding model shifts with task and time. Zirui He and four co-authors propose FinAnchor in this 2026 arXiv paper, a light framework that merges embeddings from several language models without fine-tuning any of them. One anchor embedding space is chosen, and linear maps align the other models into it.

The aligned features then combine into a single representation for prediction. Across several financial language tasks, FinAnchor beats strong single-model baselines and standard ensembles. Readers get a practical recipe for robust prediction: anchor heterogeneous representations instead of betting on one model or averaging blindly.
arxiv-2602-20959:
Reading atomic structure out of spectra is central to materials science, yet it works only for a narrow set of methods and materials. Ian Slagle, Faisal Alamgir, and Victor Fung widen that reach in this 2026 arXiv paper using ActiveStructOpt. The framework pairs graph neural network surrogates with active learning to find candidate structures that reproduce target spectra at low computational cost.

Tests on X-ray pair distribution data, and on the heavier simulations of X-ray absorption near-edge spectra and extended fine structure, show the method reliably matching spectra across diverse material classes. Under equal budgets it beats existing structure-determination methods. Readers get a flexible, data-efficient route to structural refinement across many computable spectroscopic techniques.
arxiv-2602-21059:
Automated metrics for language-model reliability miss how scientists actually judge answers. Anna Martin-Boyle, William Humphreys, Martha Brown, Cara Leckey, and Harmanpreet Kaur build an expert-grounded alternative in this 2026 arXiv paper: a schema for evaluating errors in scholarly question-answering systems. Working with domain experts, they identified twenty error patterns across seven categories from thematic analysis of sixty-eight question-answer pairs.

Validation through contextual inquiries with ten additional scientists showed which errors experts spot naturally and how structured schemas help them catch issues they had missed. Experts work through orderly routines when they judge: they test fine technical detail, weigh results against their own values, and turn back to review their own judging. The paper points toward tools built on the schema and tuned to each expert's habits and skill.
arxiv-2602-21159:
Global hypoellipticity can fail for perturbed vector fields, and the set of bad constants has a curious size. Maria Bartmeyer, Paulo Dattori da Silva, and Rafael Gonzalez measure that set topologically in this 2026 arXiv paper, using Kronecker's approximation theorem. In some situations the set is discrete and enumerable, hence meager, within the real line.

In other situations the set is a dense G-delta subset of the complex numbers, hence nonmeager, contrasting with a known result that the set has null Lebesgue measure. Readers get a topological refinement of size: measure-zero sets can still be topologically large. The contrast clarifies what different notions of smallness actually capture.
arxiv-2602-21259:
Vehicles that fly and dive could monitor coasts, infrastructure, and disaster zones, but air and water demand very different control. Ricardo Grando and five co-authors tackle persistent monitoring for hybrid aerial-underwater vehicles in this 2026 arXiv paper, combining deep reinforcement learning with transfer learning for cross-domain adaptability. A shared architecture trains on lidar data in air and sonar data underwater.

That unified policy proves feasible across both environments, handling environmental uncertainty and multiple moving targets. The framework lays groundwork for scalable autonomous monitoring with hybrid vehicles. Readers get evidence that one policy can span two domains, rather than requiring separate controllers for sky and sea.
arxiv-2603-01759:
Zichen Tian, Yaoyao Liu, and Qianru Sun tune the fine-tuning knobs of large models automatically in this 2026 work. Their test bed is remote sensing, where training a model from scratch fails for lack of data. Parameter-efficient methods update few weights, yet their fixed settings can badly cap results on new image types.

Their method, MetaPEFT, adds adaptive scalers that adjust module influence while fine-tuning runs. Three levers move together: where modules insert, which layers they touch, and how fast each learns. Tests span three transfer settings and five data sets in satellite and normal images. The method sets new top scores for cross-spectral adaptation with few trainable weights. Tail-class accuracy, often the weak spot on skewed sets, improves a lot as well.
arxiv-2603-01859:
J. Pawlowski, P. Lydzba, and M. Mierzejewski extract conserved quantities of a quantum system from just a few of its states. Their 2026 work focuses on the XXZ model, a standard chain of interacting quantum spins. Local integrals of motion, quantities that never change, define whether such a system counts as integrable.

A single energy state can already reveal if a system is integrable or chaotic, past work showed. The team shows those integrals can also be estimated from a small set of states. As system size grows, the needed share of states shrinks toward zero. A cousin model with fragmented Hilbert space breaks the pattern, since most states are needed there. That split marks a rare deep difference between true integrability and mere fragmentation of the state space.
arxiv-2603-01959:
Mehran Shakerinava, Behnoush Khavari, Siamak Ravanbakhsh, and Sarath Chandar map exactly what diagonal state-space models can and cannot track. Their 2026 work studies sequential state-tracking, where a model must follow a changing state step by step. Diagonal state-space models are fast and parallel, yet their expressive limits were unclear.

For a single layer with complex diagonal dynamics, non-Abelian group tracking proves impossible at finite precision. Non-Abelian means step order matters, a trait of many real state systems. With more layers, the reachable groups are exactly those with a layered series of Abelian factors. That places the model family precisely inside the solvable groups of algebra. Experiments add a warning: multi-layer models often fail to learn even the tracking they can express.
arxiv-2603-02459:
F Dai, E Kosov, and V Temlyakov survey sampling discretization in this 2026 mathematics paper. Discretization replaces continuous norms of functions with sums over sample points. Classic inequalities for polynomials, tied to Marcinkiewicz and Zygmund, anchor the field. The survey generalizes those results to functions in arbitrary finite-dimensional spaces.

Norms come from general probability measures, not just uniform ones. Discrete sums must approximate them faithfully for every function in the space. The authors emphasize recent advances, especially their own research line. Main proof ideas and techniques are highlighted, not just final statements. The survey complements three recent surveys on the same topic. Readers gain a map of where sampling theory stands now.
arxiv-2603-02859:
Zuzana Haniková tests whether an alternative logic of sets can capture the idea of feasible numbers. Her 2026 paper works inside Vopěnka's Alternative Set Theory, a framework often used to model vague notions. The target is Yessenin-Volpin's view that only numbers small enough to handle in practice fully count as numbers.

She tries to model Dummett's weakly infinite totalities, collections that behave as finite from some angles and endless from others. Dummett treated their coherence as the test case for the whole feasible-number idea. The verdict here is negative: the set theory captures some features of feasible numbers, but not all. Haniková stresses that one failed route does not settle the broader debate over ultrafinitism.
arxiv-2603-02959:
Julio Silva-Rodríguez and Ender Konukoglu stretch a handful of labeled medical images much further with unlabeled ones. Vision-language models adapt well to new tasks from few examples, but rare disease classes often get too few labels and drag accuracy down. Their 2026 method targets exactly that low-shot squeeze in medical imaging.

A fast semi-supervised solver spreads pseudo-labels, guided by the model's text side, from labeled to unlabeled images during adaptation. The unlabeled pool helps cover classes that annotation budgets miss. The authors report labeling effort cut by at least half in low-shot settings while keeping adaptation efficient. For hospitals, where expert annotation is the bottleneck, cheaper adaptation could decide whether these models get used at all.
arxiv-2603-03059:
Alex Binh Vinh Duc Nguyen examines a paradox in teaching architecture with generative AI. Design schools are adding these tools to the curriculum, yet learning to judge them critically means using them more, with little way to count the environmental cost. His 2026 paper views the problem through human-computer interaction research.

Three directions follow. Contextual eco-feedback would show students the footprint of their AI use as they work. Participatory scoping would let affected stakeholders help set the terms of adoption. Treating data centers as a shared study topic would tie the tool back to the built world architects shape. The paper argues generative AI is a socio-technical process, not just a new drawing tool, and education must engage it critically.
arxiv-2603-03159:
Friederike Ihssen, Renzo Kapust, and Jan Pawlowski sample probability distributions whose weights can be complex numbers. Such sign problems plague quantum field theory and real-time quantum dynamics, because negative or complex weights break standard sampling. Their 2026 paper builds a generative architecture around physics-informed kernels designed for exactly this obstacle.

The architecture preserves total probability weight while mapping the hard sampling task onto a simpler, sign-free landscape where sampling is efficient. Both burdens, the sign problem and slow sampling, are addressed by the same construction. Demonstrations cover zero-dimensional field theories with complex couplings and the real-time evolution of a quantum harmonic oscillator. Success there would point toward broader use in lattice field theory.
arxiv-2603-03359:
Swapnil Parekh audits speech recognition for accent bias, asking whether accuracy gaps across accents run deep or sit on the surface. His 2026 audit, ACES, works in three stages on a model's internal representations. It first finds the directions in representation space that carry accent information, then aims adversarial attacks along those directions, and finally tests whether deleting them would help fairness.

On a standard wav2vec model covering seven accents, tiny inaudible perturbations along the accent directions widened the error-rate gap by nearly half, far beyond random-direction controls. A label-shuffling check confirmed the effect tracks real accent structure. Surprisingly, partly removing the accent directions made both accuracy and disparity worse. Accent information is deeply entangled with recognition itself, so Parekh positions the subspaces as auditing tools, not simple erasure levers.
arxiv-2603-03459:
Peter Balogh asks how much of a transformer's heavy nonlinear machinery is actually needed. Every layer's feed-forward network transforms every token elaborately, yet many of those computations may be nearly linear. His 2026 study tests six models across two architectures and three text collections. A tiny learned gate, a single logistic classifier, decides token by token whether the full nonlinear path is required.

The gate works, but its logic resists simple rules. Whether a token needs nonlinearity cannot be predicted from the token itself: routing lists built on one corpus fail completely on another. The decision is fully contextual, best predicted by a token's contribution to the passing residual stream. Still, the gate routed a large share of computations through cheap linear paths at tiny accuracy cost in one architecture, while another family resisted more. Frozen linear layers even improved one fully retrained model.
arxiv-2603-03659:
Julia B Kieserman and four others expose a privacy leak hiding inside social media ads. TikTok, Facebook, and Instagram let advertisers aim campaigns at touchy traits. Those ads are interactive by default: anyone can comment or react. Their 2026 paper shows that this design choice lets advertisers view the profiles of all who interact, in effect naming the people who match the touchy targeting tests.

That behavior flatly contradicts the platforms' promises to keep user data hidden from advertisers. A reaction meant as a casual tap becomes an unintentional disclosure of exactly the trait the ad targeted. The authors close with design changes that would warn users about the consequences of interacting and give them a clear view before the tap. That would restore the promised protection without banning aimed ads outright.
arxiv-2603-03859:
Bart De Bruyn and Thijs van Veluw classify Hoffman colorability for connected graphs whose smallest eigenvalue is at least minus two. A graph is Hoffman colorable when the spectral Hoffman bound on its chromatic number is tight. Building on the Cameron-Goethals-Seidel-Shult classification theorem, the authors extend an earlier characterization that covered only line graphs to this whole class of graphs.

They characterize Hoffman colorability for generalized line graphs. They also completely classify the exceptional graphs that are Hoffman colorable, finding several hundred of them arranged in a natural partial order, with a small set of maximal ones. As a byproduct they also determine all graphs maximal with respect to being representable in one of the classical root systems. The results complete a chapter of spectral graph theory linking eigenvalues, colorings, and root system geometry.
arxiv-2605-00459:
Maksym Nechepurenko stress-tests his own framework for detecting information leakage, possible insider trading, on the prediction market Polymarket. His deadline-resolved leakage score had worked as a single-case proof of concept. Here he scales it to 12,708 markets from late 2020 into 2026, framing the study as scope discovery: finding where the tool actually works.

The honest headline is narrowness. Only eighty-eight candidate markets yielded computable scores at all, and only a fraction of those passed a sensitivity check, mainly because the wording of how markets resolve is often genuinely ambiguous. Raw score medians ran negative across groupings, and one baseline correction shifted some post-2024 categories to near zero while others stayed below. A modeling assumption in the earlier work was also rejected on pooled data. The conclusion directs future work at resolution typology and baselines, not just score computation.
arxiv-2605-00659:
C. R. Carvajal-Bohorquez and 66 co-authors publish the final catalogs of the NIKA2 Cosmological Legacy Survey in the COSMOS field, a deep millimeter survey of dusty star-forming galaxies. These galaxies, hidden by their own dust, built much of the universe's stars, and millimeter selection finds them at great distances. The survey mapped over a thousand square arcminutes at two wavelengths with homogeneous coverage, the largest contiguous deep survey of its kind at this depth.

The master catalog holds 323 sources passing a strict purity threshold, a third seen at both wavelengths. Counterparts were secured for most sources, and redshifts compiled from major catalogs. The redshift distribution peaks near redshift 2.8, the era of peak cosmic star formation, with sixty-six galaxies beyond redshift four. The distribution matches one leading simulation, while four other evolution models are ruled statistically inconsistent with the data.
arxiv-2605-01259:
João Marcos Brito, Edileudo M. Moreira Filho, Jefter G. M. Paz, and Rudini Sampaio determine the winner of the normal Domination partizan game on certain graph families. In the Domination game, players alternately select playable vertices, where a vertex is playable if it newly dominates at least one undominated vertex. Play ends when the chosen vertices form a dominating set. The normal variant makes the player unable to move lose.

In the partizan version, vertices are pre-colored so each player can select only their own color or a shared color. The impartial normal game was recently proved PSPACE-complete and the partizan game PSPACE-hard. The authors settle the winner for graphs whose components are complete bipartite graphs or complete split graphs, including star forests, for any initial coloring.
arxiv-2605-01359:
Alessio Donvito and Antonio Lieto rate how well computer models of analogy and metaphor match what is known about human thought. They use the Minimal Cognitive Grid, a yardstick built for judging whether an artificial system is plausible as a model of the mind.

The authors turn the grid into a formal scoring method with three parts: the balance of function and structure, how general the system is, and how well its performance matches human patterns. They then score four systems, the Structure-Mapping Engine, CogSketch, METCL, and large language models. Because all four face the same math-based rules, their strengths and gaps can be compared directly. The work gives analogy research a shared, repeatable way to argue about mental realism.
arxiv-2605-01459:
Roberto Isai Navaro-Aviña and three co-authors sharpen low-resolution photos on a tight computing budget. Blowing up a single image is ill-posed: fine detail is simply gone at large zoom factors, and the strongest current tools buy it back with heavy global models.

Their design, SRGAN-CKAN, instead makes the local step smarter. Inside an adversarial training setup, plain convolution is swapped for Kolmogorov-Arnold style units. Those units bend each patch through spline curves, a richer local map that can render textures and edges with few parts. Tests under tight hardware limits show better perceptual quality while holding fidelity scores well, a sound balance between the two. The authors offer the local-operator route as a lean complement to global architectures for phones and edge devices.
arxiv-2605-01659:
Pritam Mishra, Coloma Ballester, and Dimosthenis Karatzas summarize video without a single hand-made label. Picking the frames that carry a story is vital as video floods surveillance, teaching, and social feeds, yet supervised summarizers are costly, brittle across domains, and heavy to run.

TRIMMER works in two stages. Self-supervised learning first builds sturdy frame representations. A reinforcement learning stage then makes keep-or-drop calls over space and time, guided by information-theoretic rewards. Instead of similarity scores, entropy-based rewards reward higher-order temporal patterns and semantic variety, and they are computed straight from the chosen frame indices, which keeps the loop cheap. On standard benchmarks it leads all unsupervised and self-supervised rivals and stands close to the best supervised systems, a mix the authors offer as the scalable route to general summarization.
arxiv-2605-01759:
Xinxing Yu and seven co-authors teach 3D scene models by letting point clouds learn from each other. Self-supervised training on single scenes, one at a time, keeps each scene's meaning in its own dialect, which blocks the shared semantic space that transfer needs.

Their PointCSP framework serializes the samples in a batch into one continuous stream and runs a state-space model over it, so semantic state propagates across samples and meanings line up globally. That batch trick cannot survive to single-scene testing. A second stage distills the pretrained semantics back into a per-scene form, using mixed inputs and a feature alignment constraint to keep the transfer stable. Across several benchmark sets the method beats the state of the art on score and on semantic consistency alike. The design targets scene-level 3D vision, where labels are dear and consistency across places is the prize.
arxiv-2605-01859:
Dillip Kumar Mohapatra, Teun Verouden, and Janne-Mieke Meijer report lab work on how cube-shaped colloids join together into small clusters. By changing how strongly the cubes attract each other through their shape, the team could watch early growth change in kind. The study tracks both growth speed and how cubes shift inside clusters as they form.

Three patterns appear. At low strength, clusters grow slowly and stay ordered. In the middle, growth is faster and clusters stay disordered but can still rearrange. At high strength, clusters get stuck and cannot reorganize. The shifts between patterns can be reversed, which points to a way to design materials by choosing a growth path.
arxiv-2605-02059:
Huan Zhang and colleagues document RenCon 2025, the revival of a competition for expressive performance rendering at the ISMIR conference in Daejeon, Korea. Rendering systems turn a score into a piano performance with human-like timing and dynamics. Nine entries from groups around the world took part, using varied approaches to musical expression.

Assessment ran in two phases: an online round first, then live real-time rendering at the conference. The authors analyse the format, who took part, how systems performed, and lessons for future editions. Results show clear advances in expressive rendering since earlier contests. At the same time, reaching human-level musical expression remains an open challenge for the field.
arxiv-2605-02159:
Ujjwal Patil and Javad Ghofrani review how deep reinforcement learning reuses knowledge from trained models instead of starting each task from scratch. Deep methods have won at Atari and Go, but they cost many samples and transfer poorly. Transfer, distillation, ensembles, and federated training all aim to reuse past learning, yet their literature is scattered and hard to compare.

Following PRISMA guidance, the authors screened hundreds of records from major databases and citation tracing. Fifteen empirical studies met the final criteria for the main synthesis. They compare those studies across source-target similarity and other factors, noting how differing tasks, baselines, and compute budgets limit what published claims can show.
arxiv-2605-03059:
Omkar Kulkarni, Edward Raff, and Tim Oates address a common waste in medical imaging: experts outline regions by hand, keep only summary numbers, and discard the outlines. Training a segmentation model from those numbers alone would save that lost work, if it can be done.

Numbers alone proved too weak in their tests, but adding a few marked pixels inside the region helped a great deal. Their loss mixes image rebuild quality, match to the summary numbers, and overlap with those marked pixels. Tests cover standard images, breast ultrasound, and kidney tumor CT scans.
arxiv-2605-03159:
Reshabh K Sharma, Gaurav Mittal, and Yu Hu present a way to learn correct agent behavior from just a handful of passing execution traces. Checking long action sequences by hand is slow, exact matching is brittle, and training-based checks need far more examples than teams usually have.

Their algorithm merges two to ten good traces into a general model using prefix trees, multi-level equivalence checks, and compiler-style dominator analysis, with language model help for meaning. New runs are checked by subsequence matching, with coverage scores to explain verdicts. In controlled tests with three traces, it caught real bugs and false successes well.
arxiv-2605-03759:
JuneHyoung Kwon and five co-authors examine a flaw in benchmarks for unlearning in large vision-language models, systems that should be able to forget sensitive personal information they memorized. Current benchmarks use fictitious identities, but they skip a basic check: whether the model ever learned the target information well in the first place. Without that, unlearning scores are unreliable.

The authors diagnose under-memorization and a multi-hop curse as root causes. They then introduce ReMem, a benchmark built for reliable multi-hop and multi-image memorization. It uses principled data scaling, reasoning-aware questions, and varied visual contexts. A new Exposure metric measures how deeply information is erased from the model's internal probability distribution. That makes both learning and unlearning evaluations more trustworthy.
arxiv-2605-03859:
Sushanth Varada and four co-authors investigate nonuniform superconducting states that arise from Majorana flat bands, zero-energy bands of edge states inside a superconductor's energy gap. Flat bands can give rise to competing ordered phases. The team's platform is a topological superconductor built from magnetic adatoms hosting a flat band of Majorana edge states, studied with self-consistent calculations of the order parameter.

Two phases emerge: a pair density wave with edge-localized amplitude modulations, and a phase crystal with edge-localized phase modulations. Both lower the free energy by gapping out the Majorana flat band, and the uniform solution never survives at zero temperature. The pair density wave persists to about eighty percent of the bulk transition temperature, while the phase crystal appears only at lower temperatures.
arxiv-2605-04059:
Nicolas Michel, Maorong Wang, Jiangpeng He, and Toshihiko Yamasaki introduce continual distillation, a paradigm where a student model learns sequentially from a stream of teacher models without keeping access to earlier teachers. Model scale motivates the setup: some models need more storage than large datasets. Two challenges follow, because teacher training data are unavailable and teachers vary in expertise across domains.

The authors show external unlabeled data enables unseen knowledge transfer, letting the student acquire information about domains absent from its training data but known to a teacher. Sequential distillation, however, also causes unseen knowledge forgetting as later teachers overwrite earlier transfers. Their Self External Data Distillation method preserves output logits on external data to stabilize learning, reducing forgetting and improving cross-domain generalization across benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-04559:
Ruijun Chen and four co-authors improve how language models are aligned to produce good recommendation lists. Judging a list needs metrics like ranking quality and fairness. Those metrics cannot be trained on directly. One workaround is to generate many candidate lists at run time and keep the best. That works, but it is too costly for real deployment.

Methods that distil that search into the model suffer two flaws. They cannot rank candidates better than their static reference. Their training signal also fades as the model improves. The authors' Bayesian approach estimates candidate quality dynamically, updating the reference as the policy evolves, so list-wise guidance stays informative throughout training.
arxiv-2605-04959:
Briony Eldridge and four co-authors build a homotopy theory for directed graphs, where edges have a direction, based on cubical homotopy groups. The field studies shapes up to smooth reshaping, and a version for them could sort networks by their directed shape. Restricting the class of directed graphs at maps that preserve these groups yields an infinity-category of directed shapes.

The authors prove that this category is the same as the infinity-category of plain spaces. That sets up a directed version of the discrete homotopy hypothesis proposed by Carranza and Kapulkin. In effect, directed graphs, viewed through this theory, capture the same higher shape information as spaces themselves.
arxiv-2605-05159:
Srikar Kashyap Pulipaka describes a competition system for detecting political polarisation in text across twenty-two languages, entered in SemEval-2026 Task 9. The system fine-tunes separate Gemma models for each language using low-rank adaptation, in two sizes. Synthetic training data from a large language model supplements the real data through direct generation, paraphrasing, and contrastive pair creation, followed by multi-stage quality filtering.

Tuning decision thresholds per language on development data added several points without retraining, Pulipaka reports. A weighted ensemble of the two model sizes placed second overall among participating teams, with first place in three languages. Rival architectures that looked strong in development dropped sharply on the test set.
arxiv-2605-05359:
Sarah E. Heaps, Ian H. Jermyn, Yujiang Wang, and Darren J. Wilkinson work on a hard problem in time-series statistics. Modern sensors produce long records with many variables at once, as in genetics and neuroscience. The authors ask how to learn which variables affect which others when the system must stay stable over time.

They build a Bayesian method that forces sparsity and stability at the same time. A spike-and-slab prior keeps the model inside the stationary region, while a mixture prior handles the error structure. Tests on simulated data, plus examples from economics and neuroscience, show gains in both inference and prediction.
arxiv-2605-05459:
Location-aware search tools need a user's position, and sharing it carries privacy risks. Kennedy Edemacu, Mohammad Mahdi Shokri, Vinay M. Shashidhar, and Jong Wook Kim propose PAS, short for Privacy Anchor Substitution. Instead of blurring the true location with noise, PAS describes position relative to an anchor, using a direction and a distance range.

On synthetic city data, attackers were left with a location error of roughly four hundred meters. The system kept over half of the baseline retrieval quality, and answers stayed fairly strong. The authors also found the privacy-utility balance behaves in a non-monotonic way.
arxiv-2605-05559:
Some blockchains reward whoever performs a costly task, like generating a cryptographic proof. Maryam Bahrani, Michael Neuder, and S. Matthew Weinberg formalize the problem of buying that work from anonymous, possibly adversarial suppliers. The protocol must weigh paying more against a liveness fault, where the work simply never gets done.

They show the loss of the best protocol grows only logarithmically in the ratio between fault cost and maximum supply cost. Their mechanism pays suppliers without requiring them to reveal their identity in advance. Efficiency and coordination both enter the analysis, giving protocol designers firm bounds instead of heuristics.
arxiv-2605-05659:
Lean networks replace dense layers with low-rank ones, but their power limits are poorly mapped. Ying Chen, Aoxi Li, Jihun Kim, and Javad Lavaei study networks built from diagonal plus low-rank parts. They first expose a paradox in purely rank-1 layers: such layers can fit arbitrary scalar data exactly, yet collapse when asked to approximate functions.

Adding a diagonal component breaks the bottleneck without giving up the savings. The authors develop a structural match and broad approximation results for the combined design. Their analysis avoids strict assumptions like pretrained base matrices or specific activations.
arxiv-2605-05759:
Spectral graph neural networks filter signals by a graph's eigenvalues, and their expressiveness is capped by a classic combinatorial test. Xiaohan Wang, Deyu Bo, Longlong Li, and Kelin Xia lift the whole construction one order up. Their full-spectrum networks move signals from nodes to pairs of nodes, and filter over pairs of eigenvalues instead of single values.

Classical spectral networks reappear as a diagonal special case. The authors prove the construction breaks the old expressiveness ceiling while staying scalable. The result reframes spectral filtering as a two-dimensional problem with strictly more room to maneuver.
arxiv-2605-06159:
V. Lemes shows that spontaneous symmetry breaking changes the cohomology of a non-abelian gauge field. The argument is worked out for an SU(2) field and extends directly to SU(N). After breaking, a new field appears whose cohomological traits are characteristic of matter fields rather than gauge fields.

That shift has a practical payoff for gauge fixing. Building a renormalizable unitary gauge fixing, guided by Morse's problem of functional extremization, the Gribov condition turns out to be solved automatically on shell. The reason is that one specific combination of fields behaves in a matter like, cohomological way. Such combinations are free of the Gribov problem, so the usual obstruction to gauge fixing disappears for them.
arxiv-2605-06359:
Jihwan Woo exposes a leakage trap in how learned intrinsic image decomposition is evaluated, and urges a new community standard. Decomposition separates a photo into reflectance and shading layers, a core vision task benchmarked on the MPI Sintel data set. Several prior works split that data by frames, letting near duplicate frames of one scene land in both training and test sets, quietly inflating the scores everyone compares against, Woo argues.

Across three architectures, frame level splits inflated test scores by roughly two decibels over scene level splits, and extended training pushed the inflation past ten. Woo advocates scene level splits and supplies reference numbers for six models under the corrected protocol. A case study method with source separated uncertainty performs near a costly ensemble at a fifth of the cost, and an elaborate variant is reported as a negative result.
arxiv-2605-06559:
Alessandro Barone and five co-authors report a lattice QCD calculation of the nucleon's strange and flavor-singlet axial form factors. These quantities help decompose the proton's spin among quark flavors, alongside isovector and octet channels. The hard part is the disconnected contributions, which are crucial for extracting the strange component and are costly to compute.

Using improved Wilson fermion ensembles, the team controls errors through chiral, continuum, and infinite-volume extrapolations, building a full error budget. Combined with companion isovector and octet results, the work completes a comprehensive lattice picture of the nucleon's axial structure across flavor channels.
arxiv-2605-06659:
Tariq Yasin and Harry Desmond test a galaxy-wide acceleration relation using pulsar timing instead of galaxy rotation. The radial acceleration relation links observed acceleration to the acceleration from visible matter, and is best established in disc galaxies. Pulsar timing measures line-of-sight acceleration differences between the Sun and pulsars, probing directions outside the disc as well.

Combining twenty-six binary pulsars with literature accelerations, they compare a three-dimensional version of the measured relation against plain Newtonian gravity from baryons. The relation fits far better than Newton alone. However, a constant solar acceleration fits almost as well, showing current data are dominated by the Sun's value and cannot yet decide the test.
arxiv-2605-06859:
Ho Hin Lee and six co-authors derive scaling laws for knowledge transfer in 3D medical imaging, where one foundation model must pretrain across scan types like CT, MRI, and PET. Mixing these domains is now done by heuristic. Yet the authors observe that domains improve at different rates, and transfer is lopsided. Training on one scan type may greatly help another, with little benefit in reverse.

Both reconstruction loss and cross-domain transfer follow predictable power laws, turning data allocation into an optimization problem. The solution reveals hub domains that help many others and island domains needing direct investment. Transfer-aware mixtures beat proportional sampling by up to fifty-eight percent and hold up on disease and segmentation tasks.
arxiv-2605-07159:
Chunguo Duan and seven co-authors report the first detection of methyl carbamate in interstellar space. Glycine, the simplest amino acid, has never been found between the stars despite long searches. The team targeted a related family of molecules that might anchor glycine chemistry, using ALMA observations of a hot molecular core.

Ten clean spectral lines identify methyl carbamate, with a measured column density and a high excitation temperature. Related isomers, including glycine itself, were not detected, and the abundance pattern defies predictions based on minimum energy alone. The result supports formation on dust grain surfaces and gives astrochemists a new anchor for amino-acid chemistry.
arxiv-2605-07259:
Liron Cohen and Tomer Samara develop a semantics for chance-based programs based on explicit random tapes. A random program can be viewed as a fixed-rule one that consumes randomness from a tape, which makes reuse and linkage of randomness visible. Their evidence-tracked version builds a higher-order logic where claims are witnessed by uniform evidence carriers.

Once a chance measure on tapes is fixed, chances and averages come from summing up the tape-indexed predicates. Sound inequalities follow, and a probability-one quotient supports almost-sure reasoning. The authors also study principles lost when passing to ordinary distribution laws. Those include transport along rewiring maps and a splitting discipline enforcing separate draws.
arxiv-2605-07359:
Hanxi Li and three co-authors design an image signal processor that serves both human viewers and machine vision at once. Raw sensor data carry rich information, especially in low light, but the traditional processing pipeline that makes pictures pretty can compress away detail that recognition needs. Methods using raw data, in turn, often produce images humans dislike.

UniISP adds a hybrid attention module trained with supervision so output images stay visually appealing. A feature adapter passes informative features from the processing stage into downstream networks. Across scenarios and datasets, the framework reaches leading performance, showing one pipeline can satisfy aesthetic and recognition demands together.
arxiv-2605-07459:
Ali Asadi and three co-authors study robust Markov decision processes, a planning model where transition probabilities are uncertain and the planner guards against the worst case. They focus on the flexible version where uncertainty sets are defined by Lp norms, with a discounted cost over time. Whether efficient algorithms exist for this class was an open theoretical question.

The team shows policy iteration runs in strongly polynomial time for any compact uncertainty set, given an oracle for the inner robust chain problem. They also bound that inner problem for the L1 and L-infinity norms, and prove hardness for Lp sets with p strictly between one and infinity. Experiments confirm the iteration converges quickly in the tractable cases.
arxiv-2605-07959:
Zhengkai Sun, Dibyakanti Kumar, Alejandro Frangi, Anirbit Mukherjee, and coauthors give a rigorous account of why attention layers and low-rank adapters can be trained. Transformers rely on attention, and large models often use LoRA, a low-rank method that cuts the number of trained weights while keeping accuracy high.

Working in one unified framework, the team proves a Poincaré inequality for the Gibbs measure tied to each loss. The key constant does not grow with data dimension for LoRA, or with head dimension for multi-head attention. From this they show that a diffusion process that mimics stochastic gradient descent drives the loss down, without assuming anything about the data or model size.
arxiv-2605-08259:
Pete Rigas estimates how fast the value of a repeated multiplayer game decays when the game is played many times in parallel. Parallel repetition theorems power hardness and cryptography results, and earlier multiplayer arguments leaned on dependency-breaking and anchoring variables to strip correlations between players.

Building on a two-player analysis by Lanzenberger and Maurer, Rigas shows that monotonic concave functions can do that job instead. The approach yields quantitative decay rates for the optimal value under parallel repetition without the older machinery. The result extends the author's earlier work on quantum multiplayer games toward cleaner assumptions about how players share information.
arxiv-2605-08459:
Joeri De Ro constructs new quantum hypergroups from the actions of compact quantum groups. Starting with an ergodic action on a space, Ro combines the space's core algebra with its mirror copy through a balanced product. The result carries the full algebraic structure of a compact quantum hypergroup.

Two natural completions, reduced and universal, each carry the matching analytic structure, giving a broad family of fresh examples. Ro also characterizes when these hypergroups are coamenable, using equivariant correspondence theory. Quantum symmetry research gains both new objects to study and clear criteria for a key regularity property that governs their harmonic analysis.
arxiv-2605-08559:
Anastasis Kratsios asks whether a convex cost rule on an infinite dimensional space can be rebuilt from finitely many exact readings. Such rules appear as value functions, risk measures, and hedging prices, yet often only scattered values are known. Kratsios answers yes, giving an explicit formula that keeps convexity and the same smoothness bound while matching the true rule within any chosen error.

The rebuild uses only finitely many linear measurements and can be carried out exactly by a standard neural network form. Kratsios then defines trainable convex neural functionals where every setting stays convex automatically. Learning theory gains a firm base for fitting convex rules from limited data.
arxiv-2605-08659:
Xinwu Ye and eight coauthors train molecule and protein generators to stay diverse while chasing high scores. Reward tuning alone tends to collapse output onto one narrow family, yet diversity is a property of a whole set, not single samples. Their SGRPO method samples groups of candidate sets, scores each set's diversity, and credits individual samples by what they add when removed.

The scheme plugs into several generator and training styles without tying itself to one reward or diversity measure. Across small molecule design from scratch, pocket guided design, and protein design, it widens the frontier between utility and diversity beyond rival methods. Drug and protein discovery gain generators that keep options open while improving.
arxiv-2605-09059:
Joanna Szych and Anne Schwerk argue that judging AI-written code only by whether it runs misses much of what matters. Their study sets out a fuller way to grade code from large language models, one that also weighs quality and how usable the code feels to working programmers.

The method combines a correctness test built on a complex, multi-level class project with checks of code quality and a survey of developers who reviewed samples in a structured process. They apply it to three well-known models. Developer reviews, they find, surface problems about whether code is ready for real use that standard correctness tests alone would never show.
arxiv-2605-09159:
Nils A Herrmann, Leander Girrbach, Kirill Bykov, and Zeynep Akata ask whether large language models shift between inner personas while they reason. Their 2026 paper builds on work showing that traits such as honesty or style sit along straight directions inside a model's activity. Earlier studies used those directions as fixed handles for steering behavior.

Here the team tracks the directions over time as text is produced, calling that record a polylogue. Across four open-weight models, the tracked signals help predict whether an answer will be correct. A simple step that adjusts the signals paragraph by paragraph improves three models but harms the fourth. The authors present the polylogue as a readable tool for watching and guiding reasoning, while noting that steering is not yet reliable.
arxiv-2605-09359:
Vishe and ten colleagues treat skill evolution as ongoing two-level credit assignment, not one-step prompt engineering. Skills are reusable procedures for planning, action, and tool use. Today they improve through prompt engineering or task-model alignment to revised skills, at high cost, tied to one model, and often unusable for closed-source models.

The team frames skill evolution as bi-level optimisation over rollout selection and skill gains across generations. Skill-R1 trains a lightweight skill generator, not the task model, from task context, prior rollouts, and checked outcomes, steering a frozen task model. That design stays black-box compatible with open- and closed-source models and far cheaper than model-level updates, iterating as checked outcomes feed the next revision. Optimisation uses a bi-level group-relative policy objective: rollouts under shared skills are compared within generations, and revisions improving behaviour over generations are rewarded.
arxiv-2605-09559:
Savarino and two colleagues map the optimal nonlinear transition path in a Mach 2.15 oblique shock wave boundary layer interaction, a split shear layer that is wholly stable yet locally unstable. Linear studies can isolate candidate instabilities, but the full route to breakdown needs nonlinear tuning. Their input output frame, based on a space time spectral Navier Stokes form, captures mean flow warping, triadic energy transfers, and nonlinear stresses that switch on further instabilities.

They find a lean four stage path. First, optimal forcing of oblique first Mack mode waves. Second, self coupling making streamwise Görtler like vortices near the join zone. Third, lift up of speed streaks by those swirls. Fourth, subharmonic sinuous secondary instability leading to streak breakdown. Driving the oblique first Mack mode alone triggers the full cascade. Optimal forcing forms prove quasi steady across forcing strengths, giving a workable frame for transition forecast and control.
arxiv-2605-09859:
Wang and four colleagues tackled fine-grained image retrieval, where models trained on seen categories must find unseen ones. Training on seen categories skews models toward seen semantics rather than the look traits that carry over, hurting unseen-category retrieval. Their net, GAPan, shifts the goal from category prediction toward look modeling.

GAPan treats retrieval features with an invertible density model built on normalizing flows. In the forward pass, each seen category gets a class-conditional Gaussian prior in latent density space, trained by exact likelihood. In reverse, samples from dense prior zones map back to appearance-aware anchors that capture within-class spread. Those anchors guide alignment of embeddings with class appearance patterns, and GAPan reached state-of-the-art results on widely used fine- and coarse-grained benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-09959:
Huang and nine colleagues built G-Zero, a verifier-free framework where two models co-evolve for self-improvement in open-ended generation. Self-evolving language models excel in verifiable domains but struggle in open-ended tasks, where proxy LLM judges create capability caps and reward hacking. G-Zero learns only from its own internal dynamics, with no external judges.

The core idea is Hint-delta, an intrinsic reward measuring the predictive shift between a Generator model's plain response and its response with a self-made hint. A Proposer model trained via GRPO keeps targeting the Generator's blind spots by making hard queries and useful hints, while the Generator is tuned via DPO to take in hint-guided gains. Theory proves a best-iterate suboptimality guarantee for an idealized standard-DPO version, given broad exploration coverage and low pseudo-label score noise.
arxiv-2605-10159:
Armbruster and three co-authors present jNO, a JAX-native library for neural operators and foundation models that unifies data-driven and physics-informed training. Neural operators learn mappings between function spaces, say between opening and closing states of physical systems, and they power surrogate modelling, inverse problems and PDE-constrained learning. In practice, though, workflows fragment across separate frames for geometry, losses, model shape and training logic.

jNO's core is a tracing setup in which domains, model calls, leftovers, supervised losses and checks are written in one symbol language and built into a single tuning line. Users can move between operator regression, mesh-aware leftover testing and PDE-constrained training without rebuilding nearby code. Multi-model compositions, fine-grained parameter-level control, hyperparameter tuning and JAX-native workflows for translated PDE foundation-model families are all covered, with source code released openly.
arxiv-2605-10459:
Atsushi Oyaizu and three colleagues extend the renormalization group to nonunitary quantum dynamics. That group in physics focuses on ground-state traits of settled systems. How it extends to motion driven by dissipation and measurement backaction, without conserved energy, is unclear. Their 2026 paper extends the RG to quantum operations by coarse-graining in real time.

Contest between decoherence and coherent motion proves key for the flow. When coherent motion dominates, chaotic behavior without fixed points appears in the flow, with the parity-time transition as the example. A single qubit's PT shift is captured by a chaotic flow shift, at which fixed points disappear. For broad finite-level systems, contest between probing and unitary dynamics governs fixed-point presence. The PT shift from measurement falls in the class of the 1D Yang-Lee edge singularity, guiding lab tests of imaginary fields in lattice spin systems.
arxiv-2605-10559:
Omar French and two colleagues ask whether magnetic reconnection can power neutrino emission from active galactic nuclei coronae. They test whether merging of current sheets in near-light-speed giant black hole coronae can supply fast protons for high-energy neutrino emission in NGC 1068. Their 2026 paper models the corona as a churning, low-beta hydrogen plasma.

Combining IceCube-band neutrino brightness with X-ray brightness and Thomson light depth reduces quantities to a single family. Across this family, proton magnetization is about 0.3. In this regime, encounters with reconnecting sheets can energize hot protons up to tens of PeV before photon-meson cooling limits acceleration. Guided by PIC models of turbulence at comparable magnetization, the authors adopt a fast proton spectrum with an index set on its own. They find the forecast TeV spectrum shape in line with NGC 1068 without fitting the proton spectrum slope.
arxiv-2605-10759:
Andreas Bergmeister and colleagues derive Reinforce Adjoint Matching, a method scaling reinforcement learning post-training of diffusion and flow-matching models while keeping pretraining's regression build. Diffusion and flow-matching models grow since pretraining is watched regression: a clean sample is noised by rule and the model fits a closed-form goal.

Under KL-ruled reward growth, the best making process tilts the clean-end spread toward higher-reward samples and leaves the noising law as is. Joining this with the adjoint-matching best rule and a REINFORCE fact gives a fit loss that fixes the pretraining goal with the reward. No rollouts, backward adjoint sweeps, or reward gradients are needed. On Stable Diffusion 3.5M, the method hits the top reward on composability, text rendering, and human preference, reaching a rival's peak reward in up to fifty times fewer training steps.
arxiv-2605-11059:
William Gibson and Christoph Reisinger study uniform scaling limits in AdamW-trained transformers. The team models hidden-state dynamics as an interacting particle system coupled by attention. Joint dynamics of hidden states and backpropagated variables converge in L2, uniformly over starts, to a forward-backward ODE system. The rate is order L to the minus 1 plus L to the minus one-third times H to the minus one-half, with L as depth and H as head count.

The limiting ODE system matches a McKean-Vlasov ODE when attention heads lack causal masking. Using flow maps of this McKean-Vlasov ODE and measure concentration, the team bounds discrete-continuous model differences uniformly over compact initial-condition sets. Without a covering argument, constants are independent of token count. Under an AdamW adaptation, bounds also ignore token embedding dimension. Transformer theorists get uniform scaling limits with token-independent constants.
arxiv-2605-11359: Du and six colleagues present CVEvolve, an agent harness with a zero-code interface for finding scientific data-processing algorithms. It mixes multi-round search with tools for running code, building tests, tracking history and holdout checks. It alternates steps that find new candidates with steps that improve them. Tested on X-ray registration, peak detection, diffraction segmentation and hybrid registration, it beats baselines, while holdout tracking spots candidates that generalize best.
arxiv-2605-11459: Zhang and eight colleagues introduce Pace-and-Path Correction, a training-free inference-time fix for vision-language-action models blind to dynamics. Most such models train on single-frame observations, so they degrade badly in changing scenes even after training on dynamic data. From one quadratic cost, joint minimization splits into two channels: pace compresses execution along the planned direction, while path adds an orthogonal spatial offset. On the MoveBench benchmark it lifts success rates by up to 28 point 8 and 25 point 9 percentage points in dynamic and mixed settings.
arxiv-2605-12059: In a 2026 study, Leyi Li and four colleagues build RoboBlockly Studio. It joins block coding, a chat-based AI tutor, and a real robot that runs the code. Students write code, run it, watch the robot, and revise in a tight loop. The design came from talks with five coding teachers, with four goals: student choice, clear code behavior, classroom tasks, and time to reflect with AI help. Tests with 32 high school students showed how robot and AI feedback shaped student work with code.
arxiv-2605-12659: Rojas-Paternina and Cárdenas-Avendaño compare two light-travel prescriptions for black-hole movies. In slow light, one image mixes photons emitted at different source times, while fast light samples a single emission time for all rays. They compare the prescriptions through Kerr geodesic delays across lensing bands in a controlled semi-analytic setting. Given a geometry, spin and inclination, delay distributions are set against source correlation time. When variability timescales fall short of delay spread, high-inclination images diverge most.
arxiv-2605-12759: Antonelli and six colleagues predict Lightning Network channel closures from public gossip data. The Lightning Network is a second-layer Bitcoin protocol for fast, cheap off-chain transactions. Channels can close by mutual agreement or unilaterally through forced closure. Forced closure locks capital for a period and degrades reliability. The team frames closure prediction as temporal link classification over the channel graph. They build a set spanning two years and benchmark models ranging from MLPs through temporal graph neural networks to spectral encodings. Temporal and behavioural signals dominate.
arxiv-2605-13059: Yang and six co-authors present BrainAnytime, a pretraining framework for brain image analysis that takes whatever scans are on hand, from a lone T1 scan to a full multimodal workup. Most models assume fixed scan types, yet patients arrive with mixed, often incomplete scan sets. Trained on 34,899 3D brain scans, it learns MRI-PET links via cross-modal distillation and spotlights disease-vulnerable anatomy via atlas-guided masking. Across four tasks it largely beats single-scan and missing-scan rivals.
arxiv-2605-13259: Hahn and Geilhufe study superconductivity in a two orbital version of the Hatsugai-Kohmoto model at half filling. The model is exactly solvable, with interactions local in momentum, and offers a clean setting for strong correlations and orbital effects. For a system with fourfold symmetry, they classify the allowed gap shapes across spin, orbital and momentum degrees of freedom. They also compute critical temperatures and order parameters for chosen pairing channels as interaction and pairing strength vary.
arxiv-2605-13459: Dmitriy Ovchinnikov, Jan Schee and Zdenek Stuchlik study signs of a double-ring plus double-torus system around a Schwarzschild black hole, a black hole with no spin. They allow the two glowing parts to have tilted axes, unlike a single equatorial torus baseline. Using ray tracing in curved spacetime, they build frequency-shift maps, flux maps and spectral line profiles. Two tilted glowing structures produce multi-peak spectral profiles and lopsided flux patterns. These features offer simple diagnostics for tilted multi-part accretion structures.
arxiv-2605-13759: Claudio Mantuano, Manuel Kammermann and Philipp Baumann address fair grouping at scale, splitting objects into a set cluster count with each guarded group shown in each cluster. The goal is cutting grouping cost, the sum of squared straight gaps between objects and cluster centres, against a user-defined fairness target. The authors propose a general frame giving precise cost-fairness trade-off control, with three rules. One targets answer quality and limit freedom, one lifts scale while keeping quality, and one tops scale, solving million-object cases in seconds.
arxiv-2605-13859: Guo and five colleagues present BiSpikCLM, claimed as the first fully binary spiking language model that avoids floating-point matrix multiplication. Its softmax-free spiking attention drops both softmax and floating-point steps from autoregressive modeling, cutting energy use. A distillation method called Spike-Aware Alignment Distillation trains the spiking student against a conventional teacher across embeddings, attention maps, features and outputs.
arxiv-2605-13959: Kang and four colleagues improve flow-matching robot policies by swapping the standard Gaussian starting distribution for WarmPrior, a prior built from recent action history. The temporally grounded starting point straightens the probability paths the policy follows, echoing optimal-transport couplings in rectified flow, and lifts success rates on manipulation tasks. WarmPrior also reshapes exploration in prior-space reinforcement learning, improving sample efficiency and final performance.
arxiv-2605-14059: Ladiana links smooth real-world signals to discrete Ising-spin recall memory. Real signals are smooth and high-dimensional, while recall memory math runs on discrete spins. A layered Ising frame joins a shape-keeping signal-to-spin coder, PCA whitening plus SimHash random-plane projection, to Kanter-Sompolinsky pseudo-inverse memory links in a tri-layer hetero-associative system. The pseudo-inverse tweak tips the equal-weight mix state, so heat noise breaks cross-modal symmetry and picks one global winner.
arxiv-2605-14159: Rybak views groups by algebra and motion on spaces. They act in a general way on a delta-hyperbolic space, and the induced action on the limit set inside the Gromov boundary stays faithful. A motion-based test splits the class: groups whose limit action is topologically free, and groups whose limit action is not. Rybak shows the test matches a pure algebra trait, being mixed identity free, so tree results reach arbitrary hyperbolic spaces. As a result, the reduced C-star algebra of these groups turns out selfless.
arxiv-2605-14459: Rohner, Schwab and Xenophontos bound how well finite elements and feedforward neural networks can express solutions of a singularly perturbed elliptic boundary-value problem on a bounded interval. Working with low-regularity data, they prove parameter-robust algebraic rates for linear finite elements on graded meshes. Shallow and deep ReLU networks get matching robust rates, and deep networks with tanh units are claimed to double the finite-element rate.
arxiv-2605-14559: Afifi adds scheduling tools to PyCSP3, a Python library for building constraint models exported to XCSP3. Interval variables, sequence variables and resource functions once needed hand-built integer encodings. The extension supplies fifty-three constraints and twenty-seven expressions that compile down to standard constraints. On paired instances the compiled models match objectives on proved-optimal pairs, with speedups up to about sixfold on some families.
arxiv-2605-14659: So, Lee and No probe a puzzle in grokking, where models suddenly generalise after long training. In Needleman-Wunsch matrix generation, small Transformers reach high validation accuracy fastest at a middle data set size, not the largest. Past that sweet spot, generalisation still arrives but needs more gradient updates. Larger sets can, however, speed fitting to high training accuracy once partial competence appears. A multiplication baseline shows no such post-threshold slowdown.
arxiv-2605-15159: Calvin C. Bakker and three others simulate epithelial tissue with the cellular Potts model, tracking both cell shape and cytoskeletal activity. The runs reveal a rich phase diagram of orientational orders coexisting across scales. Raising the actin polymerization rate drives a transition into long-range flocking, while quasi-long-range nematic order emerges at large scales. Near cell size, roughly hexagonal cells produce hexanematic order like that seen in kidney-cell monolayers.
arxiv-2605-15259: Jonas Matuszak and Carlo Tasillo present TransitionListener version 2.0, a Python framework for precision predictions of gravitational waves from strong first-order cosmological phase transitions. The chain runs from a user-defined scalar potential to gravity-wave spectra and signal-to-noise ratios, aiding benchmarks and large knob scans. Version 2 adds steady transition dynamics, including true-vacuum fraction evolution, feedback on cosmic expansion, and rewarming during bubbling, plus direct mean bubble gap for mapping to simulation-based spectral patterns.
arxiv-2605-15359: A. De Sarkar and four colleagues synthesize populations of Galactic middle-aged pulsar wind nebulae, the largest very-high-energy gamma-ray source class, with detailed modeling of the reverberation phase. When the supernova remnant reverse shock compresses the nebula, dynamics and spectra shift substantially. Their hybrid TIDE+L framework evolves thousands of nebulae to 100 thousand years under varied pulsar, remnant, and environment distributions. The model predicts the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory will detect an order of magnitude more nebulae than firmly known in the TeV range.
arxiv-2605-15459: Albert Kjøller Jacobsen, Leo Uhre Jakobsen, Johanna Marie Gegenfurtner, and Georgios Arvanitidis tackle sampling the connected sets of equivalent neural-network minima rather than spreading loosely over low-loss regions. Their sampler, DiMS, uses a dynamical system with kinetic energy, a gravitational pull, and friction that drains energy, and is guaranteed to sample exactly from minimum level sets. Motivated by uncertainty quantification in Bayesian inference, it improves on earlier approaches in their tests.
arxiv-2605-15759: Wentao Qiu and four colleagues present DimMem, a dimensional memory frame that beats the cost-versus-fidelity trade-off for language-model agents. DimMem stores a memory as a unit with fields for time, location, reason, purpose, and keywords. That structure powers dimension retrieval, update, and recall without histories in context. On LoCoMo-10 and LongMemEval-S it scores 81.43 percent and 78.20 percent, beating systems while cutting per-query cost by 24 percent. After tuning on the DimMem schema, a Qwen3-4B extractor tops LightMem with GPT-4.1-mini on benchmarks and rivals extractors.
arxiv-2605-15959: Cao, So, Wang, and Wang ask why adversarial training helps physics-informed neural networks. These models solve differential equations, yet they train badly on fast-changing or multiscale solutions. Using neural tangent kernel theory, the authors show how a GAN discriminator steers training and unifies several GAN variants. Their new algorithm cut training flaws sharply in tests and often beat rival methods by wide margins.
arxiv-2605-16359: Huang and nine colleagues ask how much picture evidence vision-language models really need when the token allowance is fixed. They recast pruning as a search for task-relevant evidence. Their F^3A works before the language model sees picture tokens. It forms cues from the question, pairs them with grid tokens via frozen sparse sensing heads, and spends the allowance in locating, refining, and recovery stages. No training or extra language-model pass is needed, and the usual prompting and decoding setup stays intact.
arxiv-2605-16659: Kobayashi and colleagues model the single-turn coil, a destructive pulsed magnet that tops 100 tesla for a few microseconds before exploding. Using a full 3D model of the coil, they simulate current, heat, and magnetic field together. The results show strongly nonlinear spread of all three, driven by the skin effect, rapid heating, and coil deformation. That uneven spread explains why the field inside the coil varies so much in time and space.
arxiv-2605-17159: Gosmar and Zenezini describe MADP, a five-agent pipeline that classifies, splits, parses and extracts business documents, calling in a human only for selected checks. A feedback method lets prompts improve from corrections over time. In live use on 955 documents it automated 97 percent of the pipeline, and modeling suggests large cuts in staff time and energy use.
arxiv-2605-17359: Zhang and colleagues propose TopoPrior, a way to reuse team layouts for multi-agent language-model systems instead of searching fresh layouts per query. It learns reusable layout priors offline from sample graphs across domains, then builds query-specific starting graphs for refinement. A conditional variational graph module captures reusable structure, with adversarial alignment trimming domain mismatch. Tests show gains across backbones with lower online token use.
arxiv-2605-17559: Perets and Mannor reframe structured false-discovery control as a regularized learning problem. Classical methods treat links among hypotheses as obstacles needing cautious correction, yet proximity, links and levels can raise power. Working inside a kernel Hilbert space unifies domains, graphs and hierarchies under one method through kernel choice alone. Smooth fits replace piecewise-constant fits, data-driven tuning replaces guesswork, and inference at unseen spots supports efficient design. Two decision rules are proved to control the false discovery rate, tested on spatial data and gene expression.
arxiv-2605-17659: Shvetsov and colleagues identify negative weight drift from standard losses and biased units. They show that under MSE or cross-entropy loss, gradients for positive pre-activations are non-negative at start, driving weights down. The drift comes from optimization rather than data, and holds across architectures and asymmetric activations. Coupled with ReLU, weight drift produces sparsity near 90 percent in GPT-nano. The authors ask whether this is damaging and find models degrade above about 70 percent on average. Testing sparsity-inducing units reveals spikes in intermediate layers.
arxiv-2605-17859: Jiayi Shao and six colleagues release Multi-site PPG, an in-the-wild physiological dataset from wearables. Public PPG sets skew wrist-only or short and controlled, limiting work on new form factors. The team built four devices, an earring, ring, watch, and necklace, recording green and infrared PPG, acceleration, and temperature, with a chest strap for ECG. Participants wore them for days during routines, yielding over 350 hours of raw data. Benchmarks show body-site gaps: best heart-rate errors run 2.30 bpm on the earring but 8.68 on the necklace.
arxiv-2605-18359: Xi Leng and six colleagues address uneven attention in large multimodal models, where text and image evidence compete for focus. Their 2026 method, RAVE, adds a learned query-key bias to attention scores over visual keys, rebalancing cross-modal and within-image attention without changing the backbone. Across multimodal benchmarks it gains about three points on average, most on perception-heavy tasks like multilingual OCR and chart reading.
