Tests on a mock community recovered known interacting strains even at low abundance. Applied to stool samples from healthy donors, the pipeline named specific bacteria that bind each of two sensors. Follow-up cultures confirmed the matches. Mol and colleagues describe the platform as modular: other sensors and patient samples can be swapped in to map which microbes the immune system can actually taste.
plos-pone-0356359: An and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a protein that helps liver cancer hide from the immune system. The protein, FABP5, is the focus of their lab work. They report that it shapes a suppressive setting around the tumor through a chain involving NF-kB and PD-L1, both known immune switches. Blocking such chains is a major aim in modern cancer drug design.
plos-pone-0356759:
Haiwei Du, Runsen Lai, and Jianhua Zhu reconstructed a deadly kind of mountain disaster: the debris flow that races down steep gullies. A catchment in China's North Tianshan range served as their case. Their 2026 study combined field surveys and laboratory soil tests. It also used a validated flood simulation program. The program replayed a 2024 event and then tested how worse storms would behave.

The replay matched the real flood's depth and footprint closely. The recipe for disaster combined three things. Shattered rock supplied debris, steep slopes sped it up, and short intense rain pulled the trigger. Under a once-a-century storm, the simulated flow ran several meters deep at highway speeds. The danger zone swelled over downstream settlements. Such zonation gives engineers defensible lines for barriers and building bans.
plos-pone-0357159:
Yuri Fukai, Amane Fujiwara, and Kohei Matsuno test whether algae sleeping in Arctic seafloor mud can seed the autumn blooms now appearing on the Chukchi shelf. Stronger winds over open water stir sediments upward, and a recent field study suggested buried diatoms ride along. The team incubated natural water communities two ways, adding nutrients alone or nutrients plus microalgae-bearing sediment, and watched growth, species, and light use.

Both treatments bloomed, with diatoms leading. Sediment sped the start by adding ready cells, while growth rates and light efficiency stayed similar. Nutrient-only tanks favored open-water autumn species, while sediment tanks filled with species typical of the seafloor. Fukai and colleagues say resuspension shapes not just bloom timing but which community the Arctic gets.
plos-pone-0357259:
Ling Zong and Kexin Zhou published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on older adults in China who live with several chronic diseases at once. The study asks what family and social support do to their mental health. Using a nationally representative 2020 survey, they modeled how multimorbidity relates to mental health, and whether family or wider social support changes that link.

More diseases went with poorer mental health. Both supports were themselves linked to better mental health, but only family support changed the disease link, surprisingly: the mental health penalty of multimorbidity grew steeper where family support was higher. That effect weakened with age and vanished past eighty, while family support's direct benefit followed a U-shape across age groups. Close family involvement, they warn, is not automatically protective, and programs should work with families carefully rather than simply urging more of it.
plos-pone-0357459:
Siliang Guo, Yan Qu, and Youjia Liu published a 2026 economics study in PLOS ONE on whether education keeps Chinese families from sliding back into poverty. China has ended absolute poverty, but keeping families out is a different challenge. Using four waves of a national family panel survey from 2014 to 2020, the authors measured each household's stock of educational human capital and modeled relapse risk with several statistical approaches.

More education clearly lowered the chance of falling back into poverty. The protection ran through three channels: family members finding non-farm jobs, higher household income, and better family health. Households that themselves invested more in education got extra benefit, while heavy health spending diluted the effect. The protective impact grew stronger for families at highest relapse risk, and was larger in eastern and urban areas than elsewhere. The authors argue education budgets are anti-poverty insurance, especially where relapse risk concentrates.
plos-pone-0357759:
Ankit and coauthors published a 2026 materials paper in PLOS ONE on copper-graphite composites, blends prized for carrying current and resisting wear, made by pressing and baking metal powders. Three settings govern the result: how much graphite goes in, how hot the baking runs, and how long it lasts. Instead of trial and error, the team used response surface methodology to model how those settings jointly determine density and hardness.

A fitted quadratic model matched the measured values closely, with negligible error, and formal analysis confirmed which settings mattered. The best combination used a modest graphite share, a high sintering temperature, and a mid-length hold, giving the densest and hardest material in their tests. The model lets manufacturers dial in target density or hardness on paper first, cutting wasted runs, and gives powder metallurgy shops a template for other blends.
plos-pone-0357959:
Francisca Édla Santos Leite Gurgel and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE from Fortaleza, Brazil, on teaching pregnant women with diabetes how to care for themselves. Standard hospital handouts can be hard going for women with limited reading skills. So the team wrote the guidance as a cordel, a traditional Brazilian booklet of rhymed verse, working with health researchers and cordel poets, and tested it at two public maternity hospitals.

Hospitalized pregnant women rated every item of the booklet as fully valid, and forty expert judges nearly matched them, giving top or near-top clarity and relevance scores. Experts strongly agreed on the content overall, though they ranked individual items in quite different orders. The cordel, they say, is a culturally rooted format that makes discharge guidance easier to grasp and remember, and this early validation invites wider testing of whether it changes self-care.
plos-pone-0358259: Tang and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study that mines public data on stool fats and gene activity. Their combined computer analysis hints that the COX-2 pathway may be linked with one fat molecule, named CE(20:4). The link sits along the path from benign colon growths to cancer. A candidate link from free data can guide lab work on early colon cancer signs.
plos-pone-0358359:
Zongtao Li led a team of seven authors linking a common molecule to kidney damage in diabetes, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Lactate, known for the burn of hard exercise, may also signal renal trouble in diabetic kidney disease. The team combined animal experiments, clinical cohorts, and bioinformatics in one exploratory analysis.

Li's work ties higher serum lactate to worse kidney function across those sources. A cheap blood measure that warns early of failing kidneys would be valuable, since current markers lag behind damage. Triangulating across animals, patients, and gene data strengthens a claim that any one source could not carry. The analysis is exploratory by design, marking lactate as a lead worth testing in larger, focused studies.
plos-pone-0358459:
Braulio Tapia and colleagues studied in 2026 how fish communities differ from place to place on the rocky reefs of the Juan Fernández Archipelago. The islands, far off the coast of Chile in the southeastern Pacific, sit inside a marine protected area. The team examined demersal fish, those living near the reef floor, and asked how their groupings vary across the protected waters.

Understanding that spatial variety, called heterogeneity, is practical knowledge for conservation. A protected area drawn without it may guard plenty of water but miss the spots where particular communities thrive. The authors link their findings to the archipelago's conservation plans, showing where protection is well placed and where management may need adjusting.
plos-pone-0358659:
Muhammad Ali Ibrahim Kazi leads a team of eight studying heart outcomes in people who live with both inflammatory bowel disease and type 2 diabetes, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The pairing is dangerous, since gut inflammation and blood sugar problems feed each other's damage to blood vessels. The authors asked whether modern diabetes drugs in the GLP-1 family are linked to fewer heart events in this high risk group.

Using a large international health records network, they matched over sixteen thousand treated patients with similar untreated ones. Treated patients showed lower rates across the board: heart attack, heart failure, stroke, dangerous rhythms, and blood clots in veins and lungs. The authors caution that records based comparisons show association, not proof of cause, and that the study cannot separate the two drug types it pooled together.
plos-pone-0358759: Cui and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on hearing machine faults through noise. Bearings in spinning machines wear out, and their fault signals hide in loud, shifting conditions. The team's Wavelet-Mamba network mixes wave-based signal cleaning with a modern sequence model. Catching a failing bearing early can prevent a breakdown that stops a whole line.
plos-pone-0358959:
Rustam Akhmedov and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on exercise and women's health. It is an eight-week intervention study of indoor cycling, commonly called spinning. Outcomes cover body image, how the women see their own bodies, and anthropometric measurements, standard measures like weight and waist size.

Tracking body image alongside body measurements matters because the two do not always move together. A program can shrink a waist while leaving self-image untouched, or lift confidence before bodies change. Fitness practitioners designing women's cycling programs are the readers for evidence that joins the physical and the psychological.
plos-pone-0359559:
Joanna L'Heureux and five colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on the oral microbiome, the community of microbes living in the mouth. The authors look for signatures of ageing and of cognitive function in that community. Their cohorts come from distinct geographical regions, letting place enter the comparison.

Mouth microbes are easy to sample, so a signature tied to cognition would be a convenient window on brain health. Geography matters because diet and environment shape the microbiome strongly. Researchers of ageing and dementia screening are the readers for signatures that hold across places rather than reflecting one town's habits.
plos-pone-0359659: Shah, writing alone, published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on why muscles waste away. Using a tool called decoupleR, Shah compared the activity of transcription factors, the switches that turn genes on and off. Three causes of wasting were set side by side: space flight, old age, and lack of use. Seeing where the three match or split can point to shared targets for drugs or training plans.
plos-pone-0359859:
John Yinger published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies world-record envelopes in racing events: the outer limits that link how fast athletes can go and how far. The focus is the speed-distance trade-off, the way top speed falls as race distance grows.

An envelope here means the boundary formed by world records across distances, from sprints to marathons. Fitting that boundary shows the underlying rule connecting speed and endurance in human performance. Sports scientists use such limits to judge how close current athletes are to what bodies can do, and to spot records that break the pattern.
plos-pone-0359959:
Quang Toai Ton, Thanh Hien Vu, Thanh Nguyen Vu, and Tuong Le published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It presents HSCM-Lane, a computer vision system for lane segmentation, marking exactly which pixels in a road image belong to lane lines. The system is built on a ResNet encoder-decoder design.

Added to that base is context modeling that uses shifted windows at several levels, a way for the network to consider both fine line detail and the wider road scene. Lane marking detection is a core skill for driver assistance and self-driving cars. Engineers comparing segmentation architectures can judge whether this context modeling earns its extra complexity on road images.
plos-pone-0360059:
Ankit Singh, Varun Dutt, and Akash Rao studied in 2026 how mental effort and brain stimulation together shape the way people make decisions from experience. Their experiments vary cognitive load, how much a person's working memory is burdened, and apply prefrontal neuromodulation, gentle stimulation of the brain region behind the forehead that handles planning. They watch how these factors change exploration, risk taking, and the search for information.

Experience based decisions, learned by trying options and seeing outcomes, differ from choices made from written descriptions. Knowing how a loaded or stimulated brain explores helps explain everyday choices under pressure. The work speaks to psychology, to economics, and to the design of training for people whose risky decisions carry real costs.
pmc-13193159:
Feisal Dahir Kahie is first author on a 2026 cross-sectional study of anemia patterns among adults with diabetes at Mubende Regional Referral Hospital in Uganda. Anemia, low red blood cell levels, is a common but overlooked complication of diabetes that worsens fatigue and outcomes. Local evidence on its patterns was limited.

Among two hundred and forty-six adults, about twenty-eight percent had anemia, judged by standard cutoffs and red cell size measures. Normal-sized cell anemia was by far the commonest type, ahead of small-cell and large-cell forms. Older age, nerve damage, longer diabetes duration, obesity, and poor blood sugar control each linked independently to anemia. Routine anemia screening should join diabetes care, the authors conclude.
pmc-13196859:
Haibin Shang and colleagues published a 2026 study on sleep length and muscle loss. Sarcopenia means loss of muscle mass and strength, often with age. Past studies linked sleep to this loss, but cause and effect stayed unclear.

The team used survey data from more than five thousand adults in the United States. They paired that with a genetic method that uses gene variants as natural tests of cause. Both lines pointed to a link between longer sleep and lower odds of muscle loss. Gene work also hinted at shared risk genes for sleep and muscle traits. The authors say the link could guide care, while noting the genetic signals need care in reading.
pmc-13197159:

pmc-13197359:

pmc-13197859:
Stine Arp and colleagues surveyed young Danes on why they try to quit nicotine in a 2026 study. Use of e-cigarettes and smokeless nicotine has grown among Danish youth, and many want to quit. Services need to know what drives those attempts, and whether drivers differ by product.

pmc-13202659:

Six algorithms were trained and compared, and the gradient boosting model performed best on the held-out test data in the authors' evaluation. An explanation method ranked the strongest predictors, and the team converted the model into a bedside nomogram for timely risk decisions.
pmc-13203059:

pmc-13203359:

pmc-13213359:

pmc-13216059:

pmc-13217459:

pmc-13219159:

pmc-13224059:
Klinguer Cécile and colleagues measure a 2026 carbon audit of the central biochemistry laboratory platform at Cochin Hospital in Paris. pmc-13224159:
Mohammad Abdulsalam Soliman and colleagues follow a 2026 hospital cohort of patients recovering from mild traumatic brain injury. Among 364 patients, average scores started low, indicating marked early impairment. Scores rose sharply by three months and approached the normal range by one year, with most recovery packed into the first quarter. The authors caution that subtle higher-level difficulties may linger despite normal totals, so structured follow-up still matters.
pmc-13224759:

pmc-13225159:

pmc-13225659:

Trend analysis then tested whether that gap has narrowed over time, a question with direct consequences for screening strategies.
pmc-13232959:

pmc-13233959:

pmc-13235359:

pmc-13239259:

pmc-13239459:
Tianna Magel and team explore a patient-led research conference in a 2026 study. The event, called For Patients, By Patients, runs online each year. People with lived patient experience steer it, and the team asked what leading such an event feels like and what support it needs.

pmc-13239659:
Xuerui Li and co-authors introduce a long-running health cohort from Tianjin, China, in a 2026 profile paper. The study, launched in 2022, follows adults over time to find risk factors and intervention targets for common chronic diseases in the city.

pmc-13239959:

pmc-13240459:

pmc-13240759:

pmc-13240859:

pmc-13240959:

pmc-13241559:

pmc-13241659:

pmc-13242459:

pmc-13242659:

pmc-13243159:

pmc-13243759:

pmc-13244259:

pmc-13245059:

pmc-13245759:

pmc-13246559:

pmc-13246759:

pmc-13249559:

pmc-13250459:

pmc-13250859:

pmc-13251759:

pmc-13253759:

pmc-13253859:

pmc-13253959:

pmc-13254159:

pmc-13258559:

pmc-13259959:

The authors describe the causes of that change and show it can be reversed with drugs. Restoring the interaction sustained trap inhibition during inflammation and prevented adverse effects in their experiments.
pmc-13273759:
Yushuo Duan and co-authors reviewed RNA methylation in the immune surroundings of gastrointestinal tumors in a 2026 article. RNA methylation is a reversible chemical editing of RNA, run by writer, eraser, and reader proteins. It tunes gene activity and has been tied to cancer growth and immune control.

In gut tumors, the authors explain, this editing reshapes the immune microenvironment by changing how tumor and immune cells act and how they use energy. That reshaping helps cancers hide from immunity and alters how they respond to treatment. The review gathers the latest findings across liver, colorectal, stomach, pancreatic, and esophageal cancers. Its aim is to support strategies that pair methylation targeting drugs with immunotherapy for stronger effect.
pmc-13273859:
Gonçalo Pinto and co-authors used a large language model to generate a synthetic pregnancy dataset in a 2026 data article. Real obstetric records are hard to share because of privacy, which slows methods research. Synthetic patients can stand in for teaching and testing if they stay plausible.

Their dataset follows five thousand low risk pregnant women from before conception to after birth. An expert panel in family medicine and data science reviewed early output, and repeated prompt revisions improved consistency. Rule checks then verified internal coherence. The authors stress the data suit simulation and machine learning practice, not clinical decisions.
pmc-13274159:
Hiroshi Kobayashi wrote a 2026 review article re-reading endometrial cancer through an evolutionary lens. This womb-lining cancer is rising worldwide, especially in younger women, alongside obesity and delayed childbirth. Standard gene studies list the faults, but not why this tissue collects them so readily.

His frame is antagonistic pleiotropy: traits that help early in life can harm later. One growth pathway is vital for reproduction and womb repair, yet modern overnutrition keeps it switched on, feeding abnormal growth. The guardian protein p53 protects fertility and the placenta, but age and inflammation warp its work toward cancer. The pathways reinforce each other, he argues.
pmc-13274559:
Sufia Athar and co-authors examined emotional skill and workplace wellbeing among nurses and midwives in Qatar in a 2026 cross-sectional study. They surveyed 121 registered nurses and midwives, each with six months of experience or more, using an online questionnaire across seven skill domains. pmc-13274759:

pmc-13275359:

pmc-13276159:
Xin Li and co-authors wrote a 2026 review on exosomes as a possible new route for treating brain and nerve diseases. They rarely provoke the immune system and can cross the blood-brain barrier, a wall that blocks many drugs.

It surveys their roles in multiple sclerosis, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and stroke. The authors warn that big hurdles remain before clinic use. pmc-13276559:
Catherine Volgenant and co-authors present a 2026 population study of oral health on Sal, one of the Cape Verde islands off West Africa. Local reports suggested poor dental health, but no scientific survey existed. The team set out to measure disease, quality of life, and risk factors across the island.

Over half showed the consequences of untreated decay, like abscesses. Almost two thirds of adults had serious gum disease scores. The authors urge better prevention and access to dental services on the island.
pmc-13276759:
Iram P Rodriguez-Sanchez and a large team measure head lice among schoolchildren in two Mexican cities, in a 2026 survey. Lice infestations disrupt comfort, schooling, and family life, yet city-level Mexican data are scarce. Trained staff inspected each child's scalp directly under a standard method.

More than six thousand children were checked across Monterrey and Mérida. Overall, five hundred ninety children carried lice, with rates notably higher in Monterrey than in Mérida. Girls and children with long hair were infested most often in both cities. Links with home and hygiene factors differed between cities, so the authors advise school and family programmes tailored to each local setting.
pmc-13277659:
Md Shakhawat Hossain, Md Sahilur Rahman, and Munim Ahmed release a 2026 dataset for outlining single cell nuclei in breast cancer slides. The set holds thirty-nine patches from twenty-one patients, with more than eighteen hundred nuclei under the loose rule and fewer under full consensus. pmc-13277759:
Tae Hwa Kang and Sun Jae Park present a 2026 genetic study of how an invasive beetle spread across the Korean Peninsula. One marker set pointed to two common ancestral types, while the other split the beetles into three groups and three invasion routes. The authors settle on at least two founding populations entering through several ports, then spreading inland by hitchhiking on transport. Beetles are drawn strongly to their host plant once they arrive. Port checks may be the best choke point for control.
pmc-13278859:

One tissue marker, synaptophysin, was present, which usually points toward neuroendocrine tumours instead.

Combined platinum chemotherapy and immunotherapy shrank the metastatic cancer, and the partial response held beyond twelve months. The authors suggest this marker pattern may flag patients who benefit from that combination.
pmc-13279659:

Two readers graded study quality and bias risk with standard tools. Just four studies fit, with three hundred thirty nine patients in all. Those studies hinted that Reiki may cut fatigue in patients. Small proof calls for larger, tighter trials before firm advice.
pmc-13279759:
Carl Llor and Niels Kristian Kjaer write a 2026 commentary on combined biomarker testing in primary care. Antibiotic overuse is a top world health worry, most in chest infections seen in family care. pmc-13280159:

pmc-13280459:

pmc-13280559:

pmc-13280659:

Scans after surgery showed blood still flowed to both testicles. His sperm quality was very poor at first, then got much better over two years. The authors say fast, careful surgery can save both the glands and future fertility. They urge repair over removal when living tissue remains.
pmc-13281559:

pmc-13281859:

pmc-13282059:

pmc-13282259:

pmc-13282559:

pmc-13282859:

pmc-13284159:

pmc-13284559:

pmc-13285359:

pmc-13285559:

pmc-13285659:

pmc-13286359:

pmc-13286959:

pmc-13287159:

pmc-13287759:

pmc-13288359:

pmc-13288459:

pmc-13288559:

pmc-13288859:

pmc-13288959:

pmc-13289159:

pmc-13289259:

pmc-13289359:

pmc-13289659:

The compound lowered harmful oxidants and iron while raising protective GPX4 and related defenses. Blocking Nrf2 or silencing EGFR erased the benefit, proving the chain matters. Animal heart injury also eased with treatment.
pmc-13289759:
Muhammad Owais and coauthors recount a 2026 fatal case of desmoid-type fibromatosis hidden behind the uterus that mimicked a fibroid. This rare, locally aggressive growth makes up fewer than 0.03 percent of all tumors and can invade nearby organs silently. A 21-year-old woman with lower belly pain and a large pelvic mass on ultrasound was sent home with a fibroid label.

She came back two days later with an acute abdomen, and scans showed a 29 cm mass behind the womb lining with free air from a perforated colon. Emergency surgery removed part of the colon with a stoma, but full removal proved impossible. Tissue review fit the fibromatosis diagnosis, though confirmatory stains were not done. She died nine days after arrival.
pmc-13290659:
Teenagers in South Africa's Limpopo province are still learning what self-awareness means, T. C. Masutha and colleagues find in a qualitative study from 2026. Self-awareness underpins empathy, sound choices, and emotional resilience, so the team asked school learners how they understand and talk about it.

Forty-eight learners from six schools, evenly split between boys and girls across grades nine to eleven, took part during a nursing-model boot camp. Reflective writing and group discussion fed a thematic analysis that surfaced five themes, running from how learners define self-awareness to their strengths, weaknesses, career hopes, and ways of fixing weaknesses. The authors describe a grasp of self-awareness that is developing but uneven, tied to how committed learners feel at school and how they picture their futures. They argue teachers should build it deliberately.
pmc-13290759:
Two hippocampus circuits split memory from mood in mouse brains, Yanling Liang and colleagues show in a circuit study from 2026. The orbitofrontal cortex talks to both the dorsal and ventral ends of CA1, but how those conversations differ was unclear.

With viral tracing and targeted disconnection, the team mapped the wiring. The dorsal link runs one way and indirectly, from orbitofrontal cortex through the claustrum, with no return path found. The ventral link runs the other direction, with a direct line into the orbitofrontal cortex plus detours through thalamus, amygdala, and entorhinal cortex. Cutting the dorsal circuit hurt spatial memory only; cutting the ventral circuit produced anxiety- and depression-like behavior while memory stayed intact. Liang and colleagues read the split as a circuit-level explanation for how one region can govern both knowing and feeling.
pmc-13290959:
Stepping outside the self may be how moral injury heals, Wesley Fleming proposes in a theory paper from 2026. Moral injury leaves rigid shame and broken meaning after events that violate a person's moral code, and Fleming builds on Mindfulness-to-Meaning Theory to cast self-transcendence as the recovery mechanism.

Self-transcendence, a state of loosened self-focus, widened awareness, and prosocial meaning, is theorized to grow through mindfulness practices that train decentering and meta-awareness. In that state, attention broadens, reappraisal turns flexible, and shame-locked self-stories loosen, letting moral identity be repaired and meaning rebuilt. Fleming sketches interventions that cultivate the state directly or as modules inside other therapies. He also flags the weak spots: the state is hard to measure, readiness varies, and inducing it reliably remains unsolved.
pmc-13291159:
Shuai Wang and colleagues review the appendix and colon cancer risk in a 2026 short article. The appendix was once seen as useless. New work casts it as a home for gut microbes and immune tissue. That shift raises a fresh question about removing it.

Past studies gave mixed answers on cancer after appendix removal. Some found higher risk soon after surgery. Newer work blames early detection bias for much of that signal. Lab studies still show plausible paths through microbes and inflammation. Effects may also differ by tumor site. The authors call for care in reading old data. No simple claim that removal raises long-term risk holds up.
pmc-13291259:
A gut microbe product may shield the bowel wall. Sweta Ghosh leads a 2026 study of urolithin A in mice and human tissue. The compound switches on a gut sensor called AHR. How that switch guards the bowel was not clear.

In mouse gut cells, the compound woke a second alarm unit. That unit released one signal, IL-18, but not its close kin. IL-18 then drove mucus and defense proteins. Mice gained protection from bowel inflammation. Human bowel samples from patients showed the same signal rise. A chain from sensor to shield thus takes shape. The path may guide new bowel disease drugs.
pmc-13291359:
Listening along fiber cables can spot faults and events. Yangyang Wan leads a 2026 study of smarter sensing without real training data. Such systems need many labeled examples to learn. Real event data is scarce at most work sites.

Their method builds training data from physics itself. Models of events and of the sensing gear create fake data. A second network learns to strip background noise from signals. Tests covered public sensing data for event naming. A factory belt fault task was also tried. Fault calls hit high accuracy in a real plant. Scores matched networks trained on real data. Skills also carried across sites in one task type.
pmc-13292059:
Yang Wang and co-authors build a 2026 gene signature from lactylation-related genes to forecast outcomes and immunotherapy response in triple-negative breast cancer. Public tumor data were clustered by those genes, and a scoring model grew out of the genes separating the clusters. Lab assays then checked the model's key genes.

Patients with high scores lived better outcomes and answered immunotherapy more favorably, judging by checkpoint profiles and drug sensitivity patterns. Three genes stood out in validation: PD-L2, immunoglobulin J chain, and the CSF2 receptor beta chain. The authors present the signature as a dual-purpose tool, estimating both prognosis and likely benefit from immune treatment. They flag the three hub genes as candidates for future therapy research.
pmc-13292259:
Shynggys Nuraly and co-authors tell a 2026 case story with a rare diagnosis and a striking outcome: squamous cell carcinoma arising in the renal pelvis. Fewer than 1 percent of upper urinary tract tumors take this form. Their patient was a 58-year-old woman with anemia, and MRI showed an infiltrative mass blocking urine flow and invading the pancreatic tail.

Surgeons removed the kidney and ureter with a bladder cuff, cleared lymph nodes, and took the pancreatic segment in the same operation, achieving a complete resection despite the patient's morbid obesity. Pathology confirmed a well-differentiated keratinizing tumor with nerve invasion, staged pT4N0M0. She received no further therapy. Five years later, PET/CT showed no recurrence, a result the authors credit to thorough multivisceral surgery.
pmc-13292559:
Xunhe Huang, with co-authors, reports a 2026 genome-wide association study hunting resistance genes against avian leukosis virus in Wuhua yellow chickens, a hardy indigenous Chinese breed. The virus suppresses immunity and causes tumors across the poultry industry. Infection status came from p27 antigen testing at 46 weeks in 259 birds, of which only ten, 3.9 percent, tested positive.

Fifty-eight significant markers clustered inside one 1.03-megabase stretch of chromosome 12. The gene FHIT alone held 44 of them, and conditioning on its lead variant erased the neighboring signals, marking it the driver. Eleven candidate genes in the block mix tumor suppression, metabolism, and immune signaling themes, with the citrate cycle the top enriched pathway. The authors offer the haplotype as a breeding target for resistant lines.
pmc-13292659:
Komal Sai Pedaballe writes a 2026 letter applauding a brief report by Lin and colleagues. The report shows how rarely the kidney drug finerenone actually gets started in chronic kidney disease with type 2 diabetes. The original study used electronic health record prescriptions and found just 0.3 percent uptake, mostly in advanced, high-risk patients. The letter raises a measurement worry rather than disputing the direction.

A written prescription, Pedaballe notes, is not a filled one. Finerenone has no generic, and 77.3 percent of new users in the study sat on Medicare, where specialty copays, especially inside the coverage gap, can stall pickup. Linked pharmacy data for other cardiometabolic drugs show abandonment is common. True uptake may therefore be lower still. The letter asks the authors to cross-check orders against fills to separate doctor hesitation from patient cost barriers.
pmc-13292759:
Joshua M. Lyte joins a large expert group in a 2026 guide on best practice for gut microbe studies in poultry. The guide focuses on 16S rRNA gene sequencing, a common way to profile bacteria in the chicken gut.

Rather than force one fixed protocol, the authors set out shared steps for study design, DNA extraction, sequencing, analysis, and reporting. They stress proper positive and negative controls and fuller reporting so results can be compared across labs. Experts from universities, industry, and government wrote the guide together. It serves as a checklist meant to make poultry microbe findings more consistent and easier to repeat.
pmc-13293559:
Subhas Chandra Debnath and co-authors present three children treated for a rare blood vessel tumor growing inside the lower jaw, in a 2026 case series. These intraosseous hemangiomas account for under one percent of bone tumors and are seldom seen in young patients. Because they mimic tooth-related cysts and tumors, they are often misread, and cutting into one unprepared can trigger dangerous bleeding.

The patients, aged nine to fourteen, each had painless jaw swelling and facial asymmetry. Imaging varied from a classic sunburst pattern to hollow or destructive lesions, so needle aspiration and angiographic scans were used to reveal the vascular nature of each growth. All three underwent removal of the affected jaw segment with vessel control and reconstruction, and tissue study confirmed the diagnosis in every case.
pmc-13293659:
Nicolò Ricciardi and colleagues track, in a 2026 rat study, how a high-fat diet over 20 weeks harms both body metabolism and behavior. How thinking and mood worsen as metabolic syndrome builds, and which body signals drive each change, was still unclear.

Rats on the diet developed steady metabolic strain plus worse anxiety-like behavior and memory, each on its own timeline. Statistical modeling tied behavior shifts to fat burden, oxidative stress, leptin signaling, and ketone control acting together. Leptin signals linked most to mood changes, while redox imbalance linked most to memory loss. Thinking problems thus sit inside the syndrome itself, the authors argue.
pmc-13294159:
BKM Firmke and colleagues map an oxygen-sensing pathway in kidneys for a 2026 study. Beyond the classic hypoxia factor route, the ADO-RGS pathway tunes G-protein signals by oxygen level. Kidneys suffer easily from low oxygen, a driver of chronic disease, yet cell-by-cell maps were missing. Gene signals were charted in mouse kidneys under normal oxygen, low oxygen, and scarring, then compared with human biopsies.

The ADO enzyme stayed even across regions and states. Its RGS partners shifted sharply: Rgs4 rose in fibroblasts during anemia and scarring, Rgs5 rose in vessels and medullary fibroblasts under low oxygen, and Rgs16 marked interstitial cells in scarred tissue. Human samples echoed the split.
pmc-13294459:
Min Wei and a large team report a rare neck infection found by broad DNA sequencing in a 2026 case. A newly diagnosed person with HIV arrived with repeated pus-forming neck lymph node swelling as the first illness sign. Standard germ hunts often miss non-tuberculous mycobacteria, and Mycobacterium porcinum had almost never been tied to this picture in HIV care.

pmc-13295159:
Yu Gu and colleagues test a blood protein on airway cells in a 2026 laboratory study. Beta-2 microglobulin had already been tied by the team to emphysema through cell ageing. Whether it also disrupts the energy factories of bronchial cells, called mitochondria, was the open question.

Human bronchial cells were exposed for 48 hours to the protein or to cigarette smoke extract. Both treatments raised ageing markers, lowered mitochondrial voltage, and cut energy production while reactive oxygen climbed. Cells also grew more slowly and died more often. The pattern supports a role for the protein in airway ageing, pending animal and mechanism work.
pmc-13295759:
Jamini Bhagu and colleagues image stroke recovery by sex in a 2026 study. Stroke plays out differently in females and males, and stem cell vesicles grown in three-dimensional clusters may aid repair. Whether benefit differs by sex, tracked inside the living brain, needed testing with very strong scanners.

Labelled vesicles or salt water were delivered at vessel reopening in a temporary blockage model. Scans at extremely high field followed tissue, sodium, diffusion, and chemical changes over 21 days. Vesicle treatment trended toward smaller lesions, earlier sodium balance, and steadier brain chemicals, with females recovering somewhat better. Behaviour gaps stayed unclear.
pmc-13295959:
Ming Yi and colleagues reflect, in 2026, on a drug class that blocks PD-L1 while also trapping TGF-beta, a signal that shields tumours from immunity. An earlier drug of this kind gave mixed results, yet a newer one, retlirafusp alfa, won approval in China for stomach cancer.

The authors argue suppression by TGF-beta sits in pockets of tumour tissue and is not always the main barrier, even when PD-L1 is present. Success in one defined setting shows the approach can work when biology fits. They recommend patient selection by markers and trial measures that test the mechanism directly.
pmc-13296059:
Ultra-fast radiation in fruit flies is tested in 2026 by Marvin Kreuzer and co-authors as a stand-in for studying the FLASH effect, where rapid dosing spares healthy tissue. A clinical accelerator was adapted to deliver electron beams at thousands of times the usual rate to adult female flies.

Flies given single high ultra-fast doses lived longer than those given standard-rate doses, and split ultra-fast doses helped further. Standard dosing at a lower level caused climbing problems that ultra-fast dosing did not. Signs of a damaging cell process appeared in brains only after standard dosing. The authors promote flies as a handy model for this puzzle.
pmc-13296159:
Omar Alhumaidan, Ali Almajwal and Mohammed Alsaif update, in 2026, reference values for daily energy needs in Saudi Arabia. Older figures leaned on general equations and tended to overshoot, so the team rebuild estimates from Saudi body data, activity patterns and measured child energy use.

Infant needs rise across the first year, and children's needs climb steeply with age. For adults at current activity levels, the average requirement lands near 2,207 kilocalories daily for men and 1,708 kilocalories for women, rising sharply if activity grows. The authors offer the values as firmer ground for national food guidance.
pmc-13296859:
Lihong Shi and colleagues weave, in 2026, health communication tasks into basic medical courses for forty-two junior students in China. Students often undervalue pre-clinical science, so the team set structured talking tasks, collected written reflections and interviewed fifteen community members about the students' manner.

Reflections grouped into six themes, from clinical communication thinking to taking responsibility for public understanding. Community members rated the students clear and professional, and some planned to change health habits after talking with them. The authors suggest the blend boosts respect for basic science and speaking skills, while urging measured follow-up study.
pmc-13298859:
Maria Tziastoudi and colleagues study a gene variant's link to diabetic kidney disease through a Greek case-control study plus meta-analysis, in a 2026 genetics paper. The AKR1B1 gene has been tied to high-glucose kidney damage. Five variants were typed in patients with nephropathy, diabetic patients without it, and healthy controls.

The Greek cohort alone showed no significant association for any variant. Pooling published studies changed the picture: one promoter variant linked to nephropathy when compared against diabetic controls, and a repeat variant mattered in Asian and type 2 subgroups. The authors argue control choice shapes conclusions, and the gene may influence progression rather than diabetes itself.
pmc-13299059:
Blood and tumor tissue tell different microRNA stories in early ovarian cancer, yet the plots converge, find Shuya Cai and co-authors in a 2026 database study. Mining public gene expression collections, they compared microRNA profiles from serum and from tissue in early-stage disease.

No core microRNAs overlapped between the two compartments: serum signals mostly rose while tissue signals mostly fell. Still, their target genes funneled into the same machinery, chiefly the cell cycle and PI3K-Akt signaling. The authors argue serum microRNAs are not mere leakage from tumors but may be deliberately packaged into exosomes, which would make blood tests a faithful window for early detection.
pmc-13299459:
Hamid Mostafavi Abdolmaleky and others test whether lactate-driven acidity in the brain switches on a gene network seen in schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, in a 2026 study. Postmortem brains in both states show lactate build-up, lower pH, and raised TGFB2 expression. Stem-cell-derived neurons, astrocytes, and brain organoids were exposed to acid or alkaline shifts.

Most dysregulated genes in the patient data moved opposite to brain pH alongside TGFB2. Lactic acid raised TGFB2 expression and loosened its promoter methylation in astrocytes and organoids, while alkaline treatments did the reverse. The authors propose targeting lactate build-up or excess TGFB2 as a therapeutic direction.
pmc-13299659:
Qing-Ming Shi and others measure insecticide resistance in dengue-carrying mosquitoes from five areas of Yunnan Province, China, using samples from 2015 and 2016, reported in 2026. Larval and adult tests confirmed middling to high resistance to beta-cypermethrin everywhere. Biochemical and gene assays hunted the mechanisms behind it.

A single target-site mutation in the sodium channel gene appeared, and its share rose with resistance levels. Amounts of a detoxifying enzyme family also ran high and tracked resistance. Jointly, mutation plus metabolic change explain the pyrethroid resistance. The authors offer the data as a baseline backing steady checks and smarter vector control.
pmc-13299859:
Yu Guo and colleagues compare gut microbes in eri silkworm larvae switched between two food plants, in a 2026 insect study. The silkworm is an economically important species that eats many plants, and gut bacteria may help it adjust. Larvae fed tree-of-heaven leaves grew worse than castor-fed larvae and showed lower digestive enzyme activity in the midgut.

Short-term diet switching significantly reshaped bacterial richness, diversity, community makeup, and predicted microbial functions. One bacterial genus tracked larval weight closely. The authors conclude quick diet change alters both growth and gut community together, which matters for rearing this commercial insect on alternative host plants.
pmc-13299959:
L Jung and colleagues measure stroke risk after new atrial fibrillation appears in dialysis patients, using nationwide Korean insurance claims, reported in 2026. More than one hundred fifty thousand adults starting maintenance haemodialysis were followed, and a matched comparison balanced patients who developed the rhythm disorder against those who did not. A landmark design reduced early event bias.

New fibrillation carried a significantly higher stroke risk after matching. Annual stroke risk among affected patients averaged in the mid single digits and climbed steeply with a standard risk score, reaching the highest band at top scores. The authors stress individual risk assessment and prevention in this fragile population.
pmc-13300059:
Six genes tied to inflammation may help flag osteoarthritis, according to a 2026 computational study led by Xueya Lv. The team merged three public cartilage gene-expression datasets and corrected for batch effects before hunting for genes that separate diseased from healthy tissue. Single-cell data then checked where the candidate genes are active.

Fifty-eight genes differed between groups, mostly turned down, and six hub genes formed a diagnostic model with fair accuracy. Virtual knockouts of five hubs disturbed IL-17, NF-κB, and chemokine pathways, pointing to a shared inflammatory core. Clustering also split patients into two subtypes with different stress-response activity. The signature could guide diagnosis and future drug studies.
pmc-13300559:
Fixed spray zones only work if biting midges keep returning to the same spots, and Aaron M. Lloyd and colleagues tested that hope on a Florida residential island in a 2026 study. Trap records for Culicoides furens were checked across seasons and years for stable hot spots that control crews could target.

Catches swung widely with season and site, but no hot spot stayed fixed across years. Numbers also fell steeply from 2005 to 2007. Weather and the time of year predicted abundance better than closeness to larval habitat. For area-wide programs, the authors conclude, chasing fixed target zones is a weak strategy under Florida's legal and budget limits.
pmc-13300859:
Masaaki Akai and co-authors review low dose chemotherapy before surgery for advanced stomach and junction cancers in a 2026 retrospective study. Their regimen paired the oral drug combination S-1 with a reduced oxaliplatin dose, aiming to shrink tumors enough for complete removal in mostly elderly patients. Thirty-four patients with a median age of seventy-four went on to stomach surgery with full lymph node clearance at one center.

Complete, margin free resection was achieved in about eighty-five percent of cases, and the cancer vanished entirely under the microscope in about twenty-one percent. Nerve damage in the limbs was the commonest side effect, yet no severe grade four toxicities appeared, and serious surgical complications stayed under nine percent with no treatment related deaths. Three-year survival figures were strong for this population. The authors call the gentler dosing promising and ask for prospective trials to refine it.
pmc-13300959:
Elite water polo builds different bodies for different jobs, Milivoj Dopsaj and colleagues confirm in a 2026 study of seventy-two national-team men. Players from Serbia, Croatia, Greece, and Italy, all veterans of Olympics or world and European championships, underwent multichannel bioimpedance scanning. Ten body-structure variables were compared across playing positions.

The analysis found clear positional differences, with an effect that explained about forty percent of the variation. Body mass and body fat drove the split most strongly, with body mass index close behind. Because fat aids buoyancy while muscle powers grappling and shooting, the authors advise selectors and coaches to match recruits to position-specific profiles and to plan food and training around them.
pmc-13301159:
Y Matsuda and co-authors report long term outcomes of subcutaneous defibrillators in patients with inherited rhythm diseases, in a 2026 retrospective study. The cohort held 201 patients implanted between 2009 and 2024 at one hospital, with a mean age of forty. It spanned hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, Brugada syndrome, long QT syndrome, and a DPP6 mutation group.

Across a median follow-up near eight years, device complications touched about twenty-one percent of patients at similar rates in every disease group. Dangerous ventricular rhythms appeared in about nineteen percent, yet freedom from them differed significantly by diagnosis. The DPP6 group fared best, while the two cardiomyopathy groups carried roughly double the risk in adjusted models. Inappropriate therapy hit about seventeen percent, also varying by disease, and a wider QRS at implant predicted it. Seven patients died. The authors argue disease type, not the device, drives the long term story.
pmc-13301459:

The series covered 296 people, ninety-four with defibrillators and 202 with pacemakers, who died outside hospital and came to autopsy at eight forensic departments. Emergency reports, autopsy protocols, and device interrogations were combined to reconstruct what the heart did at the end.

A ventricular rhythm showed up in 124 patients, about forty-two percent, and more often in defibrillator carriers than pacemaker carriers, fifty-three against thirty-nine percent. Judges rated the arrhythmia the primary cause of death in about three quarters of those cases. Among defibrillator patients whose devices fought the rhythm, half degenerated into pulseless activity or standstill, and half never achieved termination. The authors attribute those failures to end stage muscle failure with no reserve left, rather than device malfunction, a limit on what implants can prevent.
pmc-13301759:
Jie Yuan and co-authors present a 2026 pot experiment on sweet potato seedlings treated with a helpful root fungus called Glomus intraradices. Such fungi live inside plant roots and trade nutrients with their hosts. The team asked whether adding the fungus would change seedling growth, nutrient uptake, root chemistry, and the bacteria living around and inside roots.

Treated seedlings gained more fresh and dry weight, took up more potassium, and stored more starch and soluble sugars. Soil near the roots held more organic matter and showed lower salt conductivity, while root chemistry shifted across hundreds of measured compounds. Bacterial groups also shifted, with certain genera becoming more common inside roots. Growers interested in cutting fertilizer use may find the potassium results especially useful.
pmc-13303659:
Aline Miranda de Vasconcelos heads a 2026 systematic review of mild electrical stimulation of the scalp and its effects on recognizing faces. Face recognition underpins daily social life, but study results in this area have stayed scattered.

Following PRISMA guidance, the team screened 261 records and kept 28 studies covering many stimulation types and groups. Stimulating vision and face areas at the back and side of the head helped in some tasks, but results clashed across studies. Small, narrow samples and wide differences in settings, tasks, and measures blocked firm conclusions. Tighter designs and clearer reporting are urged.
pmc-13303759:
Lukas Lütje and colleagues study donor brain tissue in multiple sclerosis in a 2026 pathology report. The illness varies greatly between people in damage patterns, course, and severity, and inherited factors may explain part of that spread.

Tissue from 287 donors in the Netherlands Brain Bank cohort was scored for vessel cuffs, immune cell clusters, wide-rim lesions, and repair quality. Vessel cuffs and immune clusters appeared more often in carriers of a known risk gene variant. Wide-rim lesions tied to more active damage and higher severity scores. Poor repair linked to other clinical features, helping place each donor's disease in context.
pmc-13305159:
Wendi Xu and colleagues build a light-sensing security device from a tin telluride memory cell in a 2026 study. Hardware fingerprints based on built-in randomness resist copying, yet merging secrecy with brain-like recognition in one device is hard.

The layered cell switched resistance reliably and held states for a long span, while also mimicking learning-like memory behaviors. Under light it produced jittery currents that differ from device to device by nature. Those random values became encryption keys that scrambled images, and a matching memory network read the scrambled images with high accuracy after training.
pmc-13306159:
Mirta Milić compared two slimming diets for DNA damage in adults with severe obesity in a 2026 intervention study. Fifty-three people with body mass index at or above 35.0 kg/m2 took part over three weeks.

One group ate about 600 kcal per day under hospital watch, while the other followed 1500 kcal per day at home in the reported design. Blood cell tests before and after measured fresh, oxidative and lasting DNA harm using comet and cell-block methods. The study tests whether faster energy cuts protect the genome or add stress in the short term.
pmc-13306359:
Wei Pan moved two disease resistance genes from a wild wheat ancestor into bread wheat in a 2026 breeding study. Powdery mildew and stripe rust threaten harvests worldwide, and heavy reliance on few resistance genes invites breakdown.

Three wild accessions showed strong resistance to both diseases, carrying gene forms named Pm60, Pm60b and YrU1 in marker checks. Durum hybrids acted as bridges, and repeated crossing with marker guidance produced lines holding single genes or both together. Offspring patterns confirmed the genes still worked in the new background, widening the defence pool for growers.
pmc-13306559:
Tatiana-Maria Coman and colleagues describe in 2026 the staged treatment of a twenty-one-year-old woman with severe skeletal Class II malocclusion. Her problems combined a set-back lower jaw, excess upper jaw height, gum damage, missing back teeth, and jaw joint symptoms. Specialists from orthodontics, surgery, periodontics, and prosthetics sequenced the work.

Care began with a bite splint and orthodontic preparation, then two-jaw surgery using a three-piece upper jaw cut and a lower jaw split procedure. Aligners refined the bite afterwards, while gum grafting and guided bone growth prepared sites for implants. Four years on, root coverage was complete and the skeletal correction held. Implants had integrated well, with function and appearance maintained. The case illustrates how precise planning across specialties handles problems no single field could solve alone.
pmc-13306759:
Jiajun Chen retuned a YOLO detector for tiny objects seen from drones in a 2026 study. Top-down views shrink targets, pack them densely and hide them behind clutter, so standard detectors miss many and place boxes poorly.

The ADA-YOLO design keeps the YOLOv8 backbone but rebuilds the neck and head around a high-resolution P2 branch spanning four scales. A light dynamic upsampler replaces fixed steps, and adaptive fusion calms clashes between scales in reported design goals. The authors present the combined changes as a sharper tool for traffic, farming and rescue flights.
pmc-13307159:
Basma Mostafa routed safety data in battered industrial sensor networks with fuzzy federated learning in a 2026 study. Disaster settings need critical packets favoured without central control, even as edge nodes drop out.

A fuzzy system labels packet criticality in readable rules from sensor readings, while averaging counts only reachable nodes during training. Low-confidence answers fall back to the fuzzy classifier under an auditable rule that guards against under-ranking danger. Tests on grid networks to 200 nodes at fault rates to 50% reached 99.00% critical recall in reported results. The design keeps a clear audit trail, a key need when safety calls are later checked.
pmc-13308059:
Michal Babják and colleagues test on a goat farm in 2026 whether fasting can rescue a failing worm drug. The flock's barber's pole worms already resist benzimidazole medicines, leaving few treatment options. Groups of goats received albendazole under different fasting and dose arrangements, including a twenty-four-hour fast after dosing.

The clearest gain appeared in goats fasted for a full day after receiving the drug. Slowing gut passage keeps the medicine available to the host longer, which raises its effective exposure. Raising the dose also formed part of the farm-level strategy the team examined. New drug classes are unavailable locally, so squeezing more from old ones matters commercially. The authors propose controlled fasting plus dose optimisation as a practical resistance management tool. Their findings come from real farm conditions rather than a laboratory model, which strengthens the advice.
pmc-13308459:
Tukisho Mphahlele, Thendo Gertie Makhado, and Lufuno Makhado lay out in 2026 a plan to pool studies on how HIV control shapes outcomes for rifampicin resistant tuberculosis. Their protocol follows standard rules for such reviews and spans papers and grey sources from January 2005 to December 2025.

Pairs of reviewers will screen, extract, and grade each study, with a third voice to settle clashes on close calls. Outcomes span cure, failure, death, and harms, split by virus control, CD4 based immune state, and drug resistance in HIV care. Merged proof could guide joint care for people who carry both infections in high burden lands. No results are claimed yet, as the plan comes first.
pmc-13308859:
Andrea Lo Sasso and co-authors explore in 2026 whether breath tests plus explainable artificial intelligence can flag lung cancer and gut or lung ills early, with no needle or cut. They used open data from three sets, fixed skewed class counts, and checked which breath chemicals drove each best model.

Breath holds volatile chemicals that mirror body state, and pattern tools can sort sick from well on those traces in past work. Open scoring of each chemical weight lets doctors see why a model calls a case as it does. Sample swings, weak sensors, and loose standards still block clinic use today. The frame still gives a sound base for breath based test work ahead.
pmc-13308959:
Christian Werner and a large German team report in 2026 on a home exercise programme for older adults with cognitive impairment after hospital rehabilitation. It briefly improved real walking quality, but not walking quantity. One hundred four participants, averaging eighty-two years, were randomised after discharge. Half received exercise plus activity promotion; half received a placebo motor programme.

Body-worn sensors captured real-world walking for two days at each check point. After twelve weeks, the exercise group walked with longer bouts, faster speed, and longer strides in short walks. None of the gains survived the twelve-week follow-up, and total walking amount never differed between groups. Behaviour techniques accompanied the exercises, yet habits did not stick once support ended. The authors suggest digital walking measures reveal quality changes that clinic tests miss, while lasting change needs longer support.
pmc-13309359:
Sameh Abolfotouh and co-authors survey in 2026 spine surgeons worldwide on nerve watch use during surgery, its pull, and its blocks. Their web poll of AO Spine members ran in April and May 2025. A total of 529 surgeons replied, and 55.5 percent said they can always get the watch, while 8.8 percent said they never can.

Outside firms supply the watch most often, at 59.5 percent, and techs read the traces in 63.6 percent of shops that replied. Most surgeons, 76.3 percent, run a set check list when a signal drops mid case. Cost blocks lead the complaints, at 38.2 percent, ahead of supply snags and thin training. Views ran warm overall in the poll.
pmc-13310559:
PengKun Yu and co-authors assess a modified overlapping stitch for frayed Achilles tendon tears in a 2026 study. Some tears split the tendon into strands like a horse tail, which standard repair handles poorly. The overlapping technique layers the strands before stitching to restore tendon length and strength.

Records for 57 patients treated between May 2020 and May 2024 were reviewed, with follow-up averaging within two years. Standard ankle scores rose sharply after surgery, and the top outcome grade rate reached 98.2 percent in the reported scoring. Complications stayed few: one slow wound healing, two re-tears after falls, and no nerve injury. The authors back the technique for this tear pattern.
pmc-13310659:
Emmanuel Asante-Asamani and co-authors test blood RNA markers to sharpen prostate cancer detection in a 2026 study. The standard PSA blood test flags many harmless cases and was weakly validated in men of African ancestry, who bear the highest disease burden. RNA pieces from the PVT1 gene run high in prostate tumors and may add signal.

Serum from 144 men with raised PSA who faced biopsy was tested for three PVT1 segments, alone and joined with PSA. Statistical models weighed added detection value and risk sorting, with cross-checks for overfitting. The study is the first serum test of these segments in this setting. The authors frame combined markers as a route to fewer needless biopsies, above all in high-burden groups.
pmc-13310759:
David Mhlanga reviews how artificial intelligence could improve public services and governance in Africa in a 2026 study. Many governments face weak systems, fast population growth, and split record keeping, which slow fair service delivery. Digital tools and growing data stores open new paths, but gains depend on strong oversight.

Work draws on a structured review of past studies across welfare, health care, tax, and city services. Smart tools can sharpen targeting, cut waste, and support choices made ahead of need. Gains hinge on data supply, tool skill, office capacity, and human checks. Weak systems can spread bias and exclusion, so plans must fit local needs.
pmc-13310859:
Eman A Mady led a 2026 mouse study on how mother pup separation changes breast milk and pup brain signals. Early life stress can shape later health, yet the paths that carry stress from mother to pup are unclear. Milk is a prime suspect, since it feeds both body and gut germs.

Separated mothers had higher levels of a milk fat called myristic acid. Their pups had fewer helpful gut germs, lower inosine in gut and blood, and lower serotonin gene activity in the front brain. Feeding pups the milk fat alone cut the helpful germ count. Links tie milk change to gut and brain shifts.
pmc-13310959:
Maria Cristina Robin and colleagues describe 19 patients with acid sphingomyelinase deficiency in Argentina in a 2026 case series. The rare storage disease stems from gene faults that block fat breakdown, so fat builds up in many organs. Signs vary by type and age, and diagnosis often comes late.

Cases came from seven centers for diagnoses made from 1988 to 2022. All patients had enlarged liver and spleen, and most had anemia, lung involvement, and low platelet counts. Mean delay from first signs to diagnosis was 7.5 years in length, and two patients were first misread as Gaucher disease. Broader awareness may cut delay.
pmc-13311459:
Kyle T Enriquez and co-authors describe a 2026 case study in which a generative AI tool helped draft a lung transplant infection prevention protocol. The team asked Microsoft Copilot to build a cytomegalovirus prophylaxis plan using only PubMed-indexed sources. They also had the tool model costs across four protocols, including its own. The cost models used simulated patients drawn from a real 165-patient cohort at Vanderbilt University Medical Center.

The AI-drafted protocol rested on genuine evidence with no invented sources. It leaned on older guidance, though, and raised expected cost by an average of 4,740 dollars per patient over current guideline-based plans. The tool also ran its own sensitivity analyses. Those pointed to the drug letermovir as a major cost driver in the model. The authors conclude that, with expert oversight, such tools can support the economic homework stewardship programs often lack staff to do.
pmc-13311659:
Nanuka Jalaghonia, Rumana Huque, and David Daniels wrote a 2026 commentary drawn from the eighth Global Symposium on Health Systems Research. Their question is whether new tools, digital ones and AI, can help health systems in disaster-prone places withstand shocks without leaving more people behind. Such places face repeated climate events, outbreaks, and waves of people forced from their homes, all of which interrupt care.

Talks described digital dashboards, linked data systems, AI decision aids, and local projects that improved detection and kept care going during crises. Such tools can make neglected groups visible to planners. Yet the authors warn that technology alone guarantees nothing. Tools built on data that miss whole groups, or run under weak rules, can widen exclusion instead. They argue new tools pay off only when agencies are ready, rules are clear, safeguards are real, and local people help design what gets built.
pmc-13311959:
Stefan Steiner and colleagues present their 2026 study on a new eye measure, retinal nerve fiber layer thickness slope, and its link to visual field sensitivity in early glaucoma. The slope reads how fast the fiber layer thins along its paths.

The study compared 50 early glaucoma eyes with 139 healthy eyes using wide-field scans that trace fiber routes to field test points. Glaucoma eyes showed lower sensitivity and shallower slopes in both halves of the field. Point-by-point links between slope and sensitivity reached moderate strength, strongest in the upper field near the center. The measure may sharpen early glaucoma detection.
pmc-13312159:
Akinbode Okunola, Elliott Dennis, and Matthew Hille build, in a 2026 paper, a One Health Score for judging how countries regulate medically important antimicrobials. Their framework merges the World Health Organization's importance rankings for human medicine with the animal health rankings of the World Organization for Animal Health. Human health gets the priority seat. Countries are then scored on whether their drug residue limits in food match international Codex standards.

Codex, the European Union, and the United States emerge as the reference points most other countries follow. Just over half of classified drug pairings joined the highly important human category with the top veterinary category. Among those pairings, 21 percent of countries set limits looser than Codex allows. Heavily used farm drugs are regulated most often. Some drugs vital for human care but rare on farms escape attention. The authors frame residue policy as a balance between farm economics and resistance control.
pmc-13312259:
Nadia L. Farag and colleagues report a 2026 chemistry study testing phenothiazine dyes as the positive-side liquids, or catholytes, in aqueous organic redox flow batteries. Such batteries could store grid energy cheaply, but organic catholytes often dissolve poorly and break down, so the team screened dyes already sold commercially for a workable candidate.

Azure-A performed best, and adding nicotinamide as a helper compound raised both its solubility and cycle life. Even so, only about half the expected charge capacity could be reached. Spectroscopy showed the active molecules pair up into dimers above a low concentration, leaving the dye effectively able to move just one electron in practice. Impedance analysis pointed to a further loss route: material polymerizing and coating the electrode. The authors map both limits for future dye design.
pmc-13312359:
Ruixin Mao and co-authors study, in a 2026 cross-sectional survey, how problematic smartphone use relates to mental health among Chinese senior high school students. The team surveyed 34,831 students in grades 10 to 12 in Tianmen, measuring phone habits, emotional growth mindset, well-being, and depressive symptoms under a dual-factor view of mental health.

Latent profile analysis sorted students into four groups, from very low depression with high well-being to high depression with low well-being. Heavy phone use was tied directly to poorer mental health, and also indirectly through a weaker belief that emotions can change and be managed. Having been left behind by migrant parents strengthened the first link in that chain. The authors argue that cutting screen time alone will not fix the risk for such students.
pmc-13312459:
F.J. Bruning and colleagues track, in a 2026 longitudinal study, how everyday walking recovers after total knee replacement. Surgery aims to restore mobility in end-stage knee osteoarthritis, but most follow-up relies on self-report rather than measured walking. Thirty-one patients wore inertial sensors before surgery and one and two years afterward, and their walking was compared with 31 healthy participants without joint pain.

One year after surgery, the patients' daily-life gait speed still sat 0.10 meters per second below the healthy group's, though it had improved by the same margin from before the operation. Stride length and stride timing also improved, while the longest walking bouts did not, and nothing further changed by year two. The authors judge the remaining gap minor and the gains modest, partly because these patients were already fairly functional before surgery.
pmc-13312759:
Sara Henricsson and colleagues explore, in a 2026 qualitative study, how older adults judge the faces and teeth of people their own age. Faces and dental appearance steer first impressions at every age, yet how seniors read those features in their peers, rather than in the young, had barely been asked.

The team interviewed 20 adults aged 68 to 76 drawn from a Swedish aging study and analyzed the conversations thematically. Three themes emerged. Charisma and personality could overshadow appearance entirely, warmth and expression mattering more than any feature. At the same time, judging by looks came easily: missing teeth or visibly poor oral health triggered assumptions about lifestyle, vulnerability, and self-care. Participants also expected peers to follow age-appropriate norms. The authors show peer judgment balancing kindness against quiet social rules.
pmc-13312959:
Eleanor V Thomas and Devesh C Pant write a 2026 scientific commentary on a blood biomarker study in motor neuron disease, the family that includes amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. The disease is devastating, patchy in presentation, and slow to diagnose. Progress has been blocked by the lack of easy, trustworthy blood markers that mirror its biology, since most discovery work relied on spinal fluid.

The commented study used an ultrasensitive multiplex platform to profile serum from 48 patients in the Scottish register and 38 controls, checking findings against a second assay. Neurofilament light chain stayed the single best marker, with diagnostic accuracy near 0.92 on the reported scale, but the wider protein signature around it captured more of the disease's variety. The commentators argue such multidimensional blood panels could speed diagnosis, sort patients by biology, and sharpen trial monitoring.
pmc-13313259:
Salar Saadi Hussain and Zahra Abdulqader Amin present a 2026 gene study of endometrial cancer in Kurdish women. Cancer of the womb lining varies widely, with many gene and gene-control changes, and data from this group of women were thin.

The study drew on 70 confirmed cases and tested DNA from blood. Nine cases picked for young onset or a family pattern of cancer got full exome sequencing, built through capture with tagged probes. Five variants of note turned up in five genes: CHEK2, POLE, MUTYH, USF3, and PLA2G2A. They included a missing amino acid in CHEK2, a double copy change in MUTYH, and single changes in the other three genes. The finds give a first map of inherited risk in this group and hint at which women may gain from gene screening.
pmc-13313559:
Hideyoshi Kaga and colleagues pinpoint, in a 2026 imaging study, where in the brain insulin resistance lives in type 2 diabetes. Brain insulin helps regulate appetite and body-wide glucose, and the hypothalamus is its control hub, but which of its nuclei fail was unknown. Using high-resolution functional MRI while volunteers inhaled insulin through the nose, the team compared 21 Japanese men with diabetes against 20 healthy controls.

In healthy men, insulin quieted activity in the posterior hypothalamic nucleus within five minutes. In the men with diabetes, that early suppression simply did not happen, marking a local failure of insulin responsiveness. Structural scans in a separate older group found the same posterior region shrunken in diabetic participants. Two independent methods thus converge on one small brain area. The authors propose the posterior hypothalamus as a candidate seat of brain insulin resistance, to be tested in longer and interventional studies.
pmc-13313759:
Fangfang Wang, Fengmei Ge, and Xuebin Wang present a 2026 case report, with literature review, of organizing pneumonia that returned nine years after its appearance alongside rheumatoid arthritis. Their patient, a 65-year-old woman, arrived with painful joints and recurring fever. Lung imaging showed right-sided inflammation that antibiotics failed to touch. A lung biopsy established the condition, a pattern of lung injury that is an uncommon companion to rheumatoid arthritis.

Steroid treatment with a taper, combined with the arthritis drug iguratimod, settled her fever and cough. Follow-up scans improved while her arthritis stayed quiet on maintenance therapy. Nine years later, fever and cough returned with pneumonia in both lungs. A second biopsy through an airway scope confirmed the pattern had relapsed, even though arthritis activity remained low. The authors stress that tissue diagnosis is key in such cases, since infection treatment alone would have missed the process twice.
pmc-13314759:
Habib Md Ahashan and a large surveillance team chart, in a 2026 retrospective study, three years of acute watery diarrhea at Cumilla General Hospital in Bangladesh, from 2022 to 2024. The condition floods hospitals seasonally and can signal cholera, so the team mined routine surveillance records across all ages to find who arrives, when, and with what pre-treatment history.

The burden fell heaviest on children under five, who made up most cases. Only about five percent of tested cases proved positive for cholera on rapid tests, and limited culture capacity left the true cholera share uncertain. A striking practice pattern stood out: ninety percent of patients had already taken antibiotics before reaching the hospital, a habit that feeds resistance while rarely matching the actual cause. Case loads peaked in the monsoon and post-monsoon periods. The authors argue for stronger laboratory confirmation and tighter antibiotic discipline in diarrhea care.
pmc-13315659:
Jérôme Martineau and colleagues describe, in a 2026 case report, a patient's own skin used to reinforce an abdominal wall separation. Severe rectus diastasis with ventral hernia is usually reinforced with mesh, but plastic material carries infection risk. Skin harvested during tummy surgery offers a biologic alternative. Their patient, a 36-year-old woman after three pregnancies, had a separation, 15 centimeters during surgery and 19 on CT, plus a navel hernia and skin excess.

She underwent tummy surgery with an own-tissue graft placed beneath the fascia to reinforce the repair. One week after surgery, navel necrosis required cleaning and local-flap repair, after which recovery went smoothly. At one year, no return of the defect showed on exam or ultrasound, and the patient reported functional and aesthetic satisfaction. The authors present the technique as durable even for large defects, and note the absent mesh proved advantageous when necrosis struck.
pmc-13315959:
Ruihao Lan and colleagues added polydopamine in stages in 2026 to help lab-grown lung alveolar organoids from human stem cells mature. Such organoids model lung growth and disease and speed drug hunting, yet full maturity is hard to reach, and the mussel-inspired material offers sticky, antioxidant help.

A polydopamine coating first produced more early foregut spheroids by strengthening contact between the gel and the surface, with gene data showing richer cell and matrix interaction. Later, polydopamine nanoparticles mixed into the gel at the lung progenitor stage cut harmful reactive oxygen. The timed, two-step use matched each growth stage.
pmc-13316159:
Wolfgang Trapp, Susanne Röder, and Franziska Wimmer ran a proof-of-concept study in 2026 on a playful phone app that helps people face phobias through inverted augmented reality. Exposure therapy works well for phobic disorders, yet access, acceptance, and transfer to daily life hold it back.

Twenty people with varied phobias followed a multiple-baseline plan. At a random start point they used a phone AR app, or sometimes a VR headset, to collect color-coded virtual objects while moving through places tied to their own fears. Mixed model checks showed a clear drop in self-reported situational fear after the game-like practice, with a large within-person effect.
pmc-13316459:
Simon Scheiter, Julia Brugger, and Thomas Hickler model, in a 2026 study, how stable the world's plant zones stayed through the Quaternary, the last 2.6 million years of ice age swings. They test whether long-stable zones explain why some places hold so many plant species today.

A machine learning model learned today's zone map from climate, then ran backward in thousand-year steps across the full period. Tropical forests, deserts, and boreal and temperate woods stayed put over wide areas, while northern Europe and North America churned as ice came and went. Stable zones matched rich plant life in tropical rainforests, but the global link stayed weak. Fire and local variety, they suggest, must share the credit.
pmc-13316759:
Yuanxia Wang and a team of Chinese researchers compared, in a 2026 study, mulberry wine made from whole pulp against wine made from juice alone, tracking quality through brewing and storage. Mulberries spoil fast, so wine making is a key route to value, and the starting form may shape the result.

Yeast brewing lifted antioxidant power to a 90 percent radical clearing rate in their tests, and pulp wine kept more of the fruit's phenolics and color compounds. Sixty-three scent compounds were found, with pulp adding herbal notes thanks to stem pieces. During storage, pulp wine's good compounds faded more slowly, while scent alcohols and esters dropped after 25 days in both. Pulp brewing, they conclude, preserves more of the fruit.
pmc-13316859:
Diala Bani Mustafa and colleagues introduce, in 2026, a laser method for coating surgical mesh with an antibacterial carbon layer. Polypropylene mesh is strong and well tolerated, yet bacteria can colonise it and force removal. Coating its thin fibres and knots evenly is difficult, and heat can damage the plastic.

Their one-step process uses a laser and a toner-like donor to lay porous carbon onto the mesh without melting it. Microscopy and Raman testing confirmed continuous coverage over fibres and knots, with thickness up to about forty micrometres. Tests with Escherichia coli gave a surprising pattern, where mid-range thickness near fifteen micrometres left the fewest living bacteria. The authors present the method as a programmable coating route for three-dimensional plastics.
pmc-13318059:
Mohammad Ismail and Waleed Kattan evaluate, in 2026, whether practice resuscitation drills improved real emergency performance at a Saudi tertiary hospital.
