Mock code simulations are widely used to prepare teams, yet evidence from adult hospitals in Saudi Arabia, tied to actual Code Blue events rather than drill scores, was scarce.

The team compared 37 adult Code Blue records from 2025, before and after an in-situ simulation programme began. Return of circulation and 28-day mortality did not change significantly. Process measures improved sharply, including documentation of two-minute pulse checks, rhythm identification and giving epinephrine for non-shockable rhythms, which reached full compliance. The authors recommend keeping and expanding simulation training to strengthen team performance, while noting survival gains were not shown.
pmc-13318559:
Casey A Clarke and co-authors analyse, in 2026, video of knee ligament injuries in men's Major League Soccer in the United States and Canada. Anterior cruciate ligament tears often end seasons, yet how they happen in this league was little described. Prevention programmes need that detail.

Across five and a half seasons, 65 injuries were identified and footage existed for 33. Most injuries involved no direct contact with the knee. Defensive pressing and offensive driving were the commonest actions at injury. The knee was usually bent and collapsing inward under load. Indirect-contact injuries all involved force to the upper body. Injuries clustered in the second half or overtime, more often on grass, with two peaks across the season. Training to control knee position during pressing may help.
pmc-13318759:
Qian Wang and colleagues present a 2026 prospective ultrasound study of carotid artery plaques. New tiny vessels inside a plaque make it more likely to rupture and cause stroke. The team tested a flow turbulence measure from vector flow imaging. They asked whether it can flag those inner vessels without invasive tests.

They analysed 108 plaques, of which 82 had inner vessels on sensitive microvascular imaging. Turbulence was measured before, at, and after each plaque. The downstream value at the end of the heartbeat cycle ran lower in plaques with inner vessels. A combined model reached an AUC of 0.830 in internal checks. After correction, the figure was 0.768 in their validation. The authors propose the measure as a possible noninvasive marker.
pmc-13318859:
Hai-Ming Wang and colleagues report a 2026 laboratory study creating a monoclonal antibody against pseudorabies virus. The swine herpesvirus causes heavy losses in the pig industry. Its glycoprotein B is a conserved surface protein needed for viral entry and cell fusion. That makes it a prime target for detection tools.

The team produced the outer part of glycoprotein B from the HeN1 strain in CHO cells. Mice were immunised, and fused cells yielded an antibody named 1G4. Tests showed strong specificity and reactivity. The antibody recognised multiple virus strains broadly. Labelled with a fluorescent tag and paired with another antibody, it tracked virus entry into HeLa cells under the microscope. The authors offer it as a reagent for mechanism research and immune detection.
pmc-13320259:
Zhao Wang and co-authors build a cloaked drug particle for pre surgery care of a soft tissue cancer in a 2026 study. Fibrosarcoma grows into nearby tissue, so wide cuts can cost organ function, and return plus spread stay common after surgery. Mild heat plus immune priming before surgery may shrink the mass and wake body defenses at once.

Gene checks showed an immune alarm switch runs high in this cancer, so a particle was loaded with a switch trigger plus a light active dye. A coat made from tumor cell skin, rich in an eat me signal, steers the particle to tumors and to immune trainer cells. Near infrared light then adds mild heat and cell stress, which fires the alarm in both tumor and trainer cells.
pmc-13320459:
Basavanna C and co-authors present a large text set of classical Kannada verse for language software in a 2026 data article. Kannada is a major tongue of south India with a rich verse past, yet machine ready sets for its old works barely exist. Verses from three verse forms that span the eleventh to the twentieth century were digitized, checked by hand, and paired with scholar written readings.

The set holds 24746 verses plus 22369 readings in a shared structured form, each verse tagged by form, author, and source. Forms cover short moral songs, three line verses, and a famed twentieth century wisdom poem set. The set can train tools for meaning match, logic links, search, and text making in a low resource tongue.
pmc-13320659:
Yue Bao and co-authors describe an unusual heart tracing in a 2026 case report of a young child. After repair of a hole between the heart's lower chambers, the 3-year-old developed complete heart block plus a right bundle branch block. A pacemaker using left bundle branch pacing, a more natural method favoured in children, was fitted.

During fitting, the pacing lead touched only the surface of the wall between the chambers, without deep fixing. The tracing then showed a right bundle pattern, which the team calls rare and unlike the usual left bundle pattern seen with standard pacing. No matching cases were found in prior reports, so the note alerts pacing teams to the pattern.
pmc-13321159:
Chinedu Ogbonnia Egwu and co-authors test how mixed malaria infections respond to drugs in a 2026 laboratory study. Rising tolerance to malaria drugs threatens progress against the disease, yet natural infections often carry several parasite strains at once. The team asked whether resistant strains in a mix drive the whole response.

Fifteen Gambian field samples plus two lab strains were exposed to standard drugs at low doses, and survival and reinvasion were measured. Resistant types shifted drug response clearly, most sharply for chloroquine in mixed cultures. Field samples with resistant markers survived more and reinvaded red cells at high rates after low dose exposure. Mixed infections thus cannot be judged by their weakest strain.
pmc-13321459:
Heng Shao and colleagues study pathways from childhood trauma to self-injury in teenagers with depression in a 2026 survey. Non-suicidal self-injury is a known risk in this group, but the steps between early trauma and later self-harm were unclear. The team surveyed 2308 adolescents treated at 12 psychiatric hospitals in China.

Teenagers who self-injured scored higher on trauma, sleep disturbance, and anxiety measures than those who did not. Trauma scores tracked with self-injury severity, poor sleep, and anxiety. Mediation tests found indirect paths running through sleep disturbance and anxiety, alone and in sequence. Emotional abuse, physical abuse, sexual abuse, and physical neglect each stayed linked to self-injury severity in adjusted models.
pmc-13322559:
Julie Y. L. Chow and co-authors refine how learning models handle graded outcomes in a 2026 psychology study. Classic associative models simplify learning to yes or no outcomes, such as recovery or not, and can track only an average when real outcomes vary in size. The team built a distributed version that links cues to a spread of outcome sizes.

Across four contingency learning experiments, the distributed model fit human data better than a simple delta model for nearly every participant. Keeping the full range of experienced values, rather than a single mean, seems to match how people actually encode events. The result sharpens theories of causal learning in messy, real world settings.
pmc-13323159:
Shuai Jin and colleagues track, in 2026, how often malnutrition appears on American death records for a combined heart, kidney and metabolic syndrome. Deaths tied to that syndrome fell overall across recent decades, yet how often poor nutrition was documented among them was unclear. The team used national multiple-cause mortality files spanning 1999 to 2023.

The adjusted death rate followed a U shape, falling into the early 2010s and then climbing steeply by 2023. Malnutrition's share of these deaths roughly doubled even as the total declined. Adults over sixty-five accounted for most deaths, while documentation rose fastest among younger decedents. Rates stayed highest in Black adults, grew relatively faster in White adults, and accelerated most in the West. The authors urge routine nutritional assessment in high-burden groups.
pmc-13324459:
Chang Hyun Nam and colleagues map the genome changes behind spread in uveal melanoma, the most common primary eye cancer in adults, in a 2026 analysis. Risk tools today lean on large copy number changes and miss finer details.

Whole-genome sequencing of 40 primary tumors and matched healthy tissue catalogued losses, gains, and structural breaks. Two fresh markers stood out: hidden BAP1 damage, including truncations older tests missed, and gains on chromosome 1q. Timing work showed many gains arose early in life, decades before diagnosis. Early 6p gain often excluded BAP1 damage and meant a better outlook. Spread risk may be set early, which aids detection and prognosis.
pmc-13325359:
Naushad Ahmad Khan and co-authors grow silver dendrites and flowers on gold film with a femtosecond laser in a 2026 study. Branchy silver shapes boost Raman sensing, a method that reads molecular fingerprints from scattered light.

Focused laser pulses triggered local chemistry in silver nitrate solution at room temperature. Ascorbic acid alone yielded tree-like dendrites, while adding sodium citrate gave petal-like flowers. The citrate caps growth on flat faces, steering the plate-like bloom shapes. Sharp tips and narrow gaps in both shapes create electromagnetic hotspots. Tests with Rhodamine 6G showed far stronger signals than bare gold film. The mask-free route takes minutes and could scale for sensor making.
pmc-13325459:
Amol Keshavasa Bhandage and colleagues map blood protein signatures of a chronic nerve disease in a 2026 case-control study. Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy varies widely between patients, and blood markers for it are missing.

Panels measured 92 proteins in 358 serum samples from patients with the disease, multiple sclerosis, or treated myasthenia gravis, plus healthy controls. Seven proteins, including TNFSF14, CD40, and IL8, set the nerve disease apart from every comparison group. Six more proteins shifted with immunoglobulin therapy itself. Weakness tracked with CXCL9 and CCL20 levels, while unstable active disease ran hotter on several signals. Three proteins hinted at who would improve on treatment.
pmc-13325859:
Lisa Schellenberg and co-authors chart land-made pollutants in the coastal waters of Curaçao in a 2026 study. Drugs, pesticides, and human waste products wash from shore to sea, yet their spread around an island was unmeasured.

Sampling across three campaigns in 2021 and 2022 used extraction and untargeted mass spectrometry. About 30,000 molecular features appeared, including 1,394 land-linked pollutants that thinned with distance offshore. Wet season levels in 2022 ran 3.5 times higher than in dry periods, driven by rain and slow water turnover. Local runoff paths and nearby human activity shaped fine patterns. The survey gives the island its first island-wide baseline.
pmc-13327159:
Emma Taylor and team asked if mother-child closeness takes distinct paths in families of kids with intellectual disabilities. Their 2026 study trailed 353 main-care mums across three rounds of the 1000 Families Study over eight years. Closeness was scored at each round, and a growth mixture model hunted for path groups. Closeness may shape growth for all kids, and past work hinted at sub-groups in these families.

On average, closeness held steady over time, and the study found no firm path sub-groups. Mum distress and an autism diagnosis tended to track with less closeness, while a child's talk skills and kind social acts tracked with more closeness over time. Conduct and mood troubles showed no link. The team urges support aimed at families where kids have weaker talk or social skills, an added autism diagnosis, or mums under higher distress. Bigger long-term data sets are urged too.
pmc-13327659:
Dengzhi Zhao and co-authors lay out a stepwise gene testing plan for Duchenne muscular dystrophy in a 2026 study of ten Chinese patients. Standard first tests miss some cases because they cannot spot deep hidden changes or large rearrangements in the DMD gene. The team ran tests in tiers until each case was solved.

A probe test found copy number changes in six boys, and exome sequencing solved two more, finding one frameshift and one nonsense change. Whole-genome sequencing cracked the last two, exposing a deep intronic change that switched on a false exon piece of 58 nucleotides and a 9.4 Mb chromosome inversion with a break inside the gene. Genome-level testing thus earns a place when first rounds come back empty.
pmc-13327859:
Xian Wang and Suyun Yang test whether platelet measures forecast response to radioactive iodine in thyroid cancer in a 2026 study. They reviewed 365 patients with differentiated thyroid cancer who had their first iodine-131 treatment at one large hospital. Responses were graded by 2025 guideline rules as excellent or not excellent.

Of four platelet measures checked, mean platelet volume stood out: higher values went with lower odds of a less-than-excellent response, with an odds ratio of 0.40 after adjustment in the main model. Its forecast skill was moderate, with an AUC of 0.664 and a best cutoff at 9.95 fL in their analysis. Age and a tumor marker changed the strength of the link, the authors note.
pmc-13328259:
Zheng Sun and Fan Zhang construct a scoring system for volleyball coaches' pre-match decisions in a 2026 study. Sound tactical planning before a match lifts team performance, yet the factors shaping it had no shared map. Using expert rounds and a precedence chart method, the pair built and checked an indicator system.

Expert review covered 80.6 percent of what a fuller check later found, and the final system held four main indicators, led by the decision execution system at a weight of 0.4375 against the subject system at 0.3125 in their weighting, with nine second-level and 51 third-level items. Expert and grassroots coaches ranked factors in strong agreement, giving teams a data-based frame for gathering information and planning.
pmc-13328359:
Xiaoqian Xia and a large team pair magnetic brain stimulation with brain-computer interface training after stroke in a 2026 trial. About 40 percent of stroke patients show too weak a brain rhythm response for interface training to grip, a problem dubbed BCI illiteracy. Eighteen subacute patients were randomized to interface training alone or stimulation first.

Both groups had standard rehabilitation plus ten sessions over two weeks, and the stimulation group received theta burst pulses over the affected motor cortex before each session. Arm function gains ran larger with stimulation, and interface accuracy reached 87.22 percent against 68.24 percent in the plain group on their week-four comparison, with deeper rhythm responses over the injured side. Priming the cortex may unlock training for poor responders.
pmc-13329359:
Maarten J. M. Christenhusz and many collaborators present the genome sequence of sheep's-bit, Jasione montana, in a 2026 report. The plant is a blue-flowered herb in the bellflower family, found across Europe and north-west Africa. The work forms part of the Darwin Tree of Life project, which aims to sequence named species of Britain and Ireland.

Two genome versions were built, each about 1,282 to 1,295 megabases long in the reported assembly. Most of the first version sits in 6 chromosome-like pieces. Smaller genomes for the mitochondria and plastid were also assembled. The source plant came from Trefor in Gwynedd, Wales. The sequence gives a reference for plant evolution and diversity studies.
pmc-13330659:
A. De Luca and a large study group ask what drives breast surgery choice after chemotherapy in Italy in a 2026 report. Data covered 65,926 women treated at 26 breast centres from 2017 to 2022 through the SENONET network. Of these, 4,366 women had chemotherapy before surgery.

Breast-saving surgery followed in 46 percent of that group in the reported counts. Lower saving rates tied to younger age, spread-out disease, calcium specks, ductal growth in place, and larger or node-positive tumours. Full tumour clearance, reached by 31 percent of patients, did not raise saving rates in those results. Reconstruction after removal rose over time. Choices still rest on traits seen before treatment, the authors conclude.
pmc-13331359:
Mehmet Tatlı and Selin Bulut report pufferfish poisoning far inland in eastern Turkey in a 2026 case series. Three men came to a Van hospital in December 2020 after eating a silver-cheeked toadfish that a seller mistook for an edible type. Van sits over 1000 km from the coast in the account given.

One man aged 41 years ate the liver and fell into full paralysis with breathing failure. Despite intensive care with ventilation and strong blood pressure drugs, he died on day four from unstoppable cardiac arrest. The other two ate less and no liver, had mild signs, and recovered fully within 24 hours. Seller training and supply checks are urged.
pmc-13332359:
El Mahdi Choukri and colleagues report a 2026 CT diagnosis of a rare transverse colon twist with added small bowel and colon wall changes. Transverse colon volvulus causes mechanical bowel blockage, but bedside and plain X-ray findings are often vague, making preoperative diagnosis hard. CT scanning can pinpoint the transition point, the swirling mesentery sign, added bowel involvement, and signs that bowel is in danger. The patient was a 65-year-old man with chronic lung disease and five days of blockage symptoms.

The scan showed marked dilation of small bowel and right colon upstream from a left-sided mesenteric whirl. The twist involved the transverse colon in a bird-beak shape plus a nearby upper jejunal loop, with a displaced vein.
pmc-13332659:
Craig Basman and colleagues introduce a 2026 mini-focus issue on valvular heart disease in JACC: Case Reports. The field is entering a period of rapid progress, driven by expanding catheter-based therapies, refined multi-mode imaging, and a growing evidence base that keeps reshaping when and how to intervene. As options grow, daily cases grow more complex, often running beyond standard algorithms and demanding highly individual solutions. This issue gathers cases that show that breadth and nuance.

Cases span the outpatient clinic, the catheterization laboratory, and the operating room, capturing how catheter and surgical innovation now overlap. Readers meet scenarios where timing, imaging, and judgment matter as much as device choice. The editors stress that clinical judgment stays central even as tools advance. The issue serves clinicians who need concrete, contemporary examples of valvular disease care at its expanding boundaries.
pmc-13333259:
Andi Ade Wijaya Ramlan and colleagues test a 2026 adapted healing protocol against standard care in child major gut surgery. Care around surgery in such cases often involves prolonged fasting, delayed movement, and invasive monitoring, which may raise stress responses and slow healing. Healing pathways are well established in adults but need child adaptation. The single-blind trial with random assignment enrolled children aged two months to five years undergoing major gut surgery.

Participants were assigned by chance to a modified healing group of forty or standard care of forty-two. Outcomes included time to first oral nutrition, first movement, urinary catheter removal, hospital stay length, and intraoperative glucose and electrolyte levels. Early movement was significantly faster in the healing group. The trial gives child surgeons concrete evidence for adapting adult healing pathways to young children, where fasting and immobility carry distinct risks.
pmc-13333359:
Rachel Sayko Adams and colleagues tracked recorded alcohol use disorder diagnoses in United States insurance claims from 2016 to 2023, split by disability, in a 2026 study. Surveys hint that disabled adults who drink face higher risk, but how often clinicians actually record the diagnosis in this group was unknown.

Using MarketScan claims for commercially insured adults aged 18 to 64, the team computed yearly age-adjusted diagnosis rates per 10,000 people. The overall rate climbed steadily from 85 in 2016 to 128 in 2023, growing about 5.41 percent per year. Adults with disabilities ran more than three times the rate of those without, for both men and women. Rates were especially stark for serious mental illness, over ten times higher, and acquired brain injury, over five times higher, than in people without those conditions. The authors call for care designed around disabled patients with drinking problems.
pmc-13333459:
Akihiro Maeda and co-authors recount a urethral cancer held in check for nearly three years in a 2026 case report. Clear cell adenocarcinoma of the urethra is an uncommon tumor, and with so few cases there is no playbook for advanced disease with lymph node spread.

A 60-year-old woman arrived unable to pass urine and was diagnosed at stage cT4N2M0 with pelvic node metastases. Gemcitabine plus cisplatin shrank the disease, then robot-assisted surgery removed bladder, urethra, uterus, and vagina with the pelvic nodes, leaving clean margins. Nivolumab followed but was stopped after it triggered thyroid trouble and nodes returned. Gene profiling found a stable genome with a mutation count of 1 per megabase and MET and MYC amplifications, nothing targetable. Returning to the platinum pair produced another partial response, and she remained free of progression 32 months after diagnosis. The authors credit the surgery and platinum strategy.
pmc-13334159:
Jyoti Prakash Panda and colleagues report 2026 clinical care and drug challenges in sino-cranial fungal disease after kidney transplant. A 60-year-old man underwent ABO-mismatched kidney transplant and, after a fifteen-month march of infections including drug-resistant bacterial sepsis, rifamycin-sparing TB therapy, and new-onset diabetes, presented with lasting one-sided headache. Four months earlier, sinus surgery for frontal sinus infection had yielded upper jaw debris growing Aspergillus fumigatus, then read as harmless presence.

MRI showed a left frontal pyocele with back frontal sinus table erosion and skull-base spread, and skull surgery samples confirmed the fungus on microscopy, tissue study, and culture. Surgery source control followed by systemic voriconazole, by vein then by mouth, with heavily weakened immunity, brought clinical gains. The case shows how fungal disease can hide behind harmless-presence labels in heavily immune-weakened transplant patients.
pmc-13334759:
Deepak Kumar and colleagues test 2026 serum sodium against C-reactive protein and total white cell count to spot appendix rupture in adults with sudden belly trouble. Early identification of severe belly trouble remains a medical challenge, since rupture brings increased illness, prolonged hospital stay, and adverse post-surgery outcomes. Conventional immune markers such as C-reactive protein and total white cell count have shown variable utility in spotting disease gravity. Serum sodium has recently emerged as a potential lab sign for severe belly trouble.

The prospective  study at Maharishi Markandeshwar Medical College and Hospital in Solan, India, covered 72 adult patients with acute belly trouble found by joint medical, lab, imaging, surgery, and tissue findings. The study tested serum sodium utility as a rupture sign and compared its results with C-reactive protein and total white cell count.
pmc-13335559:
Anibri Mouna and colleagues report a 2026 case of before-birth finding and after-birth care of inborn neck-face cystic lymph growth with multiple fetal defects. Cystic lymph growth is a rare benign birth malformation of the lymphatic system from abnormal embryo development of lymphatic vessels. Pregnancy scan plays a key role in early finding and follow-up.

The case concerns a 30-year-old gravida 2 para 1 woman with primary CMV infection during the first trimester. Multiple fetal defects were found on fetal scan, including large brain ventricles, small cerebellum, abnormal cerebral folding, large heart, and cystic hygroma. She was followed with serial scans until term, and vaginal delivery occurred at 39 weeks without maternal complications. The neonate presented with a neck-face cystic mass and was referred for child surgical care. Surgical excision confirmed cystic lymph growth.
pmc-13336559:
Amon Lanz leads a large team in a 2026 physics study of a layered crystal made from molybdenum, tungsten, and tellurium. Adding tungsten holds the crystal in a rare low-temperature form linked to unusual Weyl states. The group asked how stretching the crystal changes the electrons inside it.

Hard X-ray photoemission, a method that maps electron energies, tracked the bulk states while samples were pulled in two directions. Stretch along one axis drained heavy, slow-scattering states and raised conductivity. Stretch along the other axis raised resistance instead, matching transport tests. Knowing how strain steers these states may help design materials whose electric behavior can be tuned on demand.
pmc-13336959:
Chengming Zhang and colleagues build CauFinder, a causal reasoning tool for steering cell states, in a 2026 methods study. Gene data are full of correlations, so picking the true drivers of a cell's change of identity is hard. CauFinder blends causal disentanglement with network control to separate real drivers from look-alike signals.

Across simulations and real datasets it flagged regulators of cell differentiation, cancer type switching, and drug resistance shifts. In lung cancer drug resistance it nominated DAAM1, a previously unrecognized driver. Silencing DAAM1 made cells more sensitive to the drug osimertinib in lab tests, backing the prediction. Actionable, testable targets could speed therapies that push cells toward healthier states.
pmc-13337059:
Ezzoubair Bendadesse and co-authors show the electrolyte decides whether a high-capacity potassium battery anode survives in a 2026 study. Antimony-graphite anodes store much charge but swell hugely, cracking and fading fast. A localized high-concentration electrolyte changed both the surface film and the inner alloying path.

Cells with that electrolyte ran over 300 cycles holding 400 mAh per gram in the reported tests, while a standard carbonate version degraded quickly. Live Raman, diffraction, and swelling measures showed the good electrolyte favors a glassy alloy, spares the graphite, and grows a thin mineral-rich film that limits strain. The standard one built a thick organic film and damaging, uneven swelling. Fluid design may rescue alloy anodes.
pmc-13337659:
Peter W. Heger and colleagues report a 2026 trial of a rhubarb root extract for menopause complaints. The extract, called ERr 731, comes from Rheum rhaponticum and is offered as a non-hormonal option. Interest in such options has grown because of safety concerns around hormone therapy.

First, 112 women aged 45 to 55 took either the extract at 4 mg daily or a placebo for 12 weeks. Then 89 women continued openly for 52 weeks, with checks every 13 weeks. Complaint scores fell more with the extract than with placebo in the blinded phase. Scores kept falling over the open year, including for headache and migraine.
pmc-13337759:
Abdulrashid Hashi Mohamed heads a 2026 review of blood pressure swings during dialysis in Somalia. Pressure that falls or rises sharply during treatment adds to heart risk for people on hemodialysis. Data from sub-Saharan Africa on this problem have been scarce.

Charts for 149 adults treated at a Mogadishu hospital from June to September 2022 were examined. Falls in pressure affected 55.0 percent of patients and sharp rises affected 12.1 percent in the reported counts. Patient, treatment, and lab factors were tested for links to each pattern. Results give Somali clinicians a local baseline for a complication usually described from other regions.
pmc-13337859:
My Ngoc To, Ramona Beltrán, and Keli King review contemplative practices for historical trauma healing in a 2026 scoping review. Practices that build awareness and compassion can help with trauma, yet use for harm passed across generations had not been mapped. BIPOC communities were the focus.

Searches found 645 articles, and 35 intervention studies from after 1998 met the rules. Most used qualitative or mixed methods with community partners, and many involved Indigenous groups. Publication rose over the last decade as reported. Themes across studies point to shared healing paths, giving future programs a base for culturally grounded design and testing.
pmc-13338759:
Hyungji Jang and colleagues compared a combined cholesterol pill in 2026 with taking its two drugs separately in healthy Korean volunteers. Atorvastatin and fenofibrate are often paired for mixed dyslipidaemia, and a single combined pill could aid adherence. Because atorvastatin levels vary widely between people, the team used a replicated crossover design with four periods.

Blood levels of atorvastatin, its hydroxy metabolite, and fenofibric acid were tracked for 48 to 72 hours across periods. Safety was also compared. The trial tests whether the fixed dose combination matches the loose combination closely enough to swap in routine care without losing effect or adding risk.
pmc-13339159:
Shuyao Zhang, Taylor M. Estock, and Nathan D. Schley report an iridium catalyst for adding boron to chain ends in a 2026 study. Boron handles on plain carbon chains are versatile for building molecules, but saturated carbon sites lag behind flat ones. Carbonyl-bearing chains were the test set.

The catalyst, built on a dipyridylarylmethane ligand, worked at low loading with the target as the limiting material. It chose unhindered methyl ends over middle or branched spots, ignoring the carbonyl as a guide as reported. A trapped catalyst form gave structural proof. Products fed directly into palladium coupling, showing practical value.
pmc-13339459:
Joaquin A. Vizcarra framed Parkinson disease in 2026 as a systems challenge for health care, not only a clinical one. Global cases rose from two and a half million in 1990 to nearly 12 million in 2021, with projections of over 25 million by 2050. In the United States alone, about 1.04 million people lived with diagnosed disease in 2017.

Growth of that scale strains diagnosis, long term management, rehabilitation, hospital care, and palliative services within finite capacity. Ageing populations and longer survival both feed the rise. Vizcarra argues that planners must expand infrastructure and workforce now, or the Parkinson pandemic will overwhelm services built for a far smaller caseload.
pmc-13340659:
A plasma cell tumor confined to the nose is described in a 2026 case report by Diwakar Koirala and colleagues, set in a resource-limited hospital. A 59-year-old woman had months of worsening blockage on the right side of her nose, with occasional bleeding and discharge.

Scans showed a 6.2 × 3.7 × 6.5 cm mass in the right ethmoid sinus reaching into nearby structures, and tissue study confirmed extramedullary plasmacytoma. One recommended stain to exclude melanoma could not be run locally. Surgeons removed the growth with a total maxillectomy, and she went home after 7 days. The report stresses separating this tumor from myeloma and keeping up follow-up.
pmc-13341359:
Adrian Brown and colleagues surveyed kidney care providers in 2026 on weight management for patients with obesity on dialysis awaiting kidney transplant in the United Kingdom. Access to transplant for people with obesity and kidney failure is often hard, above all where publicly funded obesity services vary. An online national survey from July to December 2024 reached kidney and transplant centres by purposive and snowball sampling.

A total of 227 providers responded, with weight bias measured by the Fat Phobia Scale. Views on weight support, waitlisting criteria, and possible weight stigma were explored. The survey exposes uneven support and stigma risks that may block transplant access. Health systems can use it to standardise fairer weight pathways to transplant.
pmc-13341859:
Diabetic children's mouths fare worse than their peers', in a 2026 comparative study by Fatima Ezzahra Zidane and colleagues. One hundred children with type 1 diabetes and 100 matched controls aged 3 to 17 were examined for decay, plaque, gum inflammation, and calculus, alongside hygiene and diet questionnaires.

Decay experience matched between groups, but diabetic children showed higher plaque scores, more calculus (p = 0.001), and worse gum inflammation (p = 0.022). Poor blood sugar control tracked with inflamed gums (p = 0.043), and faulty brushing technique was commoner in the diabetes group. Prevention visits and technique coaching, not just decay checks, should anchor their dental care.
pmc-13342059:
Why palliative care nurses stay is explored by Zongwen Yi's team in a 2026 qualitative study. Fifteen nurses gave semi-structured interviews of 20 to 52 minutes, grouped by theme under a job demands and resources framework.

Demands dragging retention down included constant nearness to death, heavy emotional labor, ethically tangled talks, and physical strain. Staying was powered by team cohesion, workplace recognition, a felt sense of the work's value, plus personal mission, resilience, and hard-won peace with death. With palliative nursing in severe shortage worldwide, the balance of drains and supports offers ward heads a useful retention map.
pmc-13343159:
Liliana K. Thron and co-authors test natural killer cell therapy against HIV in humanized mice in a 2026 study. Antiretroviral drugs suppress HIV but must be taken for life, so the team tried engineered and plain activated killer cells after stopping drug treatment in infected mice.

No harm followed the cell infusions. By day 56, virus sat below detection in 62.5 percent of mice given CAR-engineered cells and 50 percent given plain cells, versus none in the salt-water control group. Engineered cells reached higher peak levels and lingered longer. Mice that controlled virus had rebounded earlier, hinting treatment timing matters for a future cure strategy.
pmc-13343859:
Lawrence P. Wackett and Randy B. Stockbridge argue, in a 2026 commentary, that microbiology's idea of salt-loving microbes is far too narrow. Halophily has meant sodium chloride tolerance for a century, yet industry now spreads fluorine, chlorine, bromine, and iodine compounds widely, and microbes answer each halide very differently.

Responses shift again with the partner cation attached and with whether the halogen sits outside the cell or gets freed inside by enzymes such as dehalogenases. Lumping all halides together, the authors warn, misreads how microbes tolerate, make, or break halogen compounds. They call for research that treats halide-philicity as a family of distinct traits, sized up one element at a time.
pmc-13343959:
Gina R. Lewin and Lily Khadempour called in 2026 for exact symbiosis words in human microbiome work. In ecology, a commensal has no effect on its host, while a mutualist benefits its host, yet microbiome writing often uses commensal loosely for any helpful organism. Old habits persist despite known gaps in word use.

The authors urge using commensal only when no host effect is known, mutualist when benefit is known, and symbiont when effect is unknown. Shared words with ecologists let microbiome workers draw on and add to vast symbiosis research. Exact words prevent false claims about microbes whose host effects stay unproved.
pmc-13346059:
Xiaoyang Xu and co-authors chart balance recovery around knee ligament surgery in 2026. Fifty participants, half awaiting anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction and half healthy, stood and walked on a high-resolution pressure mat, with the surgery group retested at two and six months after their operation.

Before surgery the injured group swayed worse standing and walking, with heavy side-to-side unevenness. Two months out, only front-back control had clearly improved. By six months most measures matched the healthy group, yet the operated leg still showed shorter gait lines and lighter forefoot pressure. Pressure mapping, the authors argue, gives rehabilitation teams an honest scoreboard for the unevenness patients still hide.
pmc-13347959:
Marianne Kotzé and co-authors gave in 2026 a brief guide to caring for young children who have faced sexual abuse in South Africa. Medical teaching there often leaves clinicians unready for forensic care. Many clinicians feel unsure. They cite scant knowledge and long legal steps. This can delay help for at-risk children.

The guide stresses that the child's best interests come first. Emotional and physical well-being take precedence, even over forensic work. It walks clinicians through checks, notes, referrals, and support. It aims to cut needless blocks to service. For busy clinicians, it gives a humane, workable start for cases that need both clinical skill and gentle handling.
pmc-13349959:
Shivansh Pandey and co-authors reported in 2026 the robotic removal of a rare cancer behind the abdominal organs, primary retroperitoneal mucinous cystadenocarcinoma. Fewer than 110 cases have been described since 1965, and diagnosis is hard because scans look nonspecific and no blood marker exists.

Their patient, a 46-year-old woman with a high-grade tumour, had complete removal using robotic assistance, which the authors believe is the first such report for the malignant form. A literature review covers how the disease presents, where it may come from, and what treatments have achieved. Surgery remains the mainstay, while the value of added drug therapy stays unsettled.
pmc-13350059:
Guannan Geng and co-authors triangulated schooling and diabetes risk in a 2026 study drawing on three kinds of evidence. UK Biobank followed over 474,000 people without diabetes at the start, a United States survey added outside validation, and genetic data tested whether the link might be causal.

More schooling tracked with clearly lower odds of having diabetes and lower risk of developing it, with degree holders faring best. Body fat, habits, and blood markers explained part of the pathway. Genetic correlation and related methods probed shared biology between education and diabetes. Combining designs that fail in different ways makes the overall case harder to dismiss.
pmc-13350259:
Qian Wang and Houqing Pang reported an extremely rare prenatal case in 2026: a fetus whose head had separated in the womb yet who survived there for weeks. Such events, usually caused by amniotic bands, most often end in early pregnancy loss.

The mother, a 32-year-old woman in her second pregnancy, had a normal scan at nine weeks with no pain, bleeding, or trauma history. Later referral imaging, including three-dimensional transvaginal ultrasound, revealed the injury in a baby previously developing normally. Only a handful of comparable cases exist in print. Documenting how the diagnosis was reached may help other teams recognise and counsel families facing the same shock.
pmc-13350359:
Wei Pan and colleagues pooled evidence in a 2026 review on nurse-led enhanced recovery care after bowel cancer surgery. Recovery bundles speed healing. They coordinate feeding, movement, and pain control. Nurses hold the pieces together.

From 2,586 records, 13 studies qualified. Outcomes such as hospital stay, readmission, and complications were pooled. The bundle examined puts nurses in charge of aligning patient teaching, early walking, and pain control. This runs across the whole surgical journey. Shorter, smoother recoveries free beds and spare patients setbacks. The synthesis tests whether giving nurses formal charge of the bundle delivers those gains.
pmc-13351159:
Thai Huyen Nguyen and colleagues published a dataset in 2026 on informal waste collectors in Hanoi, Vietnam. They are known locally as đồng nát. These collectors and aggregators have run a flexible recycling system for decades. It long predates modern waste services. It still carries much of the city's recycling.

Surveys, interviews, photographs, and records of materials were combined. Notes on streets and buildings where the work happens were added. The files cover who the collectors are, what they gather, and what they earn. They also cover movement patterns, all with names removed. The data make an unseen workforce visible to planners designing fairer waste policy.
pmc-13352659:
Amal Mubarak Alsuwaylim leads a 2026 survey study of ChatGPT use, speaking anxiety, and learner independence among foreign-language students. No prior work had modelled all three factors together. A cross-sectional survey covered 852 students at three Egyptian public universities, using validated scales for ChatGPT use, classroom speaking anxiety, and learner autonomy.

Heavier ChatGPT use linked to lower speaking anxiety and higher autonomy, while anxiety linked to lower autonomy. Mediation checks with 5,000 bootstrap resamples showed anxiety partly carried the link, accounting for 34.80 percent of the total effect. Results fit affective filter and self-determination ideas side by side. Since the design is a single snapshot, cause cannot be proven, the authors note.
pmc-13354459:
Hafsa Tariq and others studied whether dengue illness harms male fertility, in 2026. Dengue cases surged to roughly fourteen million in 2024. New reports link acute illness to brief drops in sperm count and possible rises in sperm DNA breaks, perhaps through fever-driven oxidative stress. Zika virus had already shown that bug-borne viruses can affect male breeding.

The review matches dengue's effects on sperm with Zika's, weighing the strength of the results and the ways involved. It also draws out meanings for fertility advice after illness. Doctors gain a timely summary of a missed consequence of a common tropical disease, with guidance on what to tell people.
pmc-13354959:
Nicholas A Mathias and co-authors studied a mouse smell organ in 2026 that senses scents tied to mating, social life, and danger. They focused on a protein called canopy 1, found in large amounts in one class of scent-sensing nerve cells. Mice bred without the protein were checked for cell loss, stress signs, and scent responses.

The organ formed normally, but the key nerve cells were lost over time and stopped responding to scents. Stress signals rose in the cells, receptor protein levels fell, and wiring to the brain smell center went awry. The work shows that each nerve cell type needs its own set of helper proteins to stay fit.
pmc-13355259:
Ji Ma and co-authors built a 2026 chart to predict, before surgery, whether the thin capsule around a kidney cancer is intact or breached. Capsule state hints at how aggressive clear cell kidney cancer is and shapes the surgical plan, yet it is hard to judge without cutting the tumor out. The team studied 254 patients who had contrast ultrasound scans before surgery in Shanghai.

Three scan signs on their own predicted a breached capsule: an incomplete capsule sign, weak peak brightening, and fast washout of contrast. A chart built from them sorted patients fairly well in training and check groups. The authors offer the radiation-free tool to help plan kidney surgery.
pmc-13356759:
Sunlin Luo and co-authors mapped bile acids in broiler chickens in 2026 from hatch to market age at six weeks. Bile acids help digest fats and are reshaped by gut microbes, yet their spread through the gut-liver loop in chickens was little charted. Six birds were sampled each week for bile acid levels across bile, gut sections, liver, and blood.

Bile held by far the highest levels, then the small gut and rear gut, with blood lowest. The ileum and cecum were the hot spots for microbe reshaping of bile acids. The share of reshaped forms rose sharply by week three, which the authors flag as a key maturation point for the gut microbe community.
pmc-13358759:
Yuyang Yan and co-authors review a shifting field in a 2026 paper: treatment around surgery for esophageal cancer. Surgery alone cures few patients with advanced disease, so drug and radiation treatment before or after the operation is standard. Immune therapy drugs have now entered this mix and changed the questions teams must answer.

The review covers which base treatment to choose, whether radiation adds value over drugs alone, and whether some patients can safely delay surgery. It draws on major trials and guidelines from 2005 to early 2026. The aim is care fitted to each patient's response, rather than one fixed plan for all.
pmc-13359859:
Toshiharu Onodera and co-authors review fatty kidney disease in a 2026 paper. Kidney disease is rising with obesity and diabetes. The kidney burns huge energy, and its cells must balance fat and sugar fuels with care. When that balance breaks, fat piles up in and around kidney cells, the energy factories falter, and output falls.

Over time the failure sparks inflammation and swaps healthy tissue for scar, ending in kidney failure. The review assembles how the healthy kidney makes energy, how metabolic stress breaks the system, and how the fat hugging the kidney adds injury. It also surveys new treatments meant to restore normal fuel use.
pmc-13360259:
Dávid Ádám Korda and co-authors compare two forms of internal radiation for liver cancer in a 2026 study. The treatment sends tiny radioactive beads through the liver's blood vessels to strike the tumor from inside. It serves patients who cannot have surgery or heat-based treatment. One form uses yttrium-90 and the other holmium-166, and head-to-head data on them are scarce.

The team found no clear gap between the two forms in survival, tumor response, or how long responses lasted. Both forms gave good results across early and later stages of the disease. The setups differ in how scans guide planning, yet outcomes landed in the same range. The authors say either option can be a sound choice, which helps hospitals weigh cost and access.
pmc-13361359:
Meili Hao and co-authors studied how exercise shields the obese heart in a 2026 mouse study. Exercise is a safe way to improve obesity and its harm, but the inner mechanism is not fully mapped. The team focused on sestrin2, a stress-guard protein. Male mice were fattened on a high-fat diet and then put through aerobic training.

Heart scans and tissue stains showed how much the training eased heart damage. In dish tests with rat heart cells, fat exposure harmed the cells, and adding sestrin2 let the team probe its role. They tracked damage, scarring, inflammation, and oxidative stress, plus a key energy signal path. The work aims to explain, step by step, how moving the body protects the heart in obesity.
pmc-13362459:
Xinhui Huang and a large team report a 2026 study on a fungus used in Chinese medicine and its possible role against liver cancer. Using computer maps of drug targets plus lab tests, they picked out the fungus compound most likely to matter, a sterol called polyporusterone E. The trail led to CHEK1, a gene that helps cancer cells grow and that marks a poor outlook when overactive.

Computer runs showed the compound binds CHEK1 in a stable way. In liver cancer cells, the fungus extract and the pure compound cut cell growth and lowered CHEK1 levels. Extra CHEK1 sped cell growth and spread, while silencing it did the reverse. The work gives early support for the compound as an add-on worth more study.
pmc-13363259:
Hui Luo and Yangshuai Zheng present a 2026 computer simulation of how grains share force when a dense bed of glass beads is sheared slowly under light pressure. Such beds sit in powder plants, silos, and surface soils, yet their inner mechanics at low pressure were poorly mapped. Their 3D model tracked each bead's motion and contact forces in a ring-shaped shear cell run to a steady state.

A sharp switch appeared a few millimeters deep: below it, beads moved almost as one rigid block, while above it they sheared freely and carried the strong force chains. Friction settled at a steady value that matches known theory for slow dense flow. The four inner markers lining up in one band give modelers firm numbers to test against.
pmc-13363659:
Manuel Piñon-Espitia and colleagues present a 2026 study on copper oxide nanofibers, probing rare chemical states that tune their electronic behavior. Using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, a surface chemistry tool, plus diffraction and electron microscopy, they examined fibers baked at two temperatures and a bulk comparison sample. The focus was on Cu3+-like species and missing oxygen atoms, defects that shift how the material carries charge.

The spectra and a diffraction pattern both pointed to the rare copper state, tied to a superlattice in the fibers. Crystal sizes from diffraction and from direct imaging differed, a reminder that the two methods measure different things. The authors say the defect mix should be weighed when these fibers are used in sensors and light devices.
pmc-13364759:
Sang Kim leads a wide team in a 2026 phase three trial of tegoprazan, a new fast acid block drug, to guard the gut of folks on long pain drug care. Pain drugs raise ulcer risk. Near four hundred patients took one of two guard drugs for up to 24 weeks.

The new drug matched the old guard drug on ulcer block, the main test. Heartburn free rates at week 12 ran higher on the new drug. Harm rates were low and near the same in both arms. The trial backs the new drug as a sound guard choice.
pmc-13366359:
Yuri Amemiya and Hiroshi Nishiura find in 2026 a fresh way to guess the death risk of the recent lung germ by age, from dead body checks in Tokyo. Death risk by age drives care plans, but past counts need huge blood polls plus hard death calls. Their route uses set germ tests on all dead at one law med site.

They mix test hits with death stats and blood poll counts in one math pass. Risk climbs steep with age, from a trace in youth to near four in a hundred past age 65. The ranks match past world counts, a fast path for next germs.
pmc-13367159:
Xumeng Du and others surveyed oral germ outside sacs in oral and body-wide disease, in 2026. These nanosized lipid bilayer parts sent by oral germs encapsulate virulence factors, nucleic acids, and metabolites, allowing them to cross biological barriers and modulate host cells. Their roles in disease growth were more and more seen but not fully summed.

Oral germ sacs were linked to periodontitis, dental caries, and oral cancer through immune switch-on, tissue destruction, and altered cellular conduct, with put forward body-wide effects beyond the mouth. The review maps ways connecting oral microbes to distant disease. Dental and medical teams gain a plan for a microbial influence that reaches beyond the oral cavity.
pmc-13370259:
Alessia Lunetta and co-workers hunt in 2026 for hid oil eat germs in the mud of Lake Faro, a salt lake by Messina, Italy. Lake mud can hold fouls and the germs that may clean them in place. The team takes mud from five spots and feeds test tubes with one of three oil goods as lone food.

Oil fouls in the mud read low at all spots. After 80 days, germ counts rise and 25 strains come out, most named as oil eat kin. Some strains foam well, a trait that aids oil spread. A hid clean crew sleeps in the mud.
pmc-13370659:
Katherine Wong and Clara Wong tell in 2026 of a 26 year old man whose gall sac ill mimicked cancer. He came in with gut pain and yellow skin. Scans show a mass by the gall sac and tight bile tubes, bright on a sugar scan, with no stones. That set points to a growth.

A blood mark for a rare swell ill runs high, and steroid care brings a fast, clear turn. The call lands on that ill, which scars bile tubes and the gall sac. The case warns teams to weigh the rare ill prior to a big cut in young folks.
pmc-13370859:
Ting-Hsuan Wang and co-workers build in 2026 a light drug, RuB3, that wakes to kill a harsh breast cancer type on light hit. Safe, picky care is the aim: a drug that sleeps till lit at the lump. Live cell views, scope work, and flow sorts track its acts in the test cells.

On light, the drug makes harsh oxygen bits in the cells and starts their death path. The kill jumps by a wide gap in lit cells next to dark ones, with low off aim harm. The team casts it as a firm step for light cure of this ill.
pmc-13371259:
Jie Jiao and colleagues review how brain support cells pass mitochondria to stressed nerve cells in a 2026 paper. Mitochondria are the cell powerhouses, and nerve cells are highly sensitive when they fail, a feature shared across degenerative disease, stroke, and brain injury. Astrocytes and microglia, two types of glia, often act as donors.

Healthy mitochondria from glia can restore energy in struggling nerve cells and shift disease course. The same route can also spread harm when damaged mitochondria are passed on, and in late disease even glia may lack healthy donors. The review weighs this double edge and maps the gaps that must close before mitochondria transfer can become a safe therapy.
pmc-13374159:
Sergen Arslan and co-authors asked if cancer cells can pass virus notes to clean cells in a 2026 study. Neck of the womb cancer is driven by a virus that can lodge in cell code. Sick cells shed tiny sacs that carry cell freight to new cells.

Sacs were drawn from virus-held lab cells in two ways and checked by size, shape, and marks. Their freight held virus notes. When clean cancer cells took in the sacs, they split and grew faster. The find hints that a tumor can spread growth cues with no germ at all. It also marks sacs as a point to watch in care.
pmc-13374359:
Samantha E Leonard and others map what drives inflammatory signalling molecules across European peoples in a 2026 study. Cytokine imbalance feeds chronic inflammation and immune disease, yet people determinants were poorly charted. The Rotterdam Study cohort of 3,456 adults, mean age 57, was analysed for nine plasma cytokines against age, sex, smoking, body mass, and alcohol use.

Several cytokines, including IL-10, IL-6, IL-17A, TNF, interferon-gamma, IL-18, and IL-17C, rose with age, with IL-18 and IL-17C following non-linear trends. Women had lower IL-18 and IL-17C. Findings were replicated in two independent European cohorts with identical protocols, and IL-6 links were meta-analysed across more than 4,000 people. The work gives a reproducible baseline for judging inflammation in ageing peoples.
pmc-13375659:
Matilde Ciprandi and colleagues engineer a soy protein hydrogel for local drug release in the brain in a 2026 study. Implantable materials can bypass the blood-brain barrier, a major limit for brain tumour therapy, yet tissue compatibility and release control have lagged. Soy protein isolate hydrogels were crosslinked with microbial transglutaminase, a naturally derived enzyme, at two protein levels and two crosslinker doses.

The gels held 87 to 89 percent water, swelled in a controlled way over 72 hours, and behaved as solids with shear-thinning flow suitable for injection. A 10 percent gel with 20 milligrams crosslinker per gram matched native brain stiffness near 260 pascals. That formulation released 100 to 200 nanometre liposomes in a sustained way. The gel offers a biocompatible depot for brain tumour drugs.
pmc-13375759:
Binglun Zhang and co-authors traced a fuel path in bone cancer seed cells in a 2026 study. Seed cells drive the cancer's growth, spread, and drug proof traits. A gene-code reader was high in the cancer and kept seed traits strong, the team found.

The reader grabs a marked note for a fuel burn tool and holds it firm, so more of the tool is made. A writer protein lays that mark, and the pair feeds each other. More tool meant more fuel burn and more seed strength. In live tests, cuts to the reader or tool shrank the cancer. The pair is a fresh drug aim.
pmc-13378059:
Xingyao Lu and colleagues judge the quality of short videos about common bile duct stones on TikTok and Bilibili in China in a 2026 study. Choledocholithiasis is rising and can cause severe complications, driving many people to seek health information online. The team analysed top videos on both platforms, scoring quality with Global Quality Score, modified DISCERN, and JAMA criteria, with inter-rater agreement checked.

A total of 170 videos were included, mostly from hepatobiliary surgeons, with treatment dominating at about 82 percent and little coverage of cause or diagnosis. Overall quality was mediocre, with median scores of 3 for GQS and 2 for both mDISCERN and JAMA. Surgeon videos scored higher, yet quality did not track with engagement. The study warns that popular videos are not necessarily reliable ones.
pmc-13380259:
Laxman Choudhary and co-authors present a 2026 case of an exceptionally rare wrist injury: a small wrist bone slipped out of place backwards, with no other broken or displaced bones. The patient was an adult man hurt in a high-energy road accident. He arrived with wrist pain, swelling, and visible deformity.

X-rays and detailed scans confirmed the displaced trapezoid bone at its joint near the thumb side of the wrist. Doctors put the bone back without surgery and held the wrist in a splint. At early follow-up the wrist was aligned, pain-free, and fully working. The authors stress detailed imaging, since such an injury is easily missed.
pmc-13380459:
Yao Wang and colleagues report a 2026 study breeding maize with higher levels of GABA, a natural chemical linked to human health. Maize is a staple crop worldwide, but no GABA-enriched maize had been developed before. Tomatoes had been improved this way by editing a single gene.

Using gene editing, the team altered a gene that makes GABA, a gene that breaks it down, or both together in the same plants. Editing both gave the largest rise in kernel GABA, several times the normal level. The result is a breeding stock for healthier maize. The work also shows how the two pathways together control GABA levels in the plant.
pmc-13382559:
Yong Chan Ahn wrote a 2026 editorial marking the sixtieth anniversary of the journal Cancer Research and Treatment, founded in Korea in 1966. In Korean tradition a sixtieth birthday, called Hwangap, completes the sixty-year cycle of the traditional calendar and is deeply honoured. The editorial treats the journal's milestone in the same spirit.

Ahn reflects on the journal's impact factor rising and falling over the years, and on what longevity means: not mere survival, but wisdom and integrity gathered through difficulty. With modern health care, reaching sixty is both thanks for past resilience and a launchpad for a new cycle. The piece invites readers to mark the anniversary with that dual view.
pmc-13383859:
Marc Thill and co-authors report two-year complication results from the PRO-BRA trial of implant breast reconstruction in a 2026 analysis. Operations in 269 patients used a titanized polypropylene mesh to support the implant, across 362 reconstructions. The team tested which patient and treatment factors raised the risk of problems after surgery.

Higher body mass, larger implants, and a higher illness score each linked to certain complications in single-factor tests. Radiation therapy linked to capsule tightening, while chemotherapy before surgery stood out in the combined model. The findings help surgeons flag higher-risk patients early and plan reconstruction care with clearer expectations.
pmc-13386559:
Fanyang Kong's team compared three radiation methods for bilateral breast cancer, in a 2026 dose study. The team built plans for 30 patients using VMAT, helical tomotherapy with 5-centimeter field width, and helical tomotherapy with 2.5-centimeter field width, all prescribed 50 gray in 25 fractions. Target cover and organ doses were compared.

All three methods met cover requirements. VMAT achieved the best conformity, with no difference in homogeneity. Helical methods lowered low-dose lung volume, while VMAT lowered intermediate lung doses. Heart doses also differed by method. The comparison helps planners pick the method that best balances target cover with heart and lung sparing.
pmc-13386759:
Aswathy Sreedevi's team presents a trial plan for a lifestyle toolkit in cardiometabolic multimorbidity (CMM) in India, in a 2026 paper. Lifestyle change through diet, movement, and stress care is crucial in cardiometabolic disease, yet use in Indian CMM contexts was little explored. The SHRADDHA-CMM trial uses a two-arm cluster lottery-style type III effect-rollout design.

Adults with two or more of diabetes, hypertension, stroke, or coronary heart disease will receive a locally adapted toolkit based on the WHO-HEARTS model, with a family-wide shielding angle. The village-based trial spans rural health survey cohorts. The plan tests whether an adapted toolkit can improve results where CMM meets distinct Indian risk patterns.
pmc-13388659:
Yue Zheng's team devised a general way to grow membranes from covalent organic frameworks with two pore sizes at once, aiming at fast uranium capture from water. Earlier attempts struggled because adding a support layer disturbed the growth direction of the framework network, leaving pores poorly defined.

Pre-coating framework nanoparticles onto a nylon base let the network grow in the particles' orientation. The method worked across several framework types, with pore pairs from about seven to forty-two angstroms. The best membrane moved uranyl ions faster than any comparable Schiff-base membrane, and kept working after irradiation, pointing toward uranium recovery from seawater or waste streams.
pmc-13388959:
Md Rakibul Mowla's team used recordings from inside the human brain to ask how the forebrain tracks breathing during waking, sleep, and machine ventilation. Breathing interoception, the brain's sensing of respiratory signals, matters for spotting breathing threats, yet its human circuitry was largely unknown.

Forebrain rhythms synchronised widely with breathing while awake, especially in the insula, somatosensory cortex, anterior cingulate, and amygdala, then narrowed during sleep to the amygdala and hippocampus. Nasal airflow was not required, unlike in rodents, and ventilator-driven slow deep breaths entrained more sites, hinting at how breath practices might sway emotion and thought.
pmc-13389059:
Miguel Ángel López Carrillo's team devised a way to measure the enantiomeric purity of sorted carbon nanotubes absolutely, without needing pure reference samples that do not exist. Chiroptical spectroscopy reads purity quickly and without damage, but calibrating it for single-walled nanotubes had been blocked by the lack of enantiopure standards.

Counting thousands of individual tubes by hyperspectral fluorescence imaging let them anchor ensemble circular dichroism and Raman optical activity signals to true purity, yielding universal calibration curves from the purest samples. The method extends to other tube chiralities and could make chirality sorting quantitative rather than approximate.
pmc-13390759:
Yousef E Abu Osba and Sara B Alrafayia review, in 2026, surgery choices for older men with an enlarged prostate. The condition is very common with ageing and often causes urinary symptoms that greatly reduce quality of life, while many patients also carry frailty and multiple other illnesses.

Drugs remain first-line care, but surgery is often needed when symptoms resist treatment or complications arise. The review surveys current minimally invasive and standard operations and argues for involving geriatric specialists early, across disciplines, rather than as a last consult. Urologists and geriatricians gain a patient-centred framework that weighs urinary benefit against physiological reserve, not operative technique alone.
pmc-13391359:
Deguang Song's team found that gut friendly germs make ACh in vivo, teaching the mucus immune system. Screening one hundred friendly strains in germ-free mice and in culture showed in vivo and in vitro profiles switching on G-protein-coupled sensors in varied ways. Host breakdown, germ rewiring, and dietary change drove the differences.

Several strains, including early-life Bifidobacterium and a probiotic Pediococcus, turned dietary choline to ACh. The key enzymes were found, and a cut-out strain was built. Mice settled with ACh-producing Bifidobacterium breve made more gut IgA, revealing a germ nerve-signal route to immune training.
pmc-13392159:
Shenikqua Bouges and a large team study, in 2026, how researchers can earn community trust, focusing on Black participants' views of trustworthy Alzheimer's research. Drugs for the disease have leapt ahead. Yet minority groups stay scarce in trials. That gap limits how far the findings can be stretched.

Mistrust of health research is a known participation barrier, but it is hard to measure as a single number. The study gathers participants' own descriptions of what a trustworthy study design looks like and how investigators behave. Trial teams gain firm plans, set by the people they hope to reach. The plans build trust in real streets and homes. They beat bland outreach slogans that ask for trust but do not earn it.
pmc-13392659:
Aitbay Bulashev and colleagues built a new blood test for brucellosis in cattle and sheep using a fused protein stitched from two Brucella surface proteins. Older tests lean on a sugary coating molecule that cross-reacts with other germs and triggers false alarms and needless culling. Their test coats sheep red blood cells with lab-made proteins and watches for clumping, a cheap method needing little equipment.

Fourteen hundred forty serum samples from sick and healthy herds were run through the new test alongside two standard methods. The fused-protein version caught nearly all true cases while producing no false positives in the panel, giving the best overall accuracy of the antigens tried. In a small group of slaughtered positive cattle it flagged every case, including some a commercial kit missed. The team presents it as a sharper tool for herd screening.
pmc-13393259:
Xiaoxiao Pan leads a fifteen-author team building molybdenum sulfide nanoparticles designed to wake anti-tumour immunity from inside the cancer. Molybdenum enzymes and their product uric acid help switch T cells on, so raising both inside tumours could strengthen immunotherapy. The particles were engineered to fall apart in the glutathione-rich tumour interior, releasing hydrogen sulfide gas and molybdate ions together.

The gas damages tumour mitochondria, spilling their DNA, which trips the STING alarm pathway that rouses immune attack. Molybdate amplifies that same alarm. It also rewires purine handling so uric acid climbs inside the tumour, further exciting T cells. The authors describe the pairing as metalloimmunotherapy fused with gas therapy, a metabolic-immune strategy meant to hit tumours precisely while sparing the rest of the body. Results are presented as a design proof for this class of treatment.
pmc-13393859:
Özlem Akın and Özlem Tanrıöver surveyed one hundred seventy-three adults with confirmed scabies, the intensely itchy mite infestation, to weigh its psychological and behavioural burden beyond the skin. Participants rated itch severity and duration, behaviour changes, anxiety on a standard scale, and dermatology quality of life. The analysis linked those measures with correlation and regression methods.

Itch ran severe, with a median score near the top of the scale. Itch severity tracked behaviour change, the scrubbing, washing, and avoidance rituals patients adopt, but not anxiety or quality-of-life scores directly. Quality of life instead tied to anxiety and to behaviour change, and people who had feared scabies before catching it showed nearly double the anxiety. The nodular form of the disease independently predicted worse quality of life. The authors urge clinicians to treat the mental load as part of the infestation.
pmc-13394059:
Sachin Dave and five colleagues untangle a 64-year-old woman whose progressive leg swelling and hardening skin concealed two overlapping conditions. Her legs showed the orange-peel texture and groove sign of eosinophilic fasciitis. The rare disorder thickens the deep tissue under skin. Blood work revealed an IgA-kappa monoclonal gammopathy and heavy protein in the urine. Nerve studies confirmed carpal tunnel syndrome in both wrists. The trio also raises the spectre of amyloidosis.

Steroids brought marked relief, fitting the fasciitis pattern. Marrow study settled on a benign precursor gammopathy, and kidney biopsy excluded amyloid and every monoclonal kidney injury pattern tested, arguing against kidney damage from the clone. Imaging, the authors note, can prove fascial involvement and steer biopsy choices when patients hesitate. The case shows how signature skin signs steered the diagnosis away from closer mimics.
pmc-13394259:
Giulia Maria Ruggeri leads an seventeen-author pig study testing whether donor lungs on an external perfusion circuit can be graded lobe by lobe instead of as a whole organ. Ex vivo lung perfusion lets centres assess and revive marginal donor lungs, but mixed blood sampling hides local failure. In five healthy pigs the team cannulated each lung vein separately on the circuit, then clamped first one lower bronchus and then an upper one to fake localised injury.

At baseline lobar and mixed samples matched. Clamping drove the affected lobe to near-total non-aeration with shunt approaching complete, and its oxygen measure collapsed, while the mixed sample stayed deceptively comfortable. Overall lung mechanics and pressures worsened, and tissue from the starved lower lobe showed congestion and bleeding. The authors say lobar sampling pinpoints injury and could sharpen transplant decisions.
pmc-13394559:
Feng Wang and colleagues trace a non-coding RNA pathway that promotes glioma growth in a 2026 study. Glioma, the most common primary malignant brain tumor, invades aggressively and recurs often, and new molecular targets are urgently needed.

The long non-coding RNA CROCCP2 was markedly raised in glioma tissues and cell lines, boosting proliferation, migration, and invasion. It acted by soaking up miR-5584-5p, freeing the gene HOXD11, which then suppressed autophagy as shown by lower LC3B-II and Beclin1 and higher p62. Blocking CROCCP2 or HOXD11 reversed these effects, nominating a new therapeutic axis.
pmc-13395259:
Yan Wang and co-authors study, in 2026, why women drift away from an online symptom program for ovarian cancer. The program, Nurse WRITE, pairs nurse guidance with web tools over eight weeks. The team re-read data from 68 women whose cancer had returned. They tracked board posts, site use, care plans, and symptom control.

Schooling level tracked with several forms of taking part, from word counts to finished care plans. Worse health, busy family life, and site troubles were the top blocks. Many low users quit at set stages, such as goal setting. Women who took part more also felt better symptom control. The authors urge extra help for women with less schooling.
pmc-13395559:
Sayaka Honda and co-authors recount, in 2026, a robot-aided heart valve swap in a man with a severely curved spine. The 61-year-old had bad breathlessness from a leaky aortic valve. His chest cavity was markedly narrow, with just a hand's breadth between breastbone and spine. Such tight space usually rules out robot work.

The team shifted one robot arm lower to gain a better angle and cut the aorta lengthwise for room. Retraction and suction from the bedside crew exposed the valve ring. A tissue valve went in without mishap, and the man left hospital on day twenty. The authors say careful planning opens robot care to bent chests.
pmc-13396359:
Fu and team make, in 2026, cellulose fibers with spider-silk-like toughness by copying the helical nanostructure of cherry bark. Cellulose from plant biomass is strong but brittle, with toughness usually below 50 megajoules per cubic meter. Using a scalable microfluidic spinning method, the team gave new cellulose fibers a two-way aligned internal structure, with molecular chains running along two directions instead of one.

The two-way structure spreads stress and suppresses crack growth as the fiber stretches, according to their experiments and molecular simulations. The resulting fibers reached a fracture strain of 41 percent alongside a tensile strength of 553 megapascals, a combination ordinary cellulose cannot achieve. Together these yielded a toughness of 184 megajoules per cubic meter, the same order of magnitude as natural spider silk. The improvement carried over from single fibers to woven fabrics, pointing toward greener textiles, car parts, and aerospace materials.
pmc-13396459:
Mantena and team build, in 2026, a multi-ethnic reference map of germline diversity in the genes for T cell receptors, the molecules that let T cells recognize targets. The receptor loci are repetitive and hard to sequence, so variation there has been little charted. Using long-read data from the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium and the All of Us program, covering 2,719 donors, they assembled a catalog of alleles across the V, D, and J gene segments.

The map revealed amino acid changes at almost every position within the V genes, with allele frequencies differing by group. Statistical tests found evidence of natural selection on these genes, including balancing and positive selection concentrated in the alpha chain locus. That is unusual for receptors usually assumed to diversify only within each person. Allelic differences changed T cell traits, including thymic fate and surface receptor levels, linking variation to immune response.
pmc-13396559:
Nattasha A. Mattaka and co-authors studied thyroid changes in the sickest hospital patients at a referral center in northeastern Tanzania, in a 2026 cohort study. In severe illness the thyroid hormone pattern often shifts even though the gland itself is healthy, a state called non-thyroidal illness syndrome that may mark a worse outlook.

The team enrolled 120 adults admitted to the medical intensive care unit between October 2024 and March 2025, testing three thyroid measures within a day of arrival. They recorded how common the syndrome was and hunted for traits that predicted death. Data from sub-Saharan Africa on this question were scarce, which the authors set out to remedy.
pmc-13396759:
Choi and co-authors demonstrate, in 2026, SlAction, a contact-free system that detects obstructive sleep apnea from wall-mounted near-infrared video, with analysis running on the device itself. Sleep apnea affects nearly one billion people, yet over 80 percent of moderate-to-severe cases go undiagnosed because standard testing needs an overnight laboratory study. SlAction instead reads the body movements that accompany respiratory arousals as stand-ins for breathing disturbances.

The team trained and validated the system on 936 clinical recordings totaling more than 5,000 hours from three hospitals. Across internal and external test sets, it cut apnea-hypopnea index estimation error versus prior video approaches and improved classification of severity and positional apnea, while running faster on low-cost hardware. The comparison matters because home sleep tests carry a 39 percent diagnostic error rate in a recent 20-study meta-analysis. The authors position the system as privacy-preserving screening for home use.
pmc-13396859:
Wettersten and team test, in 2026, whether kidney tubule secretion markers can predict potassium problems and treatment response in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. They used data from the TOPCAT trial: 372 participants, mean age 70 years, of whom 179 were randomized to the drug spironolactone. A summary score combined urine-to-plasma ratios of nine endogenous secretion markers measured at baseline.

In adjusted models, the score showed no link with changes in serum potassium, the study's central safety question, nor with incident high potassium during follow-up. It also failed to predict symptom improvement, natriuretic peptide changes, or heart and kidney events in the cohort. The single significant finding was modest: higher capacity tracked with a 3.5-point lower heart failure questionnaire score at twelve months, of uncertain weight. The authors conclude these biomarkers should not guide spironolactone decisions or risk prediction in this group.
pmc-13397759:
Huili Zhu and others tie Toll-like receptor signals with Eimeria tenella harm power in chickens in a 2026 study. This fierce coccidiosis agent settles in the cecum and imposes major poultry losses, yet Toll-like roles during illness were poorly defined.

Sick specific-pathogen-free chickens were watched for cecal lesions, oocyst output, and clinic signs, while ten Toll-like sensors and linked immune genes were read in cecum and spleen over time. Link reads tied sensor levels to harm marks, with marked clinic signs but no deaths. Poultry scientists gain innate immune aims for gut parasite control.
pmc-13398959:
Tomofumi Takayoshi and co-authors present a young woman whose inherited diabetes carries two gene variants at once. Their 2026 case report concerns a 21-year-old with early-onset diabetes of the maturity-onset type, called MODY, which accounts for at least 1 to 5 percent of diabetes cases in the estimates cited. Single-gene causes are the rule, and dual-variant cases are rarely reported.

Whole-exome and Sanger sequencing found a disease-causing HNF1A variant (p.Arg159Trp) plus a second variant in NEUROD1, both genes steering insulin-producing cell development. The team modelled how each change alters its protein's surface charge and stability. Pinning the exact genetic mix matters, since MODY type steers drug choice and family screening.
pmc-13400159:
Katelyn Eisner and colleagues report that the obesity drug semaglutide weakens bones in obese mice, and that the harm lifts once the drug stops, in this 2026 study. The team treated obese male mice with semaglutide for four weeks, comparing them with mice fed the same reduced calories. They measured femur mass, stiffness, and strength. A second cohort was assessed six weeks after treatment ended.

Semaglutide-treated mice ended with lighter, weaker, less stiff femurs than controls, and the deficits exceeded those of the calorie-matched mice. Ordinary weight loss alone does not explain them. Blood markers of bone-building activity fell in parallel. Six weeks after the drug stopped, femur weight, strength, and stiffness were indistinguishable from vehicle-treated animals. That shows the effect depends on continued exposure rather than permanent damage. The authors stop short of clinical claims but call for human studies.
pmc-13401059:
Xuehua Ye and colleagues build, in 2026, machine learning models to predict Parkinson disease stage five years after a dopamine imaging scan, using routine real-world data. Parkinson progression varies hugely between patients, complicating care. Most earlier models used research cohorts whose data differ from everyday clinic records, and targeted less practical measures.

Records and imaging from 343 real-world patients were harmonized with 134 patients from a research cohort, yielding 83 shared features. Two ensemble methods were trained to forecast the standard Hoehn and Yahr stage.
