pmc-13480259:
Rio Ishida and co-authors describe a 2026 study of how the timing of childhood hardship relates to thinking skills in autistic adults. The team studied 161 adults with autism and no intellectual disability. Groups split by whether hardship struck before age eleven, during the teen years, or never, and all took a standard adult intelligence battery.

The early-hardship group beat the teen-hardship group on two subtests, one on spotting missing parts in pictures and one on judging weights by logic. Gaps held after checks for schooling and trauma symptom levels, even though the early group carried heavier trauma symptoms. The authors read the pattern as a possible adaptation shaped by early vigilance, not as a benefit of hardship. Those two subtests may help flag adults whose thinking style was moulded by early adversity.
pmc-13482059:
Lorna Hardy and co-authors report a 2026 study of two kidney markers that often disagree in older cats treated for thyroid overactivity. Twenty-seven pet cats got low-dose radioactive iodine and were checked at the start plus one, six, and twelve months. Each visit measured true filtration rate beside the two blood markers, SDMA and creatinine.

The markers clashed in a wide band of cases, most often when the looser SDMA limit was used and at the start, when thyroid levels still ran high. In settled cats at one year, the looser SDMA limit caught more true filtration drops yet flagged more false alarms, while creatinine stayed the most specific. Repeat readings in the same cat wobbled by about fifteen percent for both. Vets should read a mid-range SDMA with care when creatinine looks normal.
pmc-13482359:
Pu and colleagues turn microscope slide images into a survival forecast in 2026 for advanced high-grade serous ovarian cancer, the commonest and deadliest ovarian cancer type. Standard care pairs debulking surgery with platinum chemotherapy, yet outcomes swing widely, and only about a fifth of patients survive long term. The team mined 392 patients' stained tumor slides for pathomics features, measurable patterns in tissue images, and built a signature with machine learning.

The signature split patients into risk groups with clearly different overall survival, and it also flagged which patients actually gained from the platinum chemotherapy backbone of their treatment. Its predictions held up in a separate external group of patients, strengthening the case that the signal is real rather than fitted to one hospital. Gene analysis tied high-risk scores to cell skeleton and protein processing pathways and to immune cell presence in tumors.
pmc-13483159:
Nor Asiah Muhamad and co-authors describe a 2026 trial analysis asking whether eight weeks of hepatitis C drugs clear the virus as fast as twelve. The Malaysian trial randomised 321 adults with chronic infection to shorter or standard courses of a two-drug pairing, and this study clocked days until virus levels fell below the detection line.

Median time to clearance landed at twenty-eight days in both arms. Adjusted models gave the short arm a modest edge in odds of clearing sooner, though the authors warn the study had limited power for that claim. High starting virus levels slowed clearance in everyone. A wrinkle appeared by virus type: the short course looked strong in one genotype, while the dominant local genotype needs more proof before programs shorten care across the board.
pmc-13483659:
Mohammad Bidkhori and colleagues examine links between sleep and high blood pressure in older community adults in Ardakan, Iran. Their 2026 cross-sectional analysis uses cohort data collected from 2020 to 2022 for 5,872 participants aged 50 and older. Sleep quality was scored with a validated questionnaire, and blood pressure was measured with standard methods.

Participants with hypertension slept worse on every headline measure, including longer time to fall asleep and more frequent short sleep. Sleeping six to seven hours was linked to 28 percent lower odds of hypertension compared with the reference pattern. Poor sleep quality overall showed only a borderline link once other factors were adjusted. Because the design captures a single moment, the results cannot show whether poor sleep raises pressure or high pressure ruins sleep.
pmc-13483859:
Wang and colleagues removed a little-studied protein from one lung cell type in mice and watched lung scarring develop on its own. The protein, CAP1, was deleted only in type II alveolar cells, the cells that coat air sacs and repair them after injury. Their 2026 study then tracked survival, breathing mechanics, tissue structure, and gene activity in the altered lungs.

Mice lacking CAP1 died sooner than their normal littermates in the reported follow-up. A subset declined visibly, losing weight and activity while lung stiffness rose and breathing capacity fell. Tissue sections showed scarred, disorganized air sacs with immune cells crowding in, and standard fibrosis scores climbed. Gene scans highlighted scar-building pathways and changed signaling from complement 5, part of the immune alarm system. Wang proposes CAP1 helps keep air-sac cells stable.
pmc-13484459:
Rachedi and colleagues published a 2026 study on a simple liver scarring score in diabetes care. The FIB-4 score blends age, enzymes, and platelet counts from routine bloods. The team applied it to 600 patients with type 2 diabetes at one center. Records spanned nearly nine years of follow-up at the hospital.

Sixty-one percent of patients landed in the low-risk scarring band overall. Thirty-one percent sat in the middle band, and eight percent in the high band. Patients above the middle cutoff carried more microvascular complications of every kind. Heart vessel disease also clustered in the higher-score group significantly. A cheap score could flag who needs liver checks first, they argue. Care ran through one university hospital's diabetes and nutrition department.
pmc-13485659:
Joshua Levin presents a 2026 case of a leftover urinary tube stump causing infections decades after childhood kidney surgery. The patient, a 54-year-old woman, had surgery as a child for a doubled collecting system and now suffered repeated urinary infections. Scope examination found mucus and debris pooled inside the retained stump segment near the bladder.

Surgeons removed the stump and reimplanted the working ureter in a non-refluxing fashion because of its closeness to the stump. Infections resolved after the operation. The condition, called distal ureteral stump syndrome, affects roughly one in a hundred ureter surgery patients and is usually a childhood problem. Adult cases with murky surgical histories need deliberate consideration before repeated antibiotics are accepted as the only answer.
pmc-13486059:
Kelly Fernanda Molena tests three coats that may shield tooth enamel worn by decay and by cancer radiation. In this 2026 lab study, 180 enamel bits get fake decay plus a 70 Gray dose of radiation. Coats of biosilicate, chitosan gel, or fluoride gel go on before or after the dose, in ten groups in all. Hardness, surface grain, fine imaging, and chem scans grade each coat.

Fake decay broke up the enamel rods. Clean enamel that got radiation alone stayed the hardest of all. Timing shaped the ranks of the coats. Biosilicate gel and chitosan gel did best pre-dose. Biosilicate gel and fluoride gel did best post-dose. Imaging showed shield layers of fine grains on coated bits. Such coats may aid head and neck cancer patients, whose teeth take grave harm from radiation.
pmc-13487459:
Karjalainen and colleagues in Finland asked in 2026 how nursing students judged team based mentoring during hospital practice. Older one to one mentoring is giving way to team models in many wards. The team used survey data from 397 students who trained at Oulu University Hospital in 2019 and 2020. Students rated the ward as a place to learn and the help they got from mentors, and also wrote free text answers.

Three student profiles emerged from the scores. Ratings ran high when mentors backed the student's growth as a nurse. They also ran high when goals were talked through with a mentor and then met. Free text answers backed the same points, and stressed good prep before practice starts. Most students were glad with team practice overall. The authors urge wards to keep the setup safe, clear, and goal led.
pmc-13487959:
Fan Xia and co-authors examine blood transfusion needs after CAR T-cell therapy for multiple myeloma in a 2026 post-hoc analysis. The treatment engineers a patient's own immune cells to attack the blood cancer, yet it often damages blood counts for weeks. Records covered 155 people with relapsed or treatment-resistant disease who received CAR T cells aimed at different targets.

About four in ten patients needed transfusion in the first month, linked mainly to inflammation and weak marrow reserve, with little effect on survival. Later transfusion told a darker story, tracking with shallower responses, more deaths unrelated to relapse, and much shorter survival. The authors suggest that a lasting need for blood signals lasting marrow harm.
pmc-13488259:
Tesfa Marew, Anteneh Belete, Frances J. Richmond, and Tsige Gebre-Mariam survey medicine importers in Ethiopia in a 2026 survey study. The country depends on medicines brought in from abroad, which leaves supply exposed to currency and policy shocks. Seventy-eight staff at import firms were invited through sampling by group, and seventy-one filled in an online survey about products, business conditions, and how the national drug regulator performs.

Most firms were private companies acting for makers in Asia and Europe, bringing in mainly germ-fighting drugs, painkillers, and gut and heart medicines. More than three quarters called the import climate hard to predict and stuck in a downturn, blaming shortages of foreign currency, policy barriers, and slow approvals. Views on the regulator were largely positive, though how it deals with firms and how open it is drew criticism.
pmc-13488559:
Ahmet Selim Basaran and Behchet Cosar report a 2026 case of psychosis flaring during chatbot use in a 33-year-old man with schizophrenia. He had been stable on a daily antipsychotic tablet, with past episodes built on persecution and ideas that outside events referred to him personally. About twenty days before seeking care, he began using a large language model chatbot for everyday tasks and asked it about home and device monitoring.

Generic safety tips about permissions and passwords were reinterpreted as coded personal warnings, fueling repeated checking of outlets and devices. He stopped his medication to read the supposed signals more clearly, and symptoms escalated sharply on standard scales. Restarting the prior drug dose and targeted education formed the response, and the authors advise asking about AI use in psychiatric reviews.
pmc-13491659:
Chongli Yu and four co-authors mine United States adverse event reports in 2026 for yeast infections linked to secukinumab, a psoriasis drug that blocks interleukin-17A. That immune signal helps defend skin and mucous membranes against Candida, so blocking it may invite infection. The authors catalogued which infections were reported, how serious they were, and when they began.

Reports filed from 2004 to early 2025 yielded 1,075 Candida events, most in the mouth, food pipe, or genital area. Genital candidiasis showed the strongest reporting signal, and more than half of events counted as serious. Signals ran higher in women and in adults aged eighteen to sixty-four. Most events began within two to three months, pointing to close monitoring early in treatment.
pmc-13493759:
Ko and colleagues describe who received ritlecitinib, a drug approved in the United States in June 2023 for severe alopecia areata, during its first ten months on the market. Alopecia areata is an autoimmune condition where the body attacks hair follicles and hair falls out in patches or completely. The 2026 study drew on two large American health databases and covered 2,562 patients aged 12 and older with at least one prescription.

Dermatologists wrote most prescriptions, nearly six in ten patients were female, and adolescents made up about a third of the group. Roughly a quarter had the most extensive forms of hair loss, and many carried other autoimmune, allergy-related, or mental health diagnoses alongside. Three quarters had tried another alopecia treatment in the previous year, suggesting earlier options had fallen short for them. About a quarter had no recorded prior treatment at all, which the authors read as unmet need.
pmc-13494559:
Liu and colleagues showed that the enzyme AID acts as a matchmaker that pulls distant DNA regions together, in a 2026 molecular biology study. AID starts class switch recombination, the process letting immune cells swap antibody types, by chemically altering DNA letters inside switch regions. How AID handles the DNA structures was unclear.

Liu combined biochemistry with single-molecule imaging and found AID binds and stabilizes multistranded DNA structures, including the R-loops formed when RNA sticks to DNA during gene reading. Two DNA-gripping pockets on the enzyme cooperate to hold the synapsis, the pairing of segments, together. Molecule tracking showed AID clustering as it binds. A version of the enzyme that performed its chemical editing but could not self-assemble failed at synapsis, proving the organizing role is separate from the editing chemistry. The findings recast AID as an architect of the recombination it starts.
pmc-13495159:
Đặng Phương Nam and colleagues present a 2026 case report of saving a hand after a flesh-destroying infection by Vibrio vulnificus, a sea germ that can enter through small wounds. A 62-year-old Vietnamese man with hepatitis B and alcohol use pricked his left hand on a tilapia fin. Swelling, blisters, and dying tissue followed, then septic shock that needed intensive support and a breathing machine.

Cultures confirmed the germ, and surgery found the deep infection, forcing wide removal of dead tissue. To rebuild skin and tendon in one stage, surgeons moved a combined flap from his thigh, pairing skin with a sheet of tough tissue. Wound care with suction therapy bridged the steps. At eighteen months the hand worked and looked far better. The authors stress fast, bold cleaning of the wound once the patient is stable, and name the combined flap a key tool for such salvage.
pmc-13495259:
Şekip Yazgan and co-authors test, in a 2026 study, whether inequality in ecological footprint across European Union countries fades on its own or sticks. Fair climate policy needs to know if gaps are passing shocks or lasting structure. The team tracked three inequality measures, built from footprint data from 1961 to 2024, and ran a battery of statistical tests for persistence.

The answer hinged on the test. Plain tests called the series steady, hinting gaps self-correct. Richer tests that allow bends, breaks, and slow memory found stronger signs of staying power. A long-memory model placed the process near the edge of non-steadiness, meaning shocks linger for a long time. The authors conclude that footprint gaps will not melt away unaided and that deep, long-term structural policy is needed to close them.
pmc-13495359:
Samarasiri and co-authors explored a 2026 food study fermenting okara, the soy pulp left over from tofu and soymilk making, with oyster mushroom mycelium. Okara is nutritious but perishable, rough, and bland, so most of the huge global output goes to waste. Fungal fermentation might turn it into a tasty alternative food.

The mycelium grew fastest and densest on fresh, undried okara, with wheat bran mixtures taking eleven to twelve days to colonise. Fermentation raised nitrogen content, signalling more protein, and multiplied sugars, free amino acids, and flavour nucleotides several fold. Samarasiri measured taste with an electronic tongue, an instrument that scores flavour qualities. Sourness fell while umami, the savoury taste, and richness rose clearly after fermentation.
pmc-13495859:
Pragti and colleagues design, in a 2026 chemistry study, metal-free light-activated molecules that both attack cancer cells and light up their inner compartments. Light therapy drugs work best in near-infrared, which penetrates tissue, yet most organic versions absorb only visible light. Guided by computer calculations, the team built star-shaped pyrylium dyes tuned by an electronegativity rule to drink in near-infrared light.

The dyes absorbed strongly across the deep-red band, glowed far from their absorption color, and resisted fading. Under near-infrared light the lead dye drained a key cell fuel and spawned several kinds of reactive oxygen, even where oxygen was scarce, a common shield for tumors. In breast cancer cells it wrecked the redox balance and killed efficiently, while imaging the lysosomes at fine detail. The authors frame the design rule as a template for combined therapy-and-imaging agents.
pmc-13496059:
Bunuasunthon and colleagues tackle a problem in tissue engineering: cells in the middle of thick lab-grown tissue starve for oxygen and die. One fix mixes calcium peroxide into the gel, where it slowly releases oxygen. The enzyme catalase, added to neutralise a toxic by-product, usually fizzes so fast the gel blows apart within an hour. Their 2026 strategy coats the gel's surface with catalase instead of mixing it through.

Coated gels produced bubbles several times smaller than mixed gels after a day, and the structures held together. Under near-zero oxygen, centimetre-scale constructs with the coating kept the large majority of human fibroblast cells alive after five days, against under half in uncoated versions. Human neural stem cells also survived better and grew more nerve fibres in the coated constructs. The authors propose the coating trick for building thick replacement tissues.
pmc-13498659:
Giampiero I Baroncelli leads a panel of Italian child bone specialists offering in 2026 practical guidance on fractures caused by fragile bones in children and teenagers. Many childhood breaks come from accidents, yet some signal weak bones from inherited or secondary disease, and recognition can be delayed. The panel met online between November 2024 and June 2025, combining clinical experience with a review of published work.

Their statements cover seven areas, from defining fragility fractures and childhood osteoporosis to causes, chances of natural recovery, and drug and non-drug care. Genetic testing holds a central place for inherited forms, since it can pin down the cause. Bisphosphonate drugs, which slow bone breakdown, remain the main treatment, while measures to build bone strength may help selected patients, and some damaged vertebrae can reshape as children grow.
pmc-13499159:
Brittany Lemmon and colleagues survey in 2026 public support in the United States for warning labels about added sugar on chain restaurant menus. Trials show such labels steer diners toward meals with less added sugar, and New York City has already required them. Less was known about support among groups at higher risk of diet-related disease, who might gain most, so the team asked a large online sample matched to national demographics.

Across 15,275 adults, every subgroup examined showed majority support, with opposition low everywhere. Support ran higher among people with prediabetes and among those already trying to cut added sugar. Lower income and lower education linked to somewhat lower support, and groups not trying to cut sugar often answered that they had no opinion, which the authors flag for outreach.
pmc-13499959:
Barliz Waissengrin and colleagues mine in 2026 online conversations to learn how people with cancer actually use dietary supplements during treatment. Surveys often miss unfiltered patient motives, so the team turned to the Reddit community r/cancer, using language-processing tools to find supplement posts published between November 2010 and December 2022. From 1,488 matching posts they analysed a random tenth in depth, sorting posts by purpose, intended use, and supplement type.

Most sampled posts asked questions rather than reporting experience, and intent split almost evenly between treating the cancer itself and managing symptoms. Vitamins were the supplement named most often, and breast, lung, and colorectal cancers dominated among posters who named their disease. Fatigue, nausea, pain, and emotional distress drove much of the interest, often as strategies outside conventional care, which the authors say clinicians should raise openly in visits.
pmc-13500459:
Vadim G Bogatyr and colleagues introduce in 2026 a method for watching single messenger RNA molecules as they are made in a test tube, a step toward building artificial cells. Lab transcription systems usually flood reactions with far more DNA than a real cell holds, masking single-copy behaviour. Their approach uses a molecular beacon, a hairpin probe that stays dark until it binds its target RNA and lights up. Template DNA carrying many repeats of the beacon's binding site boosts the signal.

Fluorescence tracking resolved individual transcripts both in open solution and inside giant fatty bubbles used as cell mimics. The team benchmarked several commercial transcription kits against each other with the technique and measured how single molecules behave inside the bubbles quantitatively. The method gives synthetic biology a sharper lens for the core process that turns DNA instructions into working RNA.
pmc-13500559:
Jaehyeok Lee leads a 2026 laboratory study of a Philippine medicinal plant, Premna odorata, known locally as alagaw and used traditionally for inflamed airways. Molecular proof for its effects was lacking, so the team tested its extract against the NLRP3 inflammasome, an intracellular alarm complex whose product, interleukin-1 beta, drives many inflammatory diseases. Two macrophage cell lines were primed and then triggered with standard activators.

The extract cut interleukin-1 beta release triggered through the target complex while leaving two sibling alarm complexes untouched, showing selectivity in the reported assays. It blocked assembly of the complex by preventing its adaptor protein from clumping, without killing cells or changing reactive oxygen levels. In a zebrafish inflammation model, the extract reduced inflammatory cell infiltration, giving the traditional remedy a defined molecular basis and a scaffold for targeted drug design.
pmc-13500659:
Ziheng Wu and colleagues test in 2026 a plant compound against osteosarcoma, the aggressive bone cancer of teenagers, looking for options beyond punishing chemotherapy. The compound, irisquinone, comes from the dried roots of an iris used in traditional Chinese medicine and had shown anti-tumour effects in other cancers. Computer-based target prediction pointed first at a growth signalling route called PI3K/AKT, with one protein in it flagged as the likely core target, guiding the laboratory work that followed.

Cell experiments showed the compound suppressing cancer cell growth and migration in the reported assays. Mechanistically it dampened activation of the flagged pathway and shifted the balance of two death-regulating proteins toward cell suicide, triggering programmed death in the tumour cells. A mouse graft model confirmed the anti-tumour effect and pathway control in living tissue, giving the natural product preclinical support as a candidate for drug development.
pmc-13501659:
Umit Uysal leads a nine-author team reporting a 2026 comparison of three surgical risk scores for patients having a kidney removed because of a tumour. The retrospective study covered 148 radical nephrectomy patients treated between January 2022 and March 2025. Scores tested were POSSUM, E-PASS, and its modified version mE-PASS, each computed from body and operative data. The team also checked inflammation and nutrition markers, including the prognostic nutritional index and the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, against complications graded by the Clavien-Dindo system.

Complications of grade 2 or higher struck 51 patients, some 34.5 percent of the cohort. POSSUM predicted them best, with an area under the curve of 0.810, sensitivity of 82.4 percent, and specificity of 71.1 percent on the reported figures. E-PASS reached an AUC of 0.682, while mE-PASS managed only 0.599, barely better than chance. Patients with complications also showed lower nutritional index values and higher neutrophil ratios.
pmc-13501859:
Longhao Wang leads a twelve-author team reporting a 2026 study of the enzyme USP20 as a driver of immune suppression and poor outlook in lung adenocarcinoma. The team profiled the gene across the TCGA, GTEx, and GEO cohorts, checked survival with Kaplan-Meier and Cox models, and mapped the immune landscape with estimation algorithms. Single-cell datasets resolved which cell types carry it, and tissue staining plus cell and animal experiments tested the biology.

USP20 ran high in tumours compared with normal lung, and patients with the highest levels survived less well, with the gene standing as an independent risk factor. Its copies were more often amplified than mutated. High expression came with reshaped immune cell mixtures, more suppressive populations, and higher checkpoint molecule levels. Laboratory work confirmed the protein pushes cancer cell growth and migration. The authors nominate USP20 as a prognostic marker and an immunotherapy target.
pmc-13502359:
Samuel Schwartz leads a five-author team reporting a 2026 case where an infected heart device masqueraded as a stroke. An 87-year-old man with a resynchronization defibrillator arrived after an unwitnessed fall, speaking slurred words with a drooping face and uneven limb weakness. His stroke scale score was 10, no heart murmur was heard, and head CT showed nothing acute. Magnetic imaging, the test that would settle the brain picture, could not be done: his older device was not labelled MRI-conditional.

The story turned in the blood cultures, which grew Streptococcus agalactiae as his kidneys failed, platelets fell, and bilirubin climbed. A transoesophageal echocardiogram then found a mobile vegetation clinging to the defibrillator lead, confirming device-related infective endocarditis as the true source, with brain symptoms likely embolic. The authors urge early transoesophageal imaging whenever neurological deficits meet fever, positive cultures, or systemic toxicity in a device carrier.
pmc-13503659:
Santiago García-Lloré, Richard C. Stedman, and Angela K. Fuller built a 2026 model to predict clashes between people and wildlife in parks and reserves. Such clashes harm farm income and can lead to animals being killed. Their tool is a Bayesian belief network, a chart that links causes to risk with chance values.

The team surveyed 1,011 rangers in 135 protected areas across three Andean countries. Rangers reported harm to crops and stock, killing of wild animals, and threats to people and goods. The model points to rule quality, public acceptance of wildlife, and local voice in park work as key drivers. Tests show that better rules and wider acceptance could cut risk by more than 85 percent.
pmc-13503759:
Oladoyin Kolawole, Matthew O. Sonibare, and Olufemi Olorode test whether grout can restore cracked rock around deep tunnels, in a 2026 study. Cracks from digging and stress shifts cut the strength of the rock walls. Grout is often pumped in, but how much pull strength it gives back was not well known.

The team split disc samples of limestone, dolomite, and printed rock, then grouted some and split them again. Grout did not bring back full pull strength. It did steer cracks, shorten their total length, and make breaks more local and controlled. A computer model with stick-slip crack rules matched the lab work. It showed later damage onset and more sideways energy loss after grouting.
pmc-13503859:
Yihan Xie leads a team mapping how opioid dependence reshapes brain cells in female mice that carry a human gene variant, in a 2026 study. The variant, in the main opioid receptor gene, raises the risk of addiction in people. Mice with the matching change show like shifts in drug response.

The team read gene activity cell by cell across brain regions, with maps of where each cell sat. Mice with two copies of the variant showed the strongest shifts in glial cells, the support cells of the brain, rather than in neurons. Gene network analysis tied the variant to organized changes across regions and cell types. The work sketches how inherited risk steers the brain's response to long opioid use.
pmc-13504959:
Gao and colleagues set out in 2026 how to build a rat model of recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, a throat nerve whose damage can paralyse a vocal cord. Such models guide work on nerve monitoring during thyroid surgery, but the usual pig model is costly and slow. The team operated on 24 rats, creating three injury types that mimic surgical accidents: traction, clamping, and cutting of the nerve.

Gao watched vocal cord movement with a rat-sized throat scope before surgery and weekly for four weeks after. All injury groups showed one-sided paralysis or incomplete closure in the first three weeks. By week four, the traction group had fully recovered and a few clamping rats had too, but most clamping and all cutting cases stayed impaired. Nerve signal readings fell and recovered in step with cord movement. Rat traction results matched the pig model, supporting rats as a cheaper stand-in.
pmc-13505059:
Ravi Shankar leads a team piloting a home exergaming rehab program for adults with functional disabilities in Singapore, in a 2026 study. Community rehab faces tight access and poor exercise follow-through. A game-based platform with remote therapist watch could stretch services into homes.

Ten adults from three community sites used the system at home for thirty active days inside an eighteen-week plan, with a family caregiver present at each session. On average they met about four fifths of their exercise plan, near twenty-four minutes a day. Independence, balance, and grip scores improved by the final check, and quality-of-life symptom scores eased. One walking test gain faded by follow-up. The authors call the program feasible and welcome, pending a larger trial.
pmc-13505959:
Whelan and Hall wrote a 2026 review celebrating and scrutinizing the 16S rRNA gene, the workhorse marker that microbiome science uses to census bacterial communities. The gene occurs in all prokaryotes, the group of bacteria and archaea, yet varies enough between species that sequencing its variable stretches can distinguish community members. Carl Woese pioneered its use for evolutionary relationships in the nineteen seventies, and sequencing platforms turned it into a mass tool.

Whelan traces how the method uncovered microbial diversity across environments. It illuminated the microbiome's role in gut diseases such as Crohn's disease, while warning of its limits: the full gene cannot always separate close relatives. Primer and pipeline choices skew results. With whole-genome shotgun sequencing now available, the authors argue the method still suits focused questions and budgets. The authors predict this influential gene has not finished revealing the microbial world, provided researchers heed its caveats.
pmc-13506159:
Rong and colleagues tested PainScan, a visualization-based training platform their team built, in a 2026 mixed-methods randomized trial at a Shanghai children's hospital. The platform teaches pediatric intensive care nurses how to assess pain in critically ill children. Seventy nurses were randomized to four weeks of platform training or traditional on-site training, with assessors blinded to group, and eleven platform trainees were later interviewed about the experience.

Rong found both approaches clearly raised knowledge and skill scores, but the platform produced superior skill development compared with on-site training, while knowledge gains matched. Interviewees credited realistic, vivid case presentations, flexible scheduling, and personalized features for a satisfying learning experience, and the platform cost less to run. They also flagged weak supervision, engagement, and continuity as areas to fix. The authors recommend the platform as practical training while warning that scaling it up needs those improvements.
pmc-13507059:
Yanmei Yuan leads a 2026 team that links a RNA-handling protein, TDP-43, to asthma attacks and flu spread in airway lining cells. Allergen exposure raised TDP-43 in those cells. The protein weakened a cleanup system that destroys faulty RNA copies, so harmful copies built up, including one for a receptor that tightens airways.

The same protein also helped influenza A virus copy itself in airway cells. Nose-delivered particles carrying gene-silencing strands against TDP-43 eased asthma-like disease in mice. Current asthma drugs mostly target one immune branch and do not stop return attacks. Aiming at TDP-43 could offer a new path for asthma care and for flu-worsened attacks.
pmc-13507259:
Jana Kurcova leads a 2026 team that re-tests how to monitor palladium catalysts that switch on caged drugs and dyes inside living systems, a field called bioorthogonal chemistry. Catalyst survival in salty, protein-rich fluids is doubtful, and sulfur compounds in cells can poison metal centers. Fourteen fluorescent probes, the largest such library yet, tracked activity for days in serum and hours in cells.

One ligand, triphenylantimony, gave unmatched catalyst longevity and sulfur tolerance. Probe choice mattered as much as catalyst choice: some probes shine in dishes but wash out of cells too fast for body use. Most dye products leaked from cells, limiting long tracking. Universal catalyst hopes look misplaced; pairs must be matched case by case.
pmc-13508259:
Ronghua Hong and eight co-authors test scan-guided botulinum toxin shots for the stooped posture seen in Parkinson disease, in 2026 work. Toxin shots can relax the muscles pulling the trunk forward, and a nuclear scan can show which muscles are overactive. Twenty-nine patients had the scan, a baseline posture check, then guided injections. Trunk bend angles, pain, and life quality were checked again after one month.

Results disappointed the team. Sideways bend eased a little, but forward bend did not improve as hoped, and few patients gained a large angle change. About four in ten patients still felt at least slight benefit, and a third reported clear pain relief. Eleven side effects occurred, none serious, mostly brief worsening or back pain. The authors call the approach safe but weaker than expected, and urge work to find which patients it truly helps.
pmc-13508359:
Yujun Zhang and Xingxing Jiang compare outcomes when keyhole gallbladder surgery goes smoothly against when it proves difficult in elderly patients, in 2026 work. The single-center review covered operations from January 2023 to December 2024. Patients were grouped by whether the surgery finished cleanly by keyhole or counted as a difficult case. The team compared operating time, blood loss, recovery speed, complications, and blood markers of inflammation.

The smooth group had shorter operations, less blood loss, and gentler rises in inflammation markers after surgery. Those patients also passed gas and ate sooner, stayed fewer days, and reported less pain. Complications hit 7.5 percent of the smooth group versus 30 percent of the difficult group. A high anesthesia risk class and two or more other illnesses independently predicted complications. The authors say the operation is broadly safe in older patients, with difficulty level the key warning sign.
pmc-13508459:
Yang Li, Ya-Die Liu, Zhi-Ying Jiang, and Hong-Xiang Lu hunt the starter cells that seed liver spread in pancreatic cancer, in 2026 work. Pancreatic ductal cancer is highly lethal, and liver spread decides most outcomes. The team merged bulk gene data, single-cell reading, and spatial maps from several patient groups. A learning tool sorted true cancer cells, and three trajectory methods traced which cells sit at the start of the path toward spread.

One subgroup of cancer cells stood at that origin point. These starter cells mixed shape-shifting traits with stem-like traits and carried high levels of two receptor genes. Patients rich in these cells fared worse and answered immune therapy poorly. Nearby support cells release a signal that docks on one of those receptors, and the two cell types clustered together in tissue. Dish tests backed the signal's role in movement and invasion.
pmc-13509559:
Zhou and Cai improved a search algorithm modeled on the secretary bird, a long-legged hunter. Applied it to visual design problems such as harmonious color palettes and page layouts. Their 2026 study notes that design goals are bumpy, many-peaked mathematical landscapes where the algorithm loses diversity, settles too early, and balances wide search against fine-tuning poorly.

Zhou added three fixes: a even initial population that covers the search space uniformly, a lens-based trick that flips weaker solutions to escape local traps while keeping the elite. An adaptive mutation mixing two random patterns applied to the best solution. On the CEC2017 benchmark suite across four problem sizes, checked with three statistical tests against nine rival algorithms, the enhanced version converged faster and more stably to better solutions. It also beat the original and competitors on both design tasks, confirming its value for computational aesthetics.
pmc-13509859:
Jorge Hallak, Robert John Aitken, João Sallum Hallak, Ana Flávia Quiarato Lozano, and Thiago Afonso Teixeira review oxidative stress in male fertility and how clinics should handle it, in 2026 work. Oxidative stress means an excess of reactive oxygen forms that can harm sperm. Small amounts of these reactive forms help sperm work, yet too much damages them. The review covers sources of excess, from white blood cells and infections to lifestyle, heat-related vein swelling, metabolic disease, and metal exposure.

Lab tests for oxidative stress exist in several forms, each with limits in accuracy, shared standards, and fit for daily clinic use. Taking antioxidant pills without first proving stress is present may explain mixed trial results and can even push the balance too far the other way. The authors argue for testing first, treating the root cause, and tailoring care to each man.
pmc-13511159:
Marcucci and colleagues studied how the chemistry of seminal plasma, the fluid carrying sperm, relates to sperm function in men whose semen counts as normal by World Health Organization standards. Their 2026 study measured marker chemicals and enzyme levels plus antioxidant capacity in both the fluid and the sperm cells, then tracked them against sperm shape, movement, and survival.

Marcucci found that several fluid markers, including albumin, cholesterol, a cell-damage enzyme, and homocysteine, tracked downward with normal sperm shape and forward movement. Meanwhile prostate-specific antigen tracked upward with sperm quality. Men in the low-normal range showed higher levels of these stress and inflammation markers than high-normal men. Their sperm carried more antioxidants, which the authors read as making up for stress rather than protection. The results argue that limits mark a gradient of how well the system works, not a sharp line between normal and abnormal.
pmc-13511359:
Ju Ae Shin, Min Soo Kim, and Moon-Yeon Oh compare treatment timing for a heart vessel that stays open after birth in very small newborns, in 2026 work. They also weigh its link to lung bleeding. The vessel, called the ductus, normally closes soon after birth, and a lasting opening is tied to a life-threatening bleed into the lungs. Using a national Korean registry from 2013 to 2024, the team studied 23,500 very low birth weight infants and weighted comparisons to balance illness severity.

Treating before symptoms appeared went with a lower observed risk of lung bleeding than treating after symptoms, across several checks. Preventive treatment from birth showed no such protection and carried higher risk than the pre-symptom route, likely because the sickest infants are chosen for it. The authors stress the findings generate hypotheses only and argue for planned trials of risk-based early treatment, not blanket prevention.
pmc-13513159:
Vinnie-Siow and colleagues reviewed global evidence from 2020 to 2026 on which mosquitoes carry chikungunya virus, a germ that causes fever and often long-lasting joint pain. Their 2026 review combined 56 records: 34 from field surveillance of wild mosquitoes and 22 from laboratory tests of whether mosquitoes can transmit the virus.

Aedes aegypti was the species found positive most often, confirmed in 22 of the 29 field studies that checked it. Aedes albopictus ranked second, positive in nine of 12 studies. The two species differ in habits: one thrives in cities and homes, while the other adapts to many settings and is spreading into cooler regions. The authors say knowing which species dominates locally should guide mosquito control during outbreaks.
pmc-13514259:
Zhixia Zhao, Huizi Liu, Sheng Yang, Xing Liu, Qiuxia Chen, and Jinwang Wang catalog the full bHLH switch-gene family in a salt-tough mangrove tree, in 2026 work. The family steers growth, stress adaptation, and metabolism in plants, yet it had never been mapped in Kandelia obovata, a mangrove famous for thriving where land meets sea. Searches of the genome found 118 family loci, which were sorted into eighteen branches and profiled across roots, stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits.

Organs favored different family members, suggesting three broad job groups. Salt exposure at three strengths switched 61 of the genes, clustered into ten response patterns. A co-expression network distilled twenty hub genes at the center of the response. Two hubs tied closely to secondary chemistry stand out in the full account. The authors offer the catalog as a base for breeding and engineering salt tolerance.
pmc-13514759:
Ming Chen and five co-authors chart the link between body mass index and physical fitness in a 2026 cross-sectional study of nearly fifteen thousand university students in Gansu Province, China. Their campus sits at roughly 1,483 metres, a sub-plateau setting where such data are scarce. Students completed seven fitness components, from vital capacity and sprint speed to endurance and flexibility, combined into a single standardised fitness index.

Fitness fell steadily as body mass index rose, rather than tracing the curved pattern reported in lowland groups. Underweight and normal-weight students performed about equally, while overweight and obese students scored progressively lower, and the slide ran stronger in men than in women. A weight-adjusted lung capacity measure showed the tightest tie to body mass, followed by endurance, whereas flexibility barely moved.
pmc-13515259:
Kai Xing and colleagues report an engineering study, published in 2026. It covers polishing the inner wall of metal tubing. The cobalt-chromium tubing is used for blood vessel stents. Magnetic abrasive finishing smooths the surface. It uses magnetic polishing powder. The team sought machine settings for the smoothest finish. The tubing is under two millimetres wide.

Experiments varied several settings. They covered rotation speed and magnet feed rate. Abrasive size and working gap were also varied. A model predicted surface roughness very accurately. It combined particle swarm optimisation with a support vector machine. At the model's best settings, measured roughness matched the prediction. The match was within a small fraction. This confirms the approach for stent tubing production.
pmc-13517159:
Dayan Elshan and colleagues report a coronavirus pill candidate built to be swallowed, in a 2026 drug-discovery paper. The virus's main protease cuts its own proteins into working parts, and blocking that enzyme stops replication. The best-known blocker, nirmatrelvir, uses a nitrile warhead that grips the enzyme's key cysteine. This team pursued a different grip, a hydroxymethyl ketone, prized for gentler reactivity and cleaner selectivity.

Earlier drugs of this family failed as pills because the body absorbed them poorly, forcing drip delivery. The team's lead compound, mCMX110, beat that history: stronger potency, more free drug reaching circulation, and favourable oral absorption in animal studies. Elshan and colleagues present it as proof that the alternative warhead can yield a practical tablet. Keeping chemically distinct antivirals ready matters for future outbreaks and for variants that shrug off today's drugs.
pmc-13518459:
Martin Kopáni and six colleagues take stock of the iron stored in a deep brain hub in a 2026 study. The globus pallidus gathers more iron than almost any brain region, and loose iron can feed the oxidative damage behind degeneration. Post-mortem tissue from six people without neurological disease was examined with five techniques at once: staining, Raman light fingerprints, two kinds of electron microscopy, and elemental analysis.

Iron sat in round inclusions ten to twenty micrometres wide. The fingerprints named a mixture: magnetite, maghemite, hematite, and ferritin-like material, tangled with protein and fat signals. Element scans found fellow travellers including aluminium, silicon, calcium, and nickel. The deposits were thus messy, mixed oxides of varying crystal order, not one tidy mineral. Kopáni's team notes such phases could hold reactive iron, while stressing their study measured no damage, so healthy-versus-harmful remains open.
pmc-13518859:
Hedi Jedli and five colleagues model in 2026 how activated carbon made from olive waste soaks up two common dyes, methylene blue and methyl orange, from water. Dye pollution from industry harms ecosystems and health, and adsorption onto carbon is a favored cleanup route. The team characterized their carbon with X-ray and microscope methods.

Adsorption was measured at three temperatures and fitted with a statistical physics model. Methylene blue was taken up slightly more than methyl orange. Each dye occupied roughly one to two sites per molecule, with orientation shifting as temperature changed. Warming reduced uptake, marking the process as heat-releasing, and modest energy values pointed to physical rather than chemical binding.
pmc-13518959:
Mingshi Chen and four colleagues test in 2026 whether radiomics, a texture-mining method for images, can sharpen predictions of antidepressant response in major depression from brain scans. Most patients miss out on their first-line drug, and standard scan analysis averages activity across regions, wasting detail. Their preregistered analysis used emotional-conflict fMRI from 254 trial outpatients.

Clinical variables carried the strongest signal throughout. Combined models could predict placebo response at week one, though not sertraline response. Radiomic models underperformed for sertraline, while whole-brain features helped modestly, and early clinical measures outranked every imaging feature. Chen and co-authors conclude the added value of emotional-conflict scans and radiomics looks limited for this purpose.
pmc-13519459:
Dona Soman and colleagues measured muscle and joint pain among dental practitioners in Rwanda. Published in 2026, the survey used stratified random sampling to reach 268 dentists, with questionnaires analyzed in standard statistics software. Dentistry demands long hours in fixed, awkward postures, so work-related strain is a known hazard of the craft.

More than four fifths reported a musculoskeletal disorder, with neck pain most common, followed by lower back and wrist or hand pain. Repeat motions, too few breaks between procedures, and more workdays per week each tracked with higher risk. The authors call for ergonomic training and preventive routines, from posture coaching to scheduled breaks. Readers get both a prevalence snapshot and levers clinics can pull right away.
pmc-13520359:
Jonathon Zagler and colleagues report in 2026 on a training course built with Aboriginal community partners in Australia. The course helps aged care staff give safe and respectful care to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander elders. An Aboriginal led aged care group helped design the course from the start.

Reading and a staff survey shaped the course content. Design workshops came next. A pilot then ran across city, regional and remote sites in South Australia in 2024. Staff praised the course in follow-up talks. They also named clear lessons learned. Talks covered how the course might grow to new sites while keeping its strong community roots.
pmc-13520459:
Matteo Giachino and colleagues describe in 2026 a surgical move for rare femoral head fractures. A lower inner fragment can resist straight realignment. Soft tissue folds near the fragment act like a tight strap. Forceful moves risk the blood supply of the ball.

Lifting a small flap of bone lining frees the strap while keeping its vessels whole. The fragment can then shift in a controlled way. The note covers Pipkin type I and II breaks. Type I sits below the central pit of the ball, and type II extends above it. Surgeons gain a gentle add-on when standard moves fail.
pmc-13520659:
Riley B. Pizza and colleagues survey in 2026 how holding a second marginalised identity shapes college life for science students with disabilities. Most past work looked at disability alone, which can hide sharp differences inside that group.

Responses covered 947 undergraduates at 85 United States institutions, including 379 students with disabilities. Half of the disabled group identified as LGBTQ+, a share far above the non-disabled group. LGBTQ+ students with disabilities reported notably more negative academic and social experiences than peers without that added identity. Findings suggest some hardships blamed on disability alone may partly reflect this overlap.
pmc-13522459:
Weronika Kamińska-Skrzyńska and co-authors report a 2026 qualitative study of support as experienced by cancer patients receiving palliative care in Malta. Thirty adults were interviewed in depth during the summer of 2024. Their accounts were analyzed for recurring themes about support given, support received, and what feeling supported actually meant.

Patients valued medical staff who recognized them as persons rather than treating them impersonally. Feeling supported also meant keeping up daily routines and social ties, often with encouragement from relatives. Participants gave support as well, helping family with tasks, sharing news about their illness, and preparing keepsakes to leave behind. The findings place relationships and ordinary daily life at the center of good palliative support.
pmc-13523359:
Nor Azian Mohd Zaki and colleagues measure obesity-related hypertension in Malaysian adults in a 2026 analysis of a national health survey. More than ten thousand adults surveyed in 2023 were classified using body mass, waist size, and blood pressure, with the combined condition requiring general obesity, abdominal obesity, and hypertension together. Regression accounted for the survey's complex sampling design.

One in ten adults met the combined definition, with similar shares having obesity only or hypertension only. Odds were higher in women, in adults aged sixty or older, and in those with lower education. Physical inactivity, diabetes, and high cholesterol each added independent risk, with diabetes the strongest factor. The authors call for integrated prevention in primary care and national disease programs aimed at this combined burden.
pmc-13524459:
Sripriya Rao and colleagues evaluated a vast cervical cancer screening effort across 20 Indian states built on HPV DNA testing. Women could give samples themselves or have a clinician collect them, and positive cases were treated in the same visit where possible.

The program screened 62,868 women between 2022 and 2025 and found high-risk HPV in about 8.5 percent of them. Most infections came from types other than 16 and 18, the two best-known cancer-linked strains. The see-and-treat route scored high on accuracy, yet only about half of the community women needing treatment completed it. Rao argues the model is sound but needs organised follow-up and digital tracking to close that gap.
pmc-13524859:
Sushmitha Grama Srinivasan and others describe, in a 2026 letter, the design and thinking behind a phase 1 study adding palbociclib to salvage chemotherapy for children with relapsed acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Results after relapse remain poor, and many children relapse even after cellular therapy. A drug blocking cell-cycle kinases CDK4 and CDK6 looked hopeful because the leukemia cells rarely lose the protein those kinases control.

Earlier lab work backed palbociclib alone and paired with bortezomib, and bortezomib itself had worked in relapsed disease. The trial therefore raises oral doses of the drug alongside dexamethasone, bortezomib, and doxorubicin, with approvals and guardian consent in place. The authors frame the regimen as a bridge plan, since cellular therapy works better at low disease burden and chemotherapy is needed while those cells are made.
pmc-13525059:
Yukinori Kurokawa leads a large Japanese team reporting, in a 2026 paper, three-year results from the JCOG1704 phase II trial of preoperative chemotherapy for stomach cancer with extensive lymph node spread. Such marginally resectable disease has poor prospects even after complete removal. An older two-drug regimen had set a provisional standard.

Forty-seven patients with bulky nodal disease, spread to nodes near the aorta, or both, received three cycles of docetaxel, oxaliplatin, and S-1 before surgery, followed by a year of S-1. Among 46 eligible patients, three-year overall survival reached 86.7 percent and progression-free survival 75.6 percent at the May 2025 cutoff. Outcomes held across nodal subgroups. The authors judged the regimen a provisional standard within their cooperative group without waiting for a phase III trial.
pmc-13525859:
Almaaita and colleagues survey a no-drill dentistry method in this 2026 study of pediatric dentists in Jordan. The Hall Technique treats decayed baby molars by sealing the lesion under a preformed metal crown without removing any decay, letting the sealed bacteria starve. Despite strong trial evidence, uptake varies worldwide, so the team measured knowledge, attitudes, and practices among 120 Jordanian specialists in late 2025.

Understanding and adoption both ran high: 98.3 percent grasped how sealing arrests decay, and 86.7 percent already used the technique in practice, rates above many countries. Believing it saves time was the strongest adoption predictor, multiplying the odds of use by 8.58 in the regression model, with belief in the evidence base also helping. Worries about bite changes, at 54.2 percent, and about sealing over decay and parental acceptance, each 45.0 percent, were the main brakes. Attitudes overall were strongly positive.
pmc-13526859:
Xue and co-authors presented a 2026 computing study that speeds up lattice Boltzmann simulation, a method that tracks particle distributions to model fluid flow. Step by step simulation is accurate but slow at large scales. Their neural operator learns to jump far ahead in time while keeping the physics built into its design.

The model matches key physical quantities and respects symmetry in the distribution field, so it keeps the kinetic structure of the flow. Xue trained it on coarse grids and then ran it on finer grids, even when a relaxation setting differed between them. The same design also worked across different lattice Boltzmann formulations. Tests covered vortex shedding behind obstacles, ligament breakup, and bubbles sticking to surfaces.
pmc-13527959:
Syed Abdullah Basit and Tanvir Alam present a 2026 deep-learning system that reads retinal photographs to flag cardiovascular risk. The eye's tiny blood vessels mirror the health of vessels elsewhere in the body. Their pipeline first separates arteries from veins in fundus images. It then extracts 34 measures of vessel width, branching, and winding.

Those eye measures were combined with fifteen simple clinical values, such as age, body mass index, and blood pressure. No blood tests were needed. In a Qatar Biobank group the combined model reached an area under the curve of 0.81 for sorting risk. It worked best in women and in people aged 45 to 55. The authors present the tool as a proof of concept for community screening, pending outside validation.
pmc-13528059:
Kathryn Whitehead and six colleagues present an automated workflow for microbe sequencing in a 2026 paper. Public health labs need fast, unbiased sample prep. Manual methods are slow and skew toward some germ types. Their system uses a capillary liquid handler in one cartridge. It lyses cells with enzymes, extracts DNA, and builds sequencing libraries with one operator.

Hands-on time dropped from eight to ten hours to under forty-five minutes. Libraries averaged about 80 nanograms per microliter with good quality scores. On a standard mock community, Gram-positive germs showed up 2.46 times better than with standard lysis. That fixes a known blind spot. The authors pitch the setup for small labs needing quick outbreak answers. They call it a proof of concept ready to scale.
pmc-13529659:
Ami Konno and five colleagues measure retinal blood flow across diabetes eye disease stages in a 2026 study. Laser Doppler tools give exact flow numbers, unlike most eye scans. The group held 419 people with type 2 diabetes. Most, 323, had no retinopathy yet. Others had mild, moderate, or severe early disease. Flow rose step by step with severity.

Median flow climbed from about 9.8 microliters per minute with no disease to about 11.9 at the moderate stage. Severe cases sat near 11.6. A trend test confirmed the rise. Earlier work shows flow dips below healthy levels at the very start of diabetes. The authors read the later climb as failed self-regulation. Vessels may flood under pressure they can no longer resist. Flow readings could become a stage marker, they suggest.
pmc-13530159:
Aderajew Mekonnen Girmay leads a 2026 analysis of safe food handling in Ethiopian homes. Unsafe food causes hundreds of millions of illnesses worldwide each year, and low-income settings carry a heavy share. Household survey data supported a multilevel model that weighed personal, family, and community factors together.

Only about four in ten households handled food safely by the study measure. Schooling beyond the earliest grades, paid work, and greater wealth each lifted safe practice in clear steps. Marriage, urban residence, basic hygiene services, and exposure to health information also helped. The authors urge focused programs aimed at households left furthest behind.
pmc-13531759:
Huanqi Mo and colleagues report a 2026 hybrid operation for a thymus gland tumor that had invaded a major chest vein. A 39-year-old woman carried a tumor pressing into the superior vena cava and a joining vein, a spot where biopsy itself was judged too risky. The team chose direct surgery after group review.

A camera approach through a small cut below the breastbone checked feasibility first, then a partial breastbone opening allowed removal. Surgeons rebuilt the veins in a Y shape using a synthetic graft and a shaped animal tissue tube. Recovery ran smoothly, and follow-up showed open grafts with no return.
pmc-13531959:
Rachel L King and co-authors evaluate in 2026 whether a community dementia hub in England delivers value for money. The Sage House model joins health service diagnosis, charity provision, and local partners under one roof. A natural experiment compared 65 hub users with 153 people receiving usual care over three months.

Hub care cost less while producing slightly more quality-adjusted life than usual care. The model cleared common cost-effectiveness thresholds with roughly three-in-four probability at standard willingness-to-pay levels. Dementia numbers and costs keep climbing nationally, so the authors urge a larger trial of the community approach.
pmc-13532759:
Ines Assali and colleagues present in 2026 jsPCA, a fast method to find tissue zones and key genes in spatial gene data. New tools record gene activity across a tissue slice, but the files are huge and hard to sort by hand. The method blends gene variation with how nearby spots relate in space.

Main parts drawn from that blend give a compact view for grouping spots and picking variable genes. A joint form handles many slices without aligning them first. Tests against ten other methods showed equal or better results in seconds to minutes, with clear steps readers can follow.
pmc-13532859:
August Lomholt Kvistad and colleagues test in 2026 whether weak brain stimulation boosts leg skill learning over five days. The method, called tDCS, passes a small current through the scalp and may aid practice gains. Volunteers trained on an ankle tracking task with real stimulation, sham stimulation, or plain ankle moves.

Skill practice gave clear gains that moved to the untrained leg and lasted at least one week. Stimulation did not lift learning during training, yet it improved retention after one week next to sham. Brain excitability at rest did not change, so the gain likely works through other routes.
pmc-13535259:
Elchert and colleagues studied how an enzyme that marks histones, the proteins DNA wraps around, is kept off until the right partner switches it on. The 2026 yeast study focuses on Set2, which adds methyl tags to one histone site during gene reading and thereby protects accurate transcription and genome stability. Earlier work hinted that Set2 carries its own built-in brake.

Elchert isolated multiple mutant classes of Set2 and of Spt6, a helper protein that escorts the transcription machinery along genes. Genetic tests and direct physical measurements showed Set2's catalytic region binds its own brake region, holding the enzyme inactive, and mutants that break that contact lose proper control. Genome-wide mapping of RNA and histone marks confirmed the Set2 and Spt6 partnership matters across the whole genome. The results support a model where Spt6 binding releases the brake so marking happens only during active transcription.
pmc-13535759:
Tania Bosqui and colleagues trialed a brief family program for teen mental health in Lebanon. Published in 2026, the multi-site randomized trial, called Sawa Aqwa or Stronger Together, tested a locally built family program against a waitlist. They lived in North Lebanon and Beqa'a, faced child-safety risks, and had teens in distress aged 12 to 17. Lay workers ran the program in a crisis setting.

The program lifted teen-rated family life, carer mental health, and parent skills versus control, but not teen distress itself. Finishing the program aided teen wellbeing, and father turnout linked to better teen wellbeing. Gains in family life and carer wellbeing faded by the three-month check-in. The authors present mixed but hopeful results for whole-family support in crises.
pmc-13536559:
Xing Xiong and colleagues test in 2026 whole-body MRI scoring, called MY-RADS, to gauge tumour burden in multiple myeloma. Burden guides treatment and outlook, and standard markers need blood and marrow tests that are not always handy. Records covered 108 newly diagnosed patients with varied marrow patterns on scans.

Score value depended on pattern type. For focal and mixed patterns the total score separated stage and risk groups and tracked marrow plasma cell share well. For diffuse patterns, water and fat measures carried the signal instead, supporting pattern-aware use of the score.
pmc-13536759:
Maryam Moghbel Baerz and colleagues review brain stimulation for functional seizures in a 2026 review. Functional seizures mimic true seizures but stem from brain network problems rather than faulty firing. Searches of three sources gathered 19 studies on stimulation for treatment and for testing, including magnetic and mild current methods. Wide gaps among studies meant findings are told in words, not pooled counts.

Early treatment reports, mostly small cases, linked scalp stimulation to fewer seizures and lighter mood symptoms. One spot near the side-back of the head was a frequent target. Triggering stimulation also helped provoke events during brain wave recording. Side effects were mostly mild, with headache most common. The authors call for large placebo-style trials with standard methods and long follow-up.
pmc-13538459:
Ahmed Abd Elaziz Elsayed and colleagues released a fine-grained open dataset on AI training power use. Published in 2026, the dataset logs 72 training sessions at sub-second steps: 32 on high-end H100 and B200 eight-GPU nodes and 40 on home-grade RTX 3060 cards. AI training strains data-center power and grid health, yet detailed energy profiles were scarce.

Each session tracks power draw, central-chip and graphics-chip use, per-chip power, memory use, and heat across forecasts, sorting, reward learning, and text and image making. Over 1.8 million samples passed checks on timing, hardware limits, and cross-measure links, staying inside maker heat and power caps. The dataset supports models of data-center energy, system speed, and grid-link impact. Readers get a solid base for greener, steadier AI power planning.
pmc-13540859:
Yanhui Liu and colleagues combine two kinds of data in a 2026 study. One kind comes from a large population survey. The other comes from gene activity records. Their goal is to find fat-related drivers of sleep apnoea. In that disorder, the airway collapses again and again during sleep.

In the survey data, higher triglycerides tracked with more apnoea. Harmful cholesterol tracked the same way. Protective cholesterol tracked the other way. Gene analysis produced thirty-four altered fat-related genes. Machine learning then elevated three of them. The three were CYP3A4, CYP4A22, and MED18. Network maps tied these genes to pathways for follow-up work.
pmc-13540959:
Yoo Ri Ko and colleagues build lung cancer tumoroids in a 2026 study. Each model is patient-specific. The models keep support cells and immune cells around the tumor. That neighborhood drives drug resistance in real patients. Flat organoid cultures alone cannot copy those interactions.

All cell types came from the same patient's tumor. The team recombined them in a modular well system. The system survives freezing and rebuilding. The models kept the look of the source tissue. They kept its gene programmes too. Drug responses differed from patient to patient. Adding fibroblasts dulled immune attack in some models.
pmc-13541859:
Jin Hyeong Park and colleagues ask a surgical question in 2026. Can major bowel surgery be skipped in one narrow case? The case is early colorectal cancer removed by endoscopy. The only warning sign is a positive cut edge. Guidelines push toward radical resection when any risk factor appears. That operation carries real costs.

Three Korean referral centres reviewed 250 patients. All had radical surgery after endoscopic removal. One in ten had cancer in nearby lymph nodes. Spread into vessels predicted nodal disease. A KRAS mutation predicted it too. Twenty-two patients had margin positivity as their only risk factor. None of those twenty-two had nodal spread.
pmc-13543359:
Abdul Basit and colleagues published a 2026 mixed-methods study of menstrual symptoms among rural schoolgirls in the Sylhet division of Bangladesh. Menstrual health remains neglected there, especially outside cities. The survey covered 474 girls in grades nine and ten. They rated the severity of their physical and psychological symptoms and described their cycle regularity, while 29 girls took part in in-depth interviews.

Cramps affected about 77 percent, fatigue about 69 percent, and irritability topped the psychological list at about 73 percent. Roughly a quarter reported irregular cycles, and those girls fared far worse: nearly half rated their physical symptoms severe, against under four percent of girls with regular cycles. Interviews showed heavy burdens being treated as normal through cultural beliefs passed between generations. The authors argue that normalising severe symptoms delays care and should be challenged in school health programmes.
pmc-13543559:
Diana Doukhi and colleagues published a 2026 systematic review of long-term headache after cerebral venous thrombosis. That clot in the brain's veins mainly strikes young adults and usually announces itself with headache. Recovery of movement and independence is often good, yet headaches linger. Searching two databases for studies from 2000 to 2025, the reviewers kept fifteen studies covering 2,136 patients and, because methods differed so much, summarised the findings qualitatively.

Reported headache prevalence ranged widely, from fourteen to fifty-nine percent. The headaches usually mimicked tension-type or migraine patterns, and brand-new headache was the commonest presentation, though old disorders also changed character. A previous headache history and depression predicted trouble; brain bleeding at the event did not. Some cases traced to treatable secondary causes such as raised pressure inside the skull. The authors call for a standard definition and a shared name for this neglected aftermath.
pmc-13545259:
Betsaida Bibo-Verdugo and Guy S Salvesen reviewed in 2026 the uneasy partnership between caspase-8 and cFLIP. Caspase-8 is an enzyme that can trigger programmed cell death, while cFLIP is a look-alike protein that lacks the cutting power. Which partner caspase-8 pairs with helps decide whether a cell dies quietly, dies in an inflammatory way, or survives. Mouse genetics and human disease both show what goes wrong when that balance fails.

Paired with itself, caspase-8 drives the quiet death pathway, while pairing with cFLIP restrains it yet blocks a more destructive form of death. The review walks through recent work, including a study by Newton and colleagues, that untangles these opposing roles. Readers interested in cell death signaling get a clear map of a confusing corner of the field.
pmc-13547359:
Gai Liu and colleagues read the genome of an alpine snow alga that darkens snow and speeds melting. Published in 2026, the study mapped Chloromonas typhlos, a globe-spanning snow alga whose blooms cut snow shine-back. Snow algae feed cold germs and shape melt, yet this genus lacked a strong genome model.

Long reads plus chromosome-linking data built a 200.86-million-letter genome across 31 chromosomes, with repeats at just over 11 percent. The team found 16,133 protein-coding genes and gave 82 percent a known role. The genome gives snow-alga workers a base for tracing cold coping and pigment-driven melt feedback. Readers get a model genome for a far-flung snow genus.
pmc-13547559:
Patrice Ngangue and colleagues interviewed in 2026 thirty-three English-speaking women displaced by Cameroon's Anglophone crisis into Douala, exploring how gender-based violence and mental health intertwine under displacement. The women, median age 34 and a median five years in the region, were reached through purposive and snowball sampling across city neighborhoods. Conversations were analyzed thematically through an intersectional lens.

Four themes emerged. Silence served as protection against stigma, while trauma showed up in the body and in mental shutdown. A constant anxiety about survival grew out of poverty and discrimination against English speakers. Resilience rested on informal peer networks, faith, and reframing hardship. The authors argue daily structural stressors outweigh single past events, so support must join violence prevention, livelihoods, and care in the women's own languages.
pmc-13548559:
Hongjie He, Yuanyuan Yan, and Yanming Zhang weigh proton beam therapy against standard photon radiation for liver cancer, in a 2026 meta-analysis. Protons can stop inside a tumor and spare nearby healthy liver, which matters because radiation injury to the liver is a feared complication. The team searched four databases for studies comparing the two approaches in hepatocellular carcinoma and rated the strength of the combined findings.

Only four retrospective studies qualified. Proton patients showed a lower hazard of death, yet that result carried uneven data and signs of publication bias, so the authors rate its certainty as low. The safety findings were firmer: protons cut the odds of liver injury to about a quarter, with roughly five patients treated to prevent one injury. They advise choosing case by case on liver reserve and tumor features until prospective trials report.
pmc-13548659:
Jacie T. Cooper and colleagues model whether a biomarker-based kidney risk score pays for itself in American Medicare patients, in a 2026 cost-effectiveness analysis. Diabetic kidney disease drives nearly half of new kidney failure, and protective drugs stay underused because standard staging sorts patients crudely. The KidneyIntelX score blends biomarkers with artificial intelligence to predict rapid decline, steering drug treatment toward those likeliest to progress.

Simulating lifetimes for patients in early disease stages, score-guided care produced fewer kidney failures, heart events, dialysis starts, and transplants than staging-guided care. Patients spent less time in advanced stages, gained a small amount of quality-adjusted life, and cost Medicare roughly five hundred dollars less each. pmc-13549959:
Haijun Huang and colleagues shake rounded gravel under repeated subway-like loading in a large laboratory press, in a 2026 geotechnical study. Metro tunnels increasingly pass through round gravel layers in Chinese cities, and years of train vibration can settle the ground unevenly. Using saturated samples in a dynamic triaxial machine, the team varied packing density, confining pressure, and shaking strength to watch stiffness and permanent strain evolve.

Looser, shallow gravel under strong shaking accumulated deformation that could endanger shallow tunnels, while deeper burial looked safer. Packing the gravel denser and raising confining pressure stiffened it, cut permanent and elastic strain, lowered water pressure buildup, and strengthened resistance to liquefaction. pmc-13550659:

Phone and internet access have widened their reach, while AI chat tools have become part of everyday digital life.

A respondent facing a hard question can now ask an AI tool and paste a polished, plausible answer without holding that knowledge personally. Aung notes that even well-meant help, from predictive text to search, can make answers reflect outside generation rather than lived experience, and can make responses look more alike. The piece warns researchers to rethink how such findings should be interpreted.
pmc-13551159:
Evans F Kyei and colleagues listened to Ghana's mental health nurses on drug treatment blocks. Ghana's drug response leans on crime-first rules, yet how that climate shapes treatment care was little studied.

Money strain and family systems gated access, while stigma and harsh rules scared patients off as graft eased drug supply. Clever workarounds by carers and patients rounded out the set. The authors urge health-first drug rules, wider treatment buildings, and workforce growth. Readers get frontline voices for reform in Ghana and similar cash-strapped settings.
pmc-13551859:

pmc-13554159:

Schools may gain by pairing sport with phone habits work.
pmc-13555859:

pmc-13556059:
Jiawei An and eight colleagues used genetics in 2026 to ask whether gallstones actually cause other diseases of the liver, bile ducts, and pancreas, or merely travel with them. No causal link appeared for a clotting condition of the portal vein, and reverse analyses found no sign that those diseases cause gallstones instead. pmc-13558259:

The authors gather them under one label, the electrical phenotype, and note that clinicians often notice them late, after fainting or dangerous slowing. Systematic electrical monitoring, they contend, should become a routine part of long-term care in the treatment era.
pmc-13558359:

Their patient was an 82-year-old man whose gallstones had inflamed the organ and whose other illnesses, including rheumatoid arthritis, emphysema, and a hernia, made removing it extremely risky. pmc-13559359:

Their 2026 study used health records for 512 people who had keyhole surgery to remove part of a lung. All were treated at one hospital in Kunming, China, from 2020 to 2024. The team trained five types of machine learning model, which learn patterns from past cases. It then picked the one that worked best.

The best model sorted high-risk from low-risk cases well in tests on new patients. A second tool showed which facts drove each call, so staff could see the reasons. Length of surgery was the top clue, then a lung test score, age, and a white blood cell count. The team says the tool could help staff plan care for those at high risk. pmc-13559559:
Xiaoxue Chen and colleagues explore the role of stanniocalcin-1, a protein called STC1, in laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma, a throat cancer prone to recurrence and treatment resistance. Tumors rich in STC1 showed a suppressive immune setting, with fewer killer T cells and more resting macrophages. Single-cell data placed STC1 chiefly in epithelial cells, which signaled heavily to T cells through calming pathways. The authors suggest that targeting STC1 might loosen immune suppression, a hypothesis their computational study raises rather than tests.
pmc-13559659:
Qiangzu Shao and three colleagues examine B7H4, an immune checkpoint protein, in HER2-positive gastric cancer and its effect on response to trastuzumab, the standard targeted drug for this subtype. Resistance to trastuzumab, both initial and acquired, is a central problem in this disease.

Gene sequencing after knockdown shifted programs for proliferation and movement, and the team tested whether drug sensitivity changed as well. The authors frame B7H4 as a resistance lever worth targeting alongside HER2 therapy.
pmc-13560259:
Giorgi Kanchelashvili and colleagues measure hepatitis B coinfection and awareness among tuberculosis patients in Georgia, where routine testing is not standard. Their 2026 cross-sectional study enrolled 110 people with active TB at the national center between September 2024 and February 2025. Blood tests sorted people by past or current infection and immunity, and a survey probed knowledge and vaccine views.

Four people, 3.6 percent of the group, tested positive for current hepatitis B infection. Fourteen showed past infection with immunity, seven carried an isolated core antibody pattern, and only seven had vaccine-induced immunity. The large majority, 74.5 percent, still lacked any protection in the breakdown. Awareness was patchy: half could not name how the virus spreads, and just 14.5 percent were willing to be vaccinated, with safety doubts leading the refusals. Younger ones knew more. The authors urge folding screening, teaching, and shots into TB care.
pmc-13562459:

Treated mice lost less bone. The authors propose KDM5C as a drug target for wear-particle bone loss.
pmc-13563759:

The enzyme, carbonic anhydrase, speeds the gas's conversion in living tissue. Their 2026 team purified it from cattle blood cells, drawn from a slaughterhouse, achieving an 83-fold concentration.
